lessons.title: What VLSI Is: From One Transistor to Billions on a Chip
lessons.content:
Imagine you had to build the whole of Dhaka city, every house, road, shop and traffic light, but the entire city had to fit on your fingernail. And every single brick had to work perfectly, because one broken brick could stop the city. That is roughly what a modern chip designer does. The processor in your phone holds billions of tiny switches called transistors, all connected by wires thinner than a virus, on a piece of silicon smaller than a coin. VLSI Design is the course that teaches how such a city is planned, drawn, checked and built.

What VLSI means: VLSI stands for Very Large Scale Integration. Integration means putting many electronic parts, mainly transistors and the wires between them, onto one single piece of silicon called an integrated circuit, IC or chip. Before integration, every transistor was a separate little part that a worker soldered onto a board by hand. A radio might have had a dozen of them. Very large scale means the number on one chip is huge: hundreds of thousands at the start of the VLSI era, and today many billions.

The problem it solved: In the 1950s, computers were built from separate transistors and wires. Engineers called the big headache the tyranny of numbers. More transistors meant more hand-soldered joints, and every joint was a chance for failure. A machine with 100,000 parts and 1 bad joint in 10,000 would almost never work. In 1958 and 1959, Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild independently showed that transistors, resistors and their connections could be made together on one piece of semiconductor. The wires were no longer soldered; they were printed. That idea, the integrated circuit, is the root of everything in this course.

The scales of integration: Textbooks name the eras by how much fits on one chip. SSI, small scale integration, means a few gates per chip, like a chip holding four NAND gates. MSI, medium scale, means tens to hundreds of gates, like a counter or a multiplexer. LSI, large scale, means thousands of gates, enough for a simple calculator or an early microprocessor. VLSI means hundreds of thousands of transistors and beyond. Exact boundaries differ from book to book, so remember the idea, not the cutoff numbers. Some people later used ULSI for ultra large scale, but today everyone just says VLSI for any big digital chip.

Moore's law: In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of components on a chip was doubling about every year. In 1975 he revised it to about every two years. This is not a law of physics; it is an observation about engineering and economics that the industry then used as a target. Let us check it with numbers. Intel's 4004 processor of 1971 had about 2,300 transistors. Doubling every two years for 50 years means 25 doublings. 2,300 times 2 to the power 25 is about 77 billion. Real large chips around 2021 to 2024 really did reach tens of billions of transistors, for example phone processors with around 15 to 20 billion and big GPUs with even more. So the two-year rule held surprisingly well for half a century, though it has been slowing down, which you will study in lesson 15.

Why integrate at all: Putting everything on one chip gives four big wins. First, cost: the printing process makes millions of transistors at once, so each one costs almost nothing. Second, speed: short wires on a chip mean signals travel tiny distances, so circuits switch in picoseconds instead of nanoseconds. Third, power: small transistors with short wires need far less energy to charge and discharge. Fourth, reliability: there are no soldered joints to crack, so a chip with a billion transistors can run for years. These four wins are why your phone is more powerful than a 1990s supercomputer and still fits in your pocket.

What a VLSI designer actually decides: A chip designer answers questions like these. What should the chip do, and how fast? How many transistors does each block need, and how big should each transistor be? How will the transistors be arranged on the silicon, and how will wires connect them across up to a dozen or more metal layers? How much power will it burn, and will it get too hot? How will we know the chip works before spending millions of dollars to make it, and how will the factory test each chip after it is made? This course follows that list.

Kinds of chips: Not every chip is designed the same way. In full-custom design, engineers draw every transistor by hand. It gives the best speed and smallest area, so it is still used for parts like memory cells and very fast circuits, but it takes a lot of people and time. In standard-cell design, the most common way for digital chips, the designer uses a library of pre-designed and pre-checked cells, like NAND2, flip-flop or full adder, and software places and wires them. A gate array is an older middle path where the transistors are pre-made and only the wiring is custom. An FPGA, field programmable gate array, is a chip that is already manufactured and you configure its logic and wiring with a file, in seconds. An ASIC, application specific integrated circuit, is any chip made for one particular job, usually by full-custom or standard-cell design.

Levels of abstraction: Nobody can think about a billion transistors at once. So designers climb a ladder of abstraction. At the top is the system level: blocks like CPU, memory and radio. Below that is the register transfer level, RTL, where you describe registers and the logic between them, usually in a hardware description language like Verilog. Below that is the gate level: NAND, NOR, flip-flops. Below that is the circuit level: transistors and their sizes. At the bottom is the layout level: the actual shapes of every layer on the silicon. Each level hides the details of the level below, just like you can drive a car without knowing every part of the engine.

The Gajski Y-chart: A famous picture for this is the Y-chart by Daniel Gajski and Robert Kuhn. It has three arms. The behavioural arm says what the system does, like an algorithm or a Boolean equation. The structural arm says what it is made of, like a list of gates and how they connect. The physical arm says where things are placed on the chip, like a floorplan or a layout. Rings around the centre show levels: system, RTL, logic, circuit. Designing a chip means moving from behaviour, to structure, to physical shapes, again and again at each level. When you write Verilog you are on the behavioural arm; when synthesis turns it into gates you move to the structural arm; when place and route draws it you move to the physical arm.

The chip industry: Who actually makes chips? An IDM, integrated device manufacturer, designs and also builds chips in its own factories; Intel and Samsung are classic examples. A fabless company only designs chips and sends the design files to a foundry; Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm work this way. A foundry, like TSMC, only manufactures chips designed by others. EDA companies, electronic design automation, make the software tools every designer uses, such as Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA. The factory, called a fab, can cost tens of billions of dollars, which is why most companies today are fabless.

Where Bangladesh fits: Bangladesh does not have a chip fab, but chip design and verification work happens in Dhaka. Companies such as Ulkasemi have hired many Bangladeshi engineers for design, verification and physical design work for global clients, and universities like BUET teach VLSI courses. Design is the part of the industry that needs brains and computers rather than a giant factory, which is why it is a realistic career for a CSE or EEE graduate in Bangladesh.

Real-life example 1, your phone's processor: Open your phone settings and you may see a chip name. That one chip, called a system on chip or SoC, contains CPU cores, a GPU for graphics, an image processor for the camera, a modem block, memory controllers and many small helpers. Each block was written as RTL, checked by simulation for months, turned into millions of standard cells by software, placed and wired, checked for timing and power, and finally printed at a foundry. When you open Facebook and scroll smoothly, billions of transistors switch on and off billions of times per second, and almost none of them ever fail. That reliability is the result of careful VLSI design.

Real-life example 2, a bKash POS terminal or a smart meter: The prepaid electricity meter in many Dhaka homes has a small chip inside. It reads current, calculates units, stores your balance, and talks to a card or keypad. This is not a giant chip; it might be a microcontroller made in an older, cheaper process. The same VLSI ideas apply: transistors form gates, gates form an arithmetic unit and memory, and the designer chose a process and a clock speed that keep the cost and power low. Not every chip needs to be the newest and fastest; choosing the right technology for the job is part of VLSI engineering.

What this course covers: Lessons 2 to 6 are about transistors and gates: how a MOSFET behaves, the CMOS inverter, static gates and other logic styles. Lessons 7 and 8 show how chips are manufactured and how layout is drawn. Lessons 9 to 15 are about delay, logical effort, power, low-power tricks, wires and scaling. Lessons 16 to 19 cover flip-flops, timing, datapath blocks like adders and multipliers, and memory arrays. Lessons 20 to 23 teach Verilog, the full ASIC flow and FPGAs. Lesson 24 is about testing chips, and lesson 25 puts it all together in a small chip project.

What you should already know: From Electronic Devices you know what a MOSFET is and have seen the CMOS inverter and NAND gate. From Digital Logic Design you know gates, Boolean algebra, adders, flip-flops and finite state machines. From Computer Architecture you know ALUs, pipelines and caches. We will recap these in a line or two, and go deeper into how they are built in silicon.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think Moore's law is a law of nature. It is an industry trend that is now slowing. Another mix-up is ASIC versus FPGA: an ASIC is manufactured for one job and cannot be changed, while an FPGA is a ready-made chip you reprogram. People also confuse fabless and foundry: a fabless company designs, a foundry builds. Exams often ask you to define VLSI, list the integration scales, explain Moore's law with a calculation, compare full-custom, standard-cell and FPGA design styles, draw the Y-chart, and list the benefits of integration.

Recap: VLSI means putting very many transistors on one chip. The integrated circuit solved the tyranny of numbers by printing transistors and wires together. Moore's law described transistor counts doubling about every two years, from 2,300 in 1971 to tens of billions today. Integration gives low cost, high speed, low power and high reliability. Designers use levels of abstraction and three views, behaviour, structure and physical, to manage the complexity. The industry is split into IDMs, fabless designers, foundries and EDA tool makers. Next, we zoom in on the single brick of this city: the MOS transistor as a switch.
key_points: VLSI means Very Large Scale Integration: very many transistors and wires printed together on one chip.
The integrated circuit (Kilby, Noyce, 1958-59) solved the tyranny of hand-soldered connections.
Moore's law: transistor counts doubled about every two years; 2,300 x 2^25 is about 77 billion.
Integration wins on cost, speed, power and reliability.
Design styles: full-custom, standard-cell ASIC, gate array, FPGA.
Abstraction levels: system, RTL, gate, circuit, layout; Gajski Y-chart has behavioural, structural and physical views.
Industry roles: IDM, fabless company, foundry, EDA vendor; design work happens in Bangladesh too.
lessons.tip: Keep a one-page map of the abstraction ladder (system, RTL, gate, circuit, layout) and write each new lesson's topic on the level where it lives. You will always know where you are in the city.
lessons.task: Find the name of the processor in your phone (Settings, About phone, or search the model online). Look up roughly how many transistors it has and when it was made. Then compute 2,300 x 2^n, where n is (year - 1971) / 2, and compare with the real number.

quiz.q: What problem did the integrated circuit mainly solve?
options: The tyranny of numbers: too many hand-made connections that could fail
Software was too slow to write
There was not enough silicon on Earth
quiz.explain: Printing transistors and wires together removed thousands of soldered joints, each a possible failure.

quiz.q: Starting from 2,300 transistors and doubling every two years for 40 years, about how many transistors do you get?
quiz.explain: 40 years is 20 doublings; 2,300 x 2^20 = 2,300 x 1,048,576, about 2.4 billion.

quiz.q: A company that designs chips but has no factory of its own is called:
quiz.explain: Fabless companies like Nvidia or Qualcomm design chips and pay a foundry such as TSMC to make them.

quiz.q: In the Gajski Y-chart, a floorplan showing where blocks sit on the chip belongs to which view?
quiz.explain: The physical arm is about geometry and placement; behaviour is what it does, structure is what it is made of.

quiz.q: Which design style lets you change the logic after the chip is manufactured, just by loading a new file?
quiz.explain: An FPGA is configured by a bitstream; ASICs and gate arrays are fixed once manufactured.

lessons.title: The MOS Transistor as a Switch
lessons.content:
Think of the water tap in your kitchen. Turn the handle one way and water flows; turn it the other way and the flow stops. You do not need to understand the plumbing inside the wall to use it. A MOS transistor is a tap for electric current, and the handle is a voltage. Every digital chip in this course, from a two-transistor inverter to a processor with billions of transistors, is built from this one kind of tap. So before we build anything, we must understand this brick very well: what it is made of, when it turns on, what it passes well and what it passes badly.

Why start here: In Electronic Devices you met the MOSFET as an amplifier with curves and equations. In VLSI we mostly use it as a switch, because digital circuits only care whether a signal is 0 or 1. The switch view lets you design and check gates in your head. Later, in lessons 3, 9 and 10, we add the details that the simple switch hides, like how much current flows and how long switching takes. A good designer moves between the simple switch model and the detailed model depending on the question.

The parts of a MOSFET: MOSFET stands for metal oxide semiconductor field effect transistor. Picture a flat piece of silicon, called the body or substrate. On top of it lies a very thin layer of insulating oxide, traditionally silicon dioxide, glass basically. On top of the oxide sits the gate, a conductor; in old processes it was aluminium metal, later doped polysilicon, and in modern processes metal again. On either side of the gate, the silicon is heavily doped to make two regions called the source and the drain. So the transistor has four terminals: gate, source, drain and body. The region of silicon right under the gate, between source and drain, is called the channel.

The nMOS transistor: In an nMOS transistor, the body is p-type silicon, which has few free electrons, and the source and drain are n-type, full of free electrons. With no voltage on the gate, there is no path of free electrons between source and drain: the p-type body is in the way, like a dry riverbed between two lakes. Now put a positive voltage on the gate. The gate and the body form a tiny capacitor with the oxide as the insulator. The positive gate pushes away holes and pulls electrons toward the surface right under the oxide. When the gate voltage is high enough, so many electrons gather there that the surface becomes n-type, forming a thin channel. This is called inversion. Now the two lakes are connected by a river, and current can flow from drain to source.

Threshold voltage: The gate voltage needed to form the channel, measured from gate to source, is called the threshold voltage, written Vt or Vth. In modern processes Vt for an nMOS is typically a few tenths of a volt, for example around 0.3 to 0.4 V when the supply VDD is around 1 V. The rule for the switch model is simple: if VGS is greater than Vt, the nMOS is ON; if VGS is less than Vt, it is OFF. In logic terms, an nMOS whose source is at ground turns ON when its gate is 1 and OFF when its gate is 0.

The pMOS transistor: A pMOS is the mirror image. The body is n-type (in a typical process the pMOS sits in an n-well), and the source and drain are p-type. To form a channel of holes, the gate must be pulled below the source by more than the threshold magnitude. So a pMOS turns ON when its gate is low, at 0, and OFF when its gate is high, at 1. In circuit symbols, the pMOS is drawn with a small bubble on the gate, the same bubble that means NOT in logic gates, to remind you that it is active low. Holes move more slowly than electrons, roughly 2 to 3 times slower in silicon, so a pMOS of the same size gives less current than an nMOS. Remember this; it is why pMOS transistors are often drawn wider.

Source and drain are symmetric: Physically, the source and drain of a MOSFET are identical. Which one we call source depends only on voltages: for an nMOS, the source is the terminal at the lower voltage, because electrons flow out of it; for a pMOS, the source is at the higher voltage. This matters in pass transistors, where current may flow in either direction depending on the data.

The switch-level model: Now forget the physics for a moment. An nMOS is a switch that closes when its gate is 1. A pMOS is a switch that closes when its gate is 0. That is it. With this model, you can trace any CMOS circuit by checking, for each input combination, which switches are closed and whether the output is connected to VDD (logic 1) or to ground (logic 0).

Strong and weak values: The switch model has one important twist. Suppose an nMOS has its gate at VDD and we try to pass a 0 through it: one side at 0 V. The channel stays fully on because VGS = VDD, which is far above Vt, so the other side is pulled all the way to 0 V. We say nMOS passes a strong 0. Now try to pass a 1. As the far side charges up, its voltage becomes the source voltage. When the source reaches VDD - Vt, VGS has dropped to Vt and the transistor starts to switch off. So the output stops at about VDD - Vt. With VDD = 1.0 V and Vt = 0.3 V, the output only reaches 0.7 V. We say nMOS passes a degraded or weak 1. The pMOS is the opposite: it passes a strong 1 but a weak 0, stopping at about |Vtp| above ground, for example 0.3 V.

Why this decides the shape of CMOS gates: Because nMOS passes 0 well, nMOS transistors are placed between the output and ground, in the pull-down network. Because pMOS passes 1 well, pMOS transistors are placed between VDD and the output, in the pull-up network. This is the fundamental arrangement of static CMOS logic: pMOS on top pulling up, nMOS on the bottom pulling down. If you ever put an nMOS in the pull-up, the output 1 would be weak, noise margins would shrink and the next gate might leak current. That is a classic exam trick.

The complementary pair: CMOS stands for complementary MOS. In every CMOS gate, for each input, there is an nMOS and a pMOS fed by the same signal. When the input is 1, the nMOS is on and the pMOS is off. When the input is 0, the pMOS is on and the nMOS is off. Arranged correctly, this means that for every input combination, either the pull-up or the pull-down network conducts, but never both. The output is always firmly driven, and in steady state there is no direct path from VDD to ground. That is why CMOS uses almost no power when nothing changes. You will build on this in lessons 4 and 5.

The transmission gate preview: Since nMOS passes a strong 0 and pMOS passes a strong 1, what if you put them side by side, in parallel, with opposite gate signals? When the control is 1, the nMOS gate gets 1 and the pMOS gate gets 0, so both are on, and together they pass both 0 and 1 strongly. When the control is 0, both are off. This pair is called a transmission gate, and it is a building block for multiplexers, latches and XOR gates. Lesson 6 uses it in detail.

Worked example, a switch-level trace: Take a pMOS from VDD to node Y and an nMOS from Y to ground, both gates tied to input A. Case A = 0: the pMOS is on, the nMOS is off, Y connects to VDD, so Y = 1. Case A = 1: the pMOS is off, the nMOS is on, Y connects to ground, so Y = 0. That is an inverter, traced with nothing but the switch rule. Now a broken version: put an nMOS from VDD to Y with gate A and a pMOS from Y to ground with gate A. Case A = 1: the nMOS conducts and Y rises only to VDD - Vt, 0.7 V in our example. Case A = 0: the pMOS conducts and Y falls only to about 0.3 V. The circuit is a buffer with weak outputs, which is why nobody builds it.

The gate as a capacitor: One more fact from the physics stays important. The gate is separated from the channel by oxide, so it draws essentially no DC current. It looks like a small capacitor. To switch a transistor, the previous gate must charge or discharge this capacitance. This is why a CMOS gate driving many other gates is slower: it has more capacitance to charge. Lessons 9 to 11 build the whole theory of delay on this simple fact.

Real-life example 1, the light switch and the stair switch: In many Bangladeshi houses, the stair light has two switches, one downstairs and one upstairs, and either can turn the light on or off. Inside, it is just switches in series and parallel. An nMOS pull-down network is the same idea: transistors in series act like AND (all must be closed to connect), and transistors in parallel act like OR (any one closed connects). When you look at a CMOS gate, read it like a house wiring diagram: which paths connect the output to the supply, and which connect it to ground?

Real-life example 2, the sluice gate on a canal: Farmers in Bangladesh control water in irrigation canals with a sluice gate. Raise the gate and water flows from the high side to the low side; lower it and the flow stops. Notice that water always flows from high to low, not the other way. A MOSFET is similar: the gate voltage opens or closes the channel, and current flows from the higher-voltage side to the lower one, which is why we name source and drain by voltage. The analogy also shows the weak 1 problem: if the gate operator can only lift the gate to a certain height relative to the downstream water level, as the downstream level rises the opening shrinks, and the flow stops before the two sides are equal.

Where the analogy breaks: A real transistor is not a perfect switch. When off, it still leaks a tiny current. When on, it has some resistance, so it cannot charge a load instantly. Its threshold changes a little with temperature and with the body voltage. Lesson 3 adds these effects.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often say the pMOS turns on when its gate is 1; it is the other way. Another frequent mistake is putting nMOS transistors in the pull-up network. Some forget that source and drain are named by voltage, not by position in the drawing. Exam questions include: draw the cross-section of an nMOS and label gate, oxide, source, drain, body and channel; explain inversion and threshold voltage; explain why nMOS passes a strong 0 and weak 1, with a numeric example; explain why pull-up networks use pMOS; and trace a small transistor circuit for all input combinations.

Recap: A MOSFET has gate, source, drain and body; the gate sits on thin oxide over the channel. An nMOS turns on when VGS exceeds Vt, so it acts as a switch closed by a 1. A pMOS turns on when its gate is low, so it acts as a switch closed by a 0. nMOS passes a strong 0 and a weak 1 (VDD - Vt); pMOS passes a strong 1 and a weak 0. Therefore CMOS places pMOS in the pull-up and nMOS in the pull-down, and pairs them so exactly one network conducts. Next, we open up the switch and look at how much current it actually carries.
key_points: A MOSFET has four terminals: gate, source, drain and body; the gate sits on a thin oxide over the channel.
nMOS: ON when gate is 1 (VGS > Vt); pMOS: ON when gate is 0; pMOS is drawn with a bubble.
Threshold voltage Vt is the gate-source voltage needed to form the inversion channel.
nMOS passes a strong 0 and a weak 1 (stops near VDD - Vt, e.g. 0.7 V for VDD 1.0 V, Vt 0.3 V).
pMOS passes a strong 1 and a weak 0, so pMOS goes in the pull-up and nMOS in the pull-down.
Series switches act like AND, parallel switches like OR.
The gate is a capacitor and draws no DC current; charging it is what takes time.
lessons.tip: Say it out loud until it sticks: N for Neutral ground, pulls down; P for Power, pulls up. Every CMOS gate drawing you see should obey this.
lessons.task: On paper, draw a pMOS from VDD to Y and an nMOS from Y to ground with both gates on input A. Trace Y for A = 0 and A = 1 using only the switch rule. Then swap the two transistors and trace again, writing the actual output voltages for VDD = 1.0 V and Vt = 0.3 V.

quiz.q: When is an nMOS transistor (source at ground) ON in the switch model?
quiz.explain: An nMOS turns on when VGS exceeds Vt, i.e. when its gate is at logic 1.

quiz.q: An nMOS with its gate at VDD = 1.0 V tries to pass a 1. If Vt = 0.3 V, about what voltage reaches the output?
quiz.explain: The output stops near VDD - Vt = 0.7 V because the transistor turns off as VGS drops to Vt.

quiz.q: Why are pMOS transistors used in the pull-up network?
quiz.explain: pMOS passes a full VDD, while nMOS would give only VDD - Vt.

quiz.q: Two nMOS transistors in series between output and ground conduct when:
quiz.explain: Series switches all have to be closed, which is AND behaviour.

quiz.q: Why does a pMOS of the same size give less current than an nMOS?
options: Holes move more slowly than electrons
pMOS only works at high temperature
quiz.explain: Hole mobility is roughly 2-3 times lower than electron mobility in silicon.

lessons.title: MOSFET Current: I-V Characteristics and Real-World Effects
lessons.content:
In lesson 2 the transistor was a perfect tap: fully open or fully closed. But a real tap has a size. A thin pipe fills a bucket slowly; a wide pipe fills it fast. If you want to know how quickly a chip can run, you must know how much current each transistor can push, because current is what charges and discharges the wires and gates. This lesson opens the tap and measures the flow. We will use the classic long-channel equations with real numbers, then see where modern tiny transistors break those equations.

Why this matters: Delay, power and noise all depend on current. A gate that drives more current charges its load faster, so the circuit is faster. A transistor that leaks current when it should be off wastes battery. Designers choose transistor widths based on these equations, and simulators like SPICE use much more detailed versions of them. You do not need to memorise every advanced model, but you must understand the three operating regions and the main effects.

The channel as a charged sheet: Recall that when VGS is above Vt, an inversion channel of electrons forms under the gate of an nMOS. How many electrons? The gate and channel form a capacitor, so the charge is roughly Cox times (VGS - Vt), where Cox is the oxide capacitance per unit area. The quantity VGS - Vt is called the overdrive voltage, how far above threshold the gate is. More overdrive means more electrons in the channel, which means more current for the same push from the drain.

The three regions: An nMOS works in one of three regions. Cutoff: VGS is less than Vt. No channel forms and, in the ideal model, the current ID is zero. Linear, also called triode or resistive: VGS is above Vt and VDS is small, smaller than VGS - Vt. The channel exists all the way from source to drain, and the transistor behaves roughly like a resistor controlled by the gate. Saturation: VGS is above Vt and VDS is at least VGS - Vt. Near the drain, the channel is pinched off, and the current stops increasing much with VDS. It depends mainly on VGS.

The long-channel equations: The Shockley model, also called the square-law model, gives the current. In the linear region, ID = k' (W/L) [ (VGS - Vt) VDS - VDS squared / 2 ]. In saturation, ID = (1/2) k' (W/L) (VGS - Vt) squared. Here k' is the process transconductance parameter, equal to the carrier mobility times Cox, fixed by the factory. W is the channel width and L is the channel length, which the designer chooses. W/L is the most important knob a circuit designer has: double the width and you double the current.

Worked example, saturation: Take an nMOS with k' = 200 microamps per volt squared, W/L = 2, Vt = 0.4 V. Apply VGS = 1.0 V and VDS = 1.0 V. First check the region: overdrive is 1.0 - 0.4 = 0.6 V, and VDS = 1.0 is greater than 0.6, so it is in saturation. ID = 0.5 x 200 x 2 x 0.6 squared = 0.5 x 400 x 0.36 = 72 microamps. If we doubled W/L to 4, the current would double to 144 microamps.

Worked example, linear region: Same transistor, VGS = 1.0 V, but now VDS = 0.2 V. Since 0.2 is less than 0.6, it is in the linear region. ID = 200 x 2 x [0.6 x 0.2 - 0.2 squared / 2] = 400 x [0.12 - 0.02] = 400 x 0.10 = 40 microamps. Notice that the current is smaller because the drain is not pulling hard yet.

The transistor as a resistor: For very small VDS, the squared term is tiny, so ID is approximately k' (W/L) (VGS - Vt) VDS. That is Ohm's law with resistance R = 1 / [k' (W/L) (VGS - Vt)]. With our numbers, R = 1 / (400 microamps per volt squared x 0.6 V) = about 4,167 ohms. This is the seed of the RC delay model used in lessons 9 and 10: an ON transistor behaves like a resistor whose value goes down as the width goes up.

The pMOS equations: For a pMOS, the same equations apply with signs flipped: use VSG instead of VGS, VSD instead of VDS and |Vtp| instead of Vt. Its k' is smaller because hole mobility is lower, typically about one half to one third of the nMOS value. So to get the same current as an nMOS, a pMOS needs about two to three times the width. This is why standard-cell inverters have wider pMOS transistors.

The body effect: So far we assumed the source and body are at the same voltage. In stacked transistors, like the upper nMOS in a NAND gate, the source sits above ground while the body is still at ground. A positive source-to-body voltage VSB makes it harder to form the channel, so the threshold rises. The formula is Vt = Vt0 + gamma [ square root of (2 phiF + VSB) - square root of (2 phiF) ], where gamma is the body-effect coefficient and 2 phiF is a surface potential term. Example: Vt0 = 0.4 V, gamma = 0.4 square-root volts, 2 phiF = 0.7 V and VSB = 0.5 V. The bracket is square root of 1.2 minus square root of 0.7, which is 1.095 - 0.837 = 0.259. Multiply by 0.4 to get 0.104. So Vt rises to about 0.50 V. A higher threshold means less overdrive and less current, one reason tall stacks of transistors are slow.

Channel-length modulation: In saturation, the ideal model says current does not depend on VDS. In reality, raising VDS moves the pinch-off point toward the source, shortening the effective channel slightly, so current rises a little. We model this as ID times (1 + lambda VDS). With lambda = 0.1 per volt and VDS = 1.0 V, our 72 microamps becomes 72 x 1.1 = 79.2 microamps. Shorter channels have a larger lambda.

Velocity saturation: The square law assumes electrons speed up in proportion to the electric field. But in tiny modern transistors, the field along the channel is so strong that electrons hit a maximum speed, called the saturation velocity, roughly 10 to the 7 centimetres per second in silicon. After that, more field does not make them faster. The result: current grows more slowly with overdrive, closer to linear than square. A useful empirical model is the alpha-power law, where ID is proportional to (VGS - Vt) to the power alpha, and alpha is between 1 and 2; for modern short-channel devices it is often closer to 1.

Other short-channel effects: When the channel is very short, the drain's electric field reaches toward the source and helps lower the barrier, so the threshold voltage drops as VDS rises. This is drain-induced barrier lowering, DIBL. The threshold also depends on the channel length itself, so tiny manufacturing variations in L change Vt. Mobility drops at high vertical fields too. These effects are why modern transistors moved to new shapes like FinFETs, covered in lesson 15.

Subthreshold leakage: The ideal model says the transistor is off below Vt. In reality, current drops exponentially below threshold rather than to zero. The steepness is measured by the subthreshold slope S, the gate voltage change needed to change the current by a factor of 10. At room temperature S can never be better than about 60 mV per decade for a normal MOSFET, and real devices are often 70 to 100 mV per decade. Example: if a transistor carries 1 microamp at VGS = Vt = 0.4 V and S = 100 mV per decade, then at VGS = 0 the current falls by 4 decades, to 1 microamp divided by 10,000, which is 0.1 nanoamps. That sounds tiny, but multiply by a billion transistors and you get around 0.1 amps of leakage. Lower Vt makes switching faster but leakage worse; this trade-off returns in lessons 12 and 13.

Gate leakage and other currents: When the oxide is only a few atoms thick, electrons can tunnel straight through it, causing gate leakage. This became serious in the 2000s and led to high-k dielectrics, which allow a thicker physical layer with the same capacitance. There is also small leakage through the reverse-biased source and drain junctions.

Real-life example 1, the Gulistan bus stop: Think of passengers as electrons and a bus door as the channel. In cutoff the door is shut and nobody moves. In the linear region the door is open and people walk through at a rate that depends on how hard the crowd behind pushes, like VDS. In saturation, the door width is the limit: pushing harder from behind barely changes the flow, which now depends on how wide the door is open, like VGS. Velocity saturation is like a corridor where people cannot run faster than a fixed speed no matter how loud the conductor shouts.

Real-life example 2, a phone charging chip: The charger IC in your phone uses big power MOSFETs as switches, with W/L in the thousands, so their ON resistance is tiny and they waste little power as heat. Meanwhile, the logic in the phone's processor uses tiny transistors with W/L near 1 to save area. The same equations govern both; the designer just turned the W/L knob to a very different place. This shows that W/L is a real design decision, not a fixed number.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common mistake is using the saturation equation without first checking the region. Always compute VGS - Vt and compare with VDS. Another is forgetting the factor of one half in saturation. Students also confuse W and L: current goes up with W and down with L. Some think the transistor carries exactly zero current below Vt. Typical exam questions: identify the region and compute ID for given voltages; compute the ON resistance; find the new threshold with body effect; explain velocity saturation and why current becomes more linear; compute leakage from the subthreshold slope; explain why pMOS transistors are made wider.

Recap: An nMOS is in cutoff when VGS is below Vt, linear when VDS is less than VGS - Vt, and saturated otherwise. Long-channel current is k'(W/L)[(VGS - Vt)VDS - VDS squared/2] in linear and half k'(W/L)(VGS - Vt) squared in saturation; our example gave 40 and 72 microamps. Width over length is the designer's main knob. The body effect raises Vt in stacks, channel-length modulation adds a small VDS dependence, velocity saturation makes current more linear in modern devices, and subthreshold leakage means an off transistor is never fully off. Next, we connect two transistors into the CMOS inverter and study it in depth.
key_points: Three regions: cutoff (VGS < Vt), linear (VDS < VGS - Vt), saturation (VDS >= VGS - Vt).
Saturation: ID = 0.5 k'(W/L)(VGS - Vt)^2; example gives 72 uA; linear example gives 40 uA.
W/L is the designer's main knob; an ON transistor acts like a resistor about 1/[k'(W/L)(VGS - Vt)].
pMOS has lower k' (hole mobility), so it needs about 2-3x width for equal current.
Body effect raises Vt when the source is above the body (0.40 V to about 0.50 V in the example).
Short channels bring velocity saturation, DIBL and channel-length modulation.
Subthreshold slope at least about 60 mV/decade; lower Vt means more leakage.
lessons.tip: Before plugging any number into a MOSFET equation, write one line: overdrive = VGS - Vt, compare with VDS, region = ?. Most exam errors vanish with this habit.
lessons.task: Using k' = 200 uA/V^2, W/L = 2 and Vt = 0.4 V, compute ID for VGS = 1.0 V at VDS = 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0 V. Plot the four points on paper and see the curve bend from a slope into a flat line.

quiz.q: An nMOS has VGS = 1.0 V, Vt = 0.4 V and VDS = 0.3 V. Which region is it in?
quiz.explain: Overdrive is 0.6 V and VDS = 0.3 V is smaller, so the channel is not pinched off: linear region.

quiz.q: With k' = 200 uA/V^2, W/L = 2, Vt = 0.4 V and VGS = 1.0 V in saturation, ID is:
What does the body effect do when the source is above the body voltage?
quiz.explain: A positive VSB makes inversion harder, so Vt increases and current falls.

quiz.q: With a subthreshold slope of 100 mV/decade, lowering VGS by 300 mV reduces the leakage by a factor of:
quiz.explain: 300 mV is 3 decades, so the current falls by 10^3 = 1,000.

quiz.q: Velocity saturation makes the saturation current depend on overdrive:
quiz.explain: Carriers hit a speed limit, so the alpha-power exponent moves from 2 toward 1.

lessons.title: The CMOS Inverter in Depth
lessons.content:
Picture a tug of war between two teams. One team pulls the rope toward the sky, the other pulls it toward the ground. A referee, the input, decides which team is allowed to pull: when the input says 1, only the ground team pulls; when it says 0, only the sky team pulls. The rope end, our output, always ends up firmly at one side. In the short moment while the referee changes their mind, both teams pull at once and the rope wobbles in the middle. That is the CMOS inverter, the simplest and most important circuit in all of VLSI. Every other gate is judged by comparing it to the inverter.

Why study one tiny circuit so deeply: The inverter is the yardstick of a technology. Its switching point, its noise margins, its delay and its power tell you how good a process is. Logic gates are basically inverters with more transistors in the pull-up and pull-down networks, so once you understand the inverter, NAND, NOR and complex gates follow. In lesson 20 of Electronic Devices you saw the basic idea. Here we analyse it the way a VLSI designer does: the full transfer curve region by region, the switching threshold formula with numbers, sizing, noise margins and why it restores signals.

The circuit: A pMOS connects VDD to the output Y. An nMOS connects Y to ground. Both gates connect to the input A. Both drains connect to Y. The pMOS source is at VDD, the nMOS source at ground, and in a normal process the nMOS body is at ground and the pMOS body (its n-well) is at VDD, so there is no body effect in the inverter. Output Y drives some load capacitance: the gates of the next stage plus the wires.

The voltage transfer characteristic: Slowly sweep the input from 0 to VDD and plot the output. This curve is the VTC. It starts flat at VDD, drops very steeply somewhere in the middle, and ends flat at 0. To understand its shape, we look at which region each transistor is in, using the equations from lesson 3. Remember that in steady state, with no current flowing out of the output, the nMOS current must equal the pMOS current; the output voltage settles where the two currents match.

The five regions of the VTC: Region A: input below Vtn. The nMOS is off, the pMOS is on in its linear region, the output sits at VDD. Region B: input just above Vtn. The nMOS turns on and is in saturation (its VDS is large), the pMOS is still linear; the output starts to drop a little. Region C: input near the middle. Both transistors are in saturation. Here the curve is almost vertical, because a tiny change in input causes a large change in output. Region D: input above the middle. The nMOS is now linear, the pMOS saturated, the output is close to 0. Region E: input above VDD - |Vtp|. The pMOS is off, the output sits at 0. Because the off transistor is truly off in regions A and E, the output reaches the full rails, 0 and VDD.

The switching threshold VM: VM is the input voltage at which the output equals the input, the point where the VTC crosses the line Vout = Vin. At VM both transistors are saturated, so set the nMOS saturation current equal to the pMOS saturation current and solve. With the long-channel model, VM = [Vtn + r (VDD - |Vtp|)] / (1 + r), where r is the square root of (kp' (W/L)p) divided by (kn' (W/L)n). The ratio r tells you how strong the pull-up is compared with the pull-down.

Worked example, a balanced inverter: Let VDD = 1.0 V and Vtn = |Vtp| = 0.3 V. If the pull-up and pull-down are equally strong, r = 1 and VM = [0.3 + 1 x 0.7] / 2 = 0.5 V, exactly the middle. Now suppose we made both transistors the same size, and the pMOS k' is half of the nMOS k'. Then r = square root of 0.5, about 0.707, and VM = [0.3 + 0.707 x 0.7] / 1.707 = [0.3 + 0.495] / 1.707, about 0.466 V. The weaker pull-up lets the nMOS win earlier, so the switching point slides toward ground.

Sizing the pMOS: To bring VM back to the middle, make the pMOS strong enough: kp' (W/L)p should equal kn' (W/L)n. If kp' is half of kn', make the pMOS twice as wide. This is why textbooks often say the pMOS is 2 to 3 times wider than the nMOS. The ratio of pMOS width to nMOS width is called the beta ratio or P/N ratio. A symmetric VTC also gives roughly equal rise and fall times, which is nice. But designers do not always choose perfect symmetry: because wide pMOS transistors add capacitance, a smaller ratio, around 1.4 to 2, often gives a slightly better average delay. Notice also that VM is not very sensitive to the ratio: halving the pMOS strength moved VM only from 0.5 to 0.466 V.

Noise margins: Real wires pick up noise. A gate must read a slightly noisy 0 as 0 and a slightly noisy 1 as 1. We define VIL, the highest input still surely read as 0, and VIH, the lowest input still surely read as 1. These are taken where the slope of the VTC equals -1, the edges of the steep part. VOH and VOL are the output levels for 1 and 0, which for CMOS are VDD and 0. The noise margins are NMH = VOH - VIH and NML = VIL - VOL. Example: with VDD = 1.0 V, if VIL = 0.4 V and VIH = 0.6 V, then NML = 0.4 - 0 = 0.4 V and NMH = 1.0 - 0.6 = 0.4 V. A noise spike smaller than 0.4 V cannot flip the logic value. CMOS has large noise margins because the outputs reach the rails and the middle of the curve is steep.

The regenerative property: Suppose a degraded 1 of 0.75 V arrives at an inverter. Because the VTC is flat near the ends and steep in the middle, the output is almost exactly 0. The next inverter turns that clean 0 into a clean 1. So a chain of CMOS gates cleans up small errors at every stage instead of adding them up. This is called regeneration, and it is the deep reason digital electronics is so reliable compared with analog: noise does not accumulate through a chain of gates as long as each error stays inside the noise margin.

Gain: The slope of the VTC in region C is the voltage gain. For an ideal switch, it would be infinite. Real inverters have gains of perhaps 10 to 50 in the middle, depending on the process. High gain means a sharp switching edge and good noise margins. Short-channel effects, like channel-length modulation, reduce the gain in modern processes, which is one reason noise margins shrink as transistors get smaller.

Static power: In regions A and E, one transistor is off, so no current flows from VDD to ground except tiny leakage. This is the famous property that made CMOS win over earlier logic families like nMOS-only logic, which burned power whenever the output was 0. A CMOS chip with a billion transistors sitting idle uses only leakage power.

Short-circuit current: During a transition, while the input passes through region C, both transistors are on together, and a brief current flows straight from VDD to ground. Using our earlier device, k' = 200 microamps per volt squared and W/L = 2 for both (ignoring that a real pMOS would be weaker), at VM = 0.5 V the saturation current is 0.5 x 200 x 2 x (0.5 - 0.3) squared = 8 microamps. This current only flows for the short time the input takes to cross the middle, so as long as input edges are sharp, short-circuit power is usually a small part of total power. Slow input edges make it worse, which is one reason designers limit slew rates.

The inverter as a delay yardstick: When the input switches, the output must charge or discharge the load capacitance through an ON transistor. The pull-down acts like a resistor R to ground, the pull-up like a resistor to VDD, and the delay is roughly proportional to R times C. Lesson 9 builds this RC model properly and lesson 10 uses it to define the delay unit tau and the FO4 inverter delay. Here just remember: a wider transistor means smaller R and faster switching, but also more input capacitance for the gate driving it.

Real-life example 1, a water tank with two taps: A rooftop tank in Dhaka has an inlet tap from the pump and an outlet tap to the drain. If a controller opens exactly one tap at a time, the tank is either filling or emptying, never wasting water. If the controller is slow and both are briefly open, some water flows straight from pump to drain; that is short-circuit current. If the outlet tap is a thin pipe and the inlet a fat one, the tank fills faster than it empties; that is an unbalanced beta ratio. Designers size the pipes to get the behaviour they want.

Real-life example 2, signals in a long chain of shops: Imagine a message passed by shouting from shop to shop along a crowded market lane in Old Dhaka. If every shopkeeper just repeats what they half heard, the message gets garbled. But if every shopkeeper must answer only yes or no, a slightly mumbled yes is still heard as yes and repeated loud and clear. CMOS inverters work like these disciplined shopkeepers; regeneration keeps a 1 a 1 across thousands of gates.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often say VM is always VDD/2; it is only VDD/2 when the pull-up and pull-down are balanced and thresholds are equal. Another mistake is assuming no current ever flows; current flows during switching to charge loads and briefly through both transistors. Some mix up NMH and NML. Exam questions: draw the VTC and label the five regions with transistor states; derive and compute VM for given parameters; size the pMOS for VM = VDD/2; compute noise margins from given VIL and VIH; explain regeneration; explain static, short-circuit and dynamic power in an inverter.

Recap: The CMOS inverter is a pMOS pull-up and an nMOS pull-down sharing one input. Its VTC has five regions and a steep middle where both transistors are saturated. VM = [Vtn + r(VDD - |Vtp|)] / (1 + r); balanced devices give 0.5 V, while a pMOS half as strong gives about 0.466 V. Making the pMOS about 2 to 3 times wider balances it. Noise margins are large, outputs reach the rails, regeneration cleans signals, and static power is nearly zero. Next, we turn the inverter into NAND, NOR and any complex gate.
key_points: CMOS inverter: pMOS from VDD to Y, nMOS from Y to ground, gates tied to input.
VTC has five regions; in the steep middle both transistors are saturated.
VM = [Vtn + r(VDD - |Vtp|)] / (1 + r), r = sqrt(beta_p / beta_n); balanced gives 0.5 V, weak pMOS gives 0.466 V.
Make the pMOS about 2-3x wider for a symmetric VTC; ratio around 1.4-2 can give better average delay.
Noise margins NMH = VOH - VIH, NML = VIL - VOL; CMOS margins are large.
Regeneration: steep VTC restores degraded levels, so noise does not accumulate.
Static power is nearly zero; short-circuit current flows only during transitions.
lessons.tip: Draw the VTC once by hand, writing next to each region which transistor is off, linear or saturated. If you can redraw that annotated picture from memory, you understand the inverter.
lessons.task: With VDD = 1.2 V and Vtn = |Vtp| = 0.35 V, compute VM for r = 1, r = 0.7 and r = 1.4. Write down how far VM moves each time, and decide which r you would choose for equal rise and fall.

quiz.q: In the steep middle region of the inverter VTC, the transistors are:
quiz.explain: Region C has both devices in saturation, which gives the high gain and steep slope.

quiz.q: VDD = 1.0 V, Vtn = |Vtp| = 0.3 V and r = 1. What is VM?
If the pMOS k' is half of the nMOS k', how should you size the pMOS for a symmetric inverter?
options: Twice as wide as the nMOS
quiz.explain: Doubling W compensates for half the k', making the pull-up as strong as the pull-down.

quiz.q: VIL = 0.4 V, VOL = 0 V, VIH = 0.65 V, VOH = 1.0 V. What is NMH?
Why does noise not pile up along a long chain of CMOS inverters?
options: The supply voltage increases along the chain
Each stage regenerates full logic levels from slightly degraded inputs
quiz.explain: The flat ends and steep middle of the VTC push small errors back to clean 0 or VDD at each stage.

lessons.title: Static CMOS Logic Gates: From Expression to Transistors
lessons.content:
Think about how a building's main door and fire exit work together. The main door is open when the guard is present AND the time is daytime. The fire exit, wired the opposite way, is open in exactly every situation where the main door is closed. At every moment, exactly one of them is open, never both and never neither. A static CMOS gate is built with the same discipline: a pull-up network made of pMOS transistors that connects the output to VDD, and a pull-down network made of nMOS transistors that connects it to ground, wired so that for every input combination exactly one of them conducts. In this lesson you will learn to turn any inverting Boolean expression into such a pair of networks by hand.

Why this matters: Standard-cell libraries, the bricks of every digital ASIC, are mostly static CMOS gates: inverters, NAND, NOR, AOI, OAI, multiplexers and flip-flops. Knowing how they are built tells you why some gates are faster, why NAND is preferred over NOR, why a 4-input gate is slow and how a library designer chooses transistor sizes. It also lets you answer the most common VLSI exam question: draw the transistor-level circuit for this function.

The general structure: Every static CMOS gate has one output. Between VDD and the output sits the pull-up network, PUN, made only of pMOS. Between the output and ground sits the pull-down network, PDN, made only of nMOS. Each input drives one pMOS in the PUN and one nMOS in the PDN. When the PDN conducts, the output is 0. When the PUN conducts, the output is 1. The networks are complementary: whenever one conducts, the other does not. This guarantees a full-swing output and no static current, just like the inverter.

Series and parallel rules: In the PDN, transistors in series form AND: all must be on for a path to ground. Transistors in parallel form OR: any one on gives a path. Because nMOS turn on with a 1, the PDN conducts when its AND/OR expression of the inputs is true, and the output becomes 0. So the gate computes the complement: Y = NOT(PDN function). This is why a single static CMOS stage is always inverting. A non-inverting function like AND needs two stages: a NAND followed by an inverter.

Duality: The PUN is the dual of the PDN. Wherever the PDN has transistors in series, the PUN has them in parallel, and wherever the PDN has them in parallel, the PUN has them in series. Because pMOS turn on with a 0, this dual structure conducts exactly when the PDN does not, which is De Morgan's theorem in hardware. For example, if the PDN is A AND B, the PUN conducts when NOT A OR NOT B, which is exactly NOT(A AND B).

NAND2 and NOR2 recap: For the NAND2, Y = NOT(A AND B). The PDN has two nMOS in series; the PUN has two pMOS in parallel. Four transistors total. For the NOR2, Y = NOT(A OR B). The PDN has two nMOS in parallel; the PUN has two pMOS in series. Also four transistors. Check NAND2 with A = 1, B = 0: the series nMOS path is broken because B is off; the pMOS with gate B is on, so Y = 1. Correct, because NOT(1 AND 0) = 1.

Step-by-step method for any complementary gate: Step 1: write the function as Y = NOT(expression) where the expression uses only AND and OR of uncomplemented inputs. Step 2: build the PDN from the expression: AND becomes series, OR becomes parallel. Step 3: build the PUN as the dual: series becomes parallel and parallel becomes series. Step 4: connect the PDN between Y and ground, the PUN between VDD and Y. Step 5: check with a few input combinations. If the expression contains complemented inputs, you need inverters to make those signals first.

Worked example, Y = NOT(A AND (B OR C)): Step 2: B OR C is two nMOS in parallel; AND with A means put nMOS A in series with that parallel pair. So the PDN is: Y to nMOS A, then from there to ground through nMOS B and nMOS C in parallel. Step 3: the dual: pMOS A in parallel with the series pair pMOS B and pMOS C. So from VDD, one branch is pMOS A to Y, the other branch is pMOS B then pMOS C to Y. Step 5: check A = 1, B = 0, C = 1: PDN path A on, C on, so Y connects to ground, Y = 0; PUN: pMOS A is off, and in the series branch B = 0 turns pMOS B on but C = 1 turns pMOS C off, so that branch is broken too. Y = 0 and the expression gives NOT(1 AND 1) = 0. Correct. The gate uses 6 transistors.

Compound gates, AOI and OAI: An AND-OR-INVERT gate computes NOT of an OR of ANDs. The AOI22 computes Y = NOT(A AND B OR C AND D). Its PDN has two series pairs (A-B and C-D) in parallel; its PUN has two parallel pairs in series. Total 8 transistors. Building the same function from separate gates would take two AND2 gates (each a NAND2 plus inverter, 6 transistors each) and one NOR2 (4 transistors), 16 transistors and three gate delays. The compound gate is half the size and one stage. OAI gates, OR-AND-INVERT, are the duals, for example OAI21: Y = NOT((A OR B) AND C). Standard-cell libraries contain many AOI and OAI variants because synthesis tools love them.

Transistor sizing for equal drive: We want every gate to drive about as strongly as a reference inverter. Take the unit inverter as nMOS width 1 and pMOS width 2, since the pMOS is about half as strong. In the NAND2, the two nMOS are in series, so each must be twice as wide, width 2, for the stack to match a single width-1 nMOS. The pMOS are in parallel, and in the worst case only one is on, so each stays at width 2. In the NOR2, the nMOS are in parallel, width 1 each, but the pMOS are in series, so each must be width 4. The general rule: transistors in a series stack of k are made k times wider.

Why NAND beats NOR: Compare input capacitance, which is proportional to the total gate width one input sees. In the inverter, one input sees 1 + 2 = 3. In the NAND2, each input sees 2 + 2 = 4. In the NOR2, each input sees 1 + 4 = 5. The NOR2 has bigger, slower pMOS transistors in series, so it costs more area and loads its driver more. That is why designers and synthesis tools prefer NAND-based logic, and why lesson 11 assigns NAND2 a logical effort of 4/3 and NOR2 5/3. Total transistor width: NAND2 is 2+2+2+2 = 8, NOR2 is 1+1+4+4 = 10.

Fan-in limits: A NAND with many inputs has a tall stack of series nMOS. With 4 inputs, each nMOS is 4 times wider, so each input drives a lot of capacitance, and the stack also has internal node capacitances and body effect that slow it down. Delay grows roughly with the square of fan-in in the worst case. In practice, designers rarely use more than 4 inputs per gate; a wide AND is built as a tree, for example an 8-input AND as two NAND4 gates followed by a NOR2.

The mirror full adder: The 1-bit full adder computes Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin and Cout = majority(A, B, Cin) = AB + ACin + BCin. A clever static CMOS design called the mirror adder computes the complements of Cout and Sum with transistor networks whose PUN has the same shape as the PDN, which works because the majority and parity functions are self-dual. It uses 24 transistors for the two complemented outputs, plus two inverters, 28 transistors in all. This 28-transistor adder is the classic textbook answer; lesson 18 uses many of them to build fast adders.

Input ordering inside a stack: In a series stack, the transistors are not all equal. In a NAND2, the nMOS nearest the output must also discharge the small capacitance of the internal node between the two transistors, while the one nearest ground does not. So if one input arrives later than the others, a designer connects that late input to the transistor closest to the output. By the time it arrives, the lower transistors are already on and the internal node is already discharged, so only the top transistor's switching remains. This small trick, called input ordering, can save a noticeable amount of delay on a critical path, and library cells often mark which input pin is the fast one.

Non-complementary pitfalls: If the PUN and PDN are not true duals, there may be an input combination where both conduct, creating a short from VDD to ground and an output stuck somewhere in the middle, or one where neither conducts, leaving the output floating and holding an old value. Both are bugs in static logic. The quickest check is to confirm that for every input combination exactly one network has a closed path; for a 3-input gate that is only 8 cases to trace on paper.

Real-life example 1, the hostel gate rule: A boys' hostel in Dhaka has a rule: the gate stays locked when (the warden is out) AND (it is after 11 pm OR it is an exam night). Draw this as a PDN where locked means output 0: nMOS warden-out in series with the parallel pair late and exam-night. The PUN is its dual. Every possible situation either locks or unlocks the gate, never both. If you can draw this, you can draw any compound gate.

Real-life example 2, standard cells in a real chip: When a synthesis tool turns Verilog for a traffic-signal controller into gates, it picks from a library of perhaps a few hundred cells: NAND2, NAND3, NOR2, AOI21, AOI22, OAI21, inverters in several sizes, flip-flops. Each cell exists in several drive strengths, like X1, X2, X4, which are the same circuit with wider transistors. The tool chooses an AOI22 instead of four separate gates because it is smaller and faster. Everything you did by hand in this lesson is exactly what the library designers did, once, very carefully.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common error is forgetting duality and drawing the PUN with the same series-parallel shape as the PDN. Another is putting complemented inputs directly on transistors without generating them. Students also forget that one static CMOS stage is always inverting, so they try to build AND in one stage. Some forget to upsize series transistors. Exam questions: draw the transistor circuit for a given expression; count transistors; size transistors for equal drive with an inverter of pMOS 2 and nMOS 1; compare NAND and NOR; explain why fan-in is limited; draw an AOI or OAI gate; explain the mirror adder.

Recap: A static CMOS gate is a pMOS pull-up network and an nMOS pull-down network that are duals of each other. Series means AND and parallel means OR in the PDN, and the output is the complement of the PDN function. Build the PDN from the expression, then flip series and parallel for the PUN. Compound AOI and OAI gates save area and delay, for example 8 transistors instead of 16 for AOI22. Series stacks are upsized, which makes NAND cheaper than NOR and limits fan-in to about 4. Next, we look at logic styles that break the static CMOS rules to gain speed or area.
key_points: Static CMOS gate = pMOS pull-up network + nMOS pull-down network, duals of each other.
In the PDN, series = AND and parallel = OR; output = NOT(PDN function), so one stage is always inverting.
Method: PDN from expression, PUN by swapping series and parallel, then check with input cases.
AOI22 = NOT(AB + CD) needs 8 transistors versus 16 using separate gates.
Series stacks are upsized: NAND2 nMOS width 2, NOR2 pMOS width 4 (unit inverter 1/2).
Input capacitance per input: inverter 3, NAND2 4, NOR2 5, so NAND is preferred.
Keep fan-in to about 4; the mirror full adder uses 28 transistors.
lessons.tip: Always check your gate with at least two input combinations: one that should give 0 and one that should give 1. Trace the PDN and the PUN separately and confirm exactly one conducts.
lessons.task: Draw the transistor-level static CMOS circuit for Y = NOT((A OR B) AND (C OR D)). Size it for equal drive with a unit inverter of nMOS 1 and pMOS 2, then write down the input capacitance seen by input A.

quiz.q: In a static CMOS pull-down network, nMOS transistors in series implement:
quiz.explain: All series switches must be on to connect output to ground, which is AND.

quiz.q: How many transistors does a static CMOS AOI22 gate use?
quiz.explain: Four nMOS in the PDN and four pMOS in the PUN; using separate gates would take 16.

quiz.q: If the PDN is nMOS A in series with (B parallel C), what is the PUN?
options: pMOS A in series with (B parallel C)
pMOS A in parallel with (B series C)
pMOS A, B and C all in series
pMOS A, B and C all in parallel
quiz.explain: The PUN is the dual: series becomes parallel and parallel becomes series.

quiz.q: With a unit inverter of nMOS 1 and pMOS 2, what width does each pMOS get in a NOR2 sized for equal drive?
quiz.explain: Two pMOS in series must each be twice the inverter's pMOS width: 2 x 2 = 4.

quiz.q: Why can't one static CMOS stage implement AND directly?
options: One stage always gives the complement of its PDN function
quiz.explain: The PDN pulls the output low when its function is true, so a single stage is always inverting; AND = NAND + inverter.

lessons.title: Beyond Static CMOS: Pass Transistors, Transmission Gates, Ratioed and Dynamic Logic
lessons.content:
Static CMOS is like a family car: safe, reliable, economical, and good enough for almost every trip. But sometimes you need a motorbike to weave through Dhaka traffic, or a truck to carry a heavy load. Chip designers also have other vehicles. Some logic styles use fewer transistors, some are faster, some trade power for speed. Each breaks one of the comfortable rules of static CMOS, and each comes with a danger you must understand. This lesson tours the main alternatives: pass-transistor logic, transmission gates, ratioed pseudo-nMOS logic, dynamic logic, domino logic and differential logic.

Why learn other styles: Static CMOS needs two transistors per input and always inverts. For some functions, like multiplexers and XOR, that is wasteful. For the fastest paths in high-performance processors, its big pMOS transistors add capacitance and slow things down. Alternative styles appear inside standard cells you use every day: multiplexers and flip-flops are built with transmission gates, and many memory and high-speed circuits use dynamic precharge. Understanding them also explains classic bugs like charge sharing, which appear in exams and in real chips.

Pass-transistor logic: Instead of using a transistor to connect the output to VDD or ground, pass-transistor logic uses it to pass an input signal straight through to the output. A 2-to-1 multiplexer can be built with just two nMOS transistors: one passes input D0 when select S is 0 (its gate driven by NOT S), the other passes D1 when S is 1. That is two transistors plus an inverter for NOT S, compared with a dozen or so in static CMOS. Very compact.

The weak 1 problem returns: Recall from lesson 2 that an nMOS passes only a weak 1, reaching about VDD - Vt. With VDD = 1.0 V and Vt = 0.3 V, the multiplexer output reaches only about 0.7 V, and with the body effect even less. If this degraded 1 drives a static CMOS inverter, the inverter's pMOS is not fully off, because its gate is 0.3 V below VDD, about at its threshold. So a small current leaks from VDD to ground through the inverter, wasting static power, and the noise margin shrinks. Chaining several pass transistors makes it worse. Pass-transistor logic therefore usually restores levels with a static gate after one or two pass stages.

The transmission gate: The fix is to pair the nMOS with a pMOS in parallel, driven by complementary control signals. When the control C is 1, the nMOS gate gets 1 and the pMOS gate gets NOT C = 0: both are on. The nMOS passes 0 strongly and the pMOS passes 1 strongly, so together they pass any value with full swing. When C is 0, both are off and the gate is an open switch. This is the transmission gate, TG, drawn as two overlapping triangles or a pair of transistors with a bubble on one control.

TG multiplexer and XOR: A 2-to-1 multiplexer made from two TGs needs 4 transistors plus 2 for the inverter making NOT S, 6 total, and it gives full-swing outputs. An XOR gate can be built with TGs in about 6 to 8 transistors, versus about 12 for a static CMOS XOR built from complementary networks with input inverters. TGs also form the heart of most latches and flip-flops, which you will meet in lesson 16. The catch: a TG is not a driver. It adds resistance and capacitance to the path but no gain, so the signal weakens through a chain of TGs. The rule of thumb is to put a buffer after a few TGs in series.

Ratioed logic, pseudo-nMOS: Another idea is to replace the whole pull-up network with a single pMOS whose gate is tied permanently to ground, so it is always on, like a resistor pulling the output up. The pull-down network is the usual nMOS network. When the PDN is off, the always-on pMOS pulls the output to VDD. When the PDN is on, it fights the pMOS and wins, because the pMOS was deliberately made weak, about a quarter of the nMOS strength. An N-input gate needs only N + 1 transistors. An 8-input NOR needs 9 transistors instead of 16, and has no tall pMOS stack, so it can be fast.

The cost of pseudo-nMOS: When the output is 0, both the pMOS and the PDN are on, so current flows continuously from VDD to ground. That is static power, exactly what CMOS was supposed to avoid. Example: if each gate draws 50 microamps at VDD = 1.0 V while its output is low, that is 50 microwatts per gate; 10,000 such gates would burn 0.5 W doing nothing. Also, the output low level VOL is not exactly 0 but a small voltage set by the ratio of the two transistors, which is why it is called ratioed logic: the sizes must be chosen carefully or the output will not go low enough. Pseudo-nMOS is used in special spots, like wide NOR decoders in memories, often with the pMOS turned off when idle.

Dynamic logic: Dynamic logic removes the static pull-up altogether and uses the clock. A dynamic gate has a pMOS precharge transistor from VDD to the output node, the nMOS PDN below the output, and an nMOS evaluate or foot transistor between the PDN and ground. Both clocked transistors are driven by the clock. In the precharge phase, clock = 0: the pMOS is on, the foot is off, and the output charges to 1. In the evaluate phase, clock = 1: the pMOS is off, the foot is on, and if the PDN function is true, the output discharges to 0; otherwise it stays at 1, held only by charge on its capacitance. An N-input dynamic gate needs N + 2 transistors: a dynamic NAND4 needs 6 instead of 8, and its input capacitance is about one third smaller because there are no pMOS on the inputs. Faster and smaller.

The monotonicity problem: Dynamic gates have a serious rule. During evaluation the output can only fall, never rise again, because there is no pull-up. So inputs must only rise during evaluation. Now chain two dynamic gates. At the start of evaluation, the first gate's output is still precharged high. The second gate sees that 1 and may wrongly discharge its own output before the first gate's output falls. Once discharged, it cannot recover until the next precharge. The result is a wrong answer. Dynamic gates must not feed dynamic gates directly.

Domino logic: The classic fix is domino logic: put a static CMOS inverter after each dynamic gate. During precharge, the dynamic node is 1, so the inverter output is 0. During evaluation, the dynamic node can only fall, so the inverter output can only rise. Rising outputs feed the next dynamic gate safely, and the gates switch one after another like a row of falling dominoes. The limitation is that each domino stage is non-inverting, so domino logic alone cannot compute an inverting function; designers use tricks like dual-rail logic, computing both the true and complemented signals. Domino logic was used in the fastest parts of many high-performance processors.

Charge sharing: A dynamic output holds its 1 only as charge on a capacitor. Suppose the output node has 20 fF and is precharged to 1.0 V. Inside the PDN, an internal node between two series nMOS has 10 fF and was left at 0 V. During evaluation, the upper nMOS turns on but the lower one stays off, so the output should stay at 1. But now the output charge spreads over both capacitances: 20 fF x 1.0 V = 20 fC shared over 30 fF gives 20 / 30, about 0.67 V. The output has dropped by a third without any real path to ground. If the next inverter's switching threshold is near 0.5 V, this is dangerously close. Fixes include precharging internal nodes too and adding a keeper.

Keepers and leakage: A dynamic node held only by charge also slowly loses it through subthreshold leakage, so dynamic logic cannot be stopped for long with the clock frozen. A keeper is a small, weak pMOS from VDD to the dynamic node, controlled by the output of the domino inverter. While the node is high, the inverter output is low, so the keeper is on and gently tops up the charge, fighting leakage and charge sharing. When the PDN really discharges the node, it overpowers the weak keeper. Like pseudo-nMOS, this is a small ratioed fight, so the keeper must be sized carefully.

Differential logic, CVSL: Cascode voltage switch logic computes both Y and NOT Y using two complementary nMOS networks and two cross-coupled pMOS transistors. Whichever network conducts pulls its side low, and the cross-coupled pMOS pull the other side fully high. It gives both polarities for free, which suits XOR-heavy circuits like adders and avoids inverters, at the cost of more transistors and some contention during switching.

Choosing a style: For most logic, use static CMOS: robust, low static power, easy for tools. Use transmission gates for multiplexers, XOR and latches. Use pseudo-nMOS only in special wide-NOR structures where speed matters and static power can be managed. Use dynamic or domino logic only for the most critical high-speed paths, and only with careful design for charge sharing, leakage, noise and clocking. Most standard-cell ASIC flows are almost entirely static CMOS plus TG-based cells, because automated tools and timing analysis handle them reliably.

Real-life example 1, a rickshaw toll gate versus a pumped tank: A static CMOS gate is like a road with a guard who actively pushes every rickshaw to the correct side. A dynamic gate is like an overhead water tank filled every morning: during the day it can only drain, never refill, so if a pipe leaks a little or water slips into a side pipe (charge sharing), the level drops and you cannot fix it until the next morning's pump (precharge). It is cheaper and quicker to use, but you must plan carefully.

Real-life example 2, the multiplexer inside your phone's camera path: Image processing chips move huge amounts of data through selection points: choose this pixel or that one, this filter or that one. Multiplexers there are commonly built with transmission gates because they are compact and give full-swing outputs. Meanwhile, the address decoders inside on-chip memories have historically used wide dynamic or ratioed NOR structures because they must decide very quickly which of many rows to activate.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget that nMOS pass gates give a degraded 1 and that this causes static current in the next inverter. Many think dynamic logic has no static power issues but forget charge sharing and leakage. Another mistake is cascading dynamic gates without domino inverters. Exam questions: draw a TG-based 2:1 MUX and explain why both transistors are needed; draw a pseudo-nMOS NOR and explain its static power; draw a dynamic NAND and explain precharge and evaluate; explain the monotonicity problem and domino logic; compute the voltage after charge sharing; compare transistor counts of styles.

Recap: Pass transistors pass signals instead of driving them, but nMOS alone degrades a 1. Transmission gates pair nMOS and pMOS to pass full-swing values and build compact MUXes, XORs and latches. Pseudo-nMOS uses a weak always-on pMOS, needs N + 1 transistors, but burns static power when the output is low. Dynamic logic precharges and evaluates with N + 2 transistors, is fast, but suffers from monotonicity, charge sharing (20 fF with 10 fF gives 0.67 V) and leakage; domino and keepers address these. Next, we leave circuits for a moment and visit the factory that makes them.
key_points: nMOS pass transistors degrade a 1 to about VDD - Vt, causing leakage in the next static gate.
Transmission gate = nMOS + pMOS in parallel with complementary controls; passes full swing.
TG 2:1 MUX uses about 6 transistors; TGs build MUXes, XORs and latches but have no gain.
Pseudo-nMOS: always-on weak pMOS pull-up, N + 1 transistors, static power when output is low, ratioed VOL.
Dynamic logic: precharge (clock 0) and evaluate (clock 1), N + 2 transistors, output can only fall.
Domino adds a static inverter after each dynamic gate to keep inputs monotonic rising.
Charge sharing example: 20 fF at 1.0 V shared with 10 fF gives about 0.67 V; keepers fight leakage.
lessons.tip: For each style, remember one strength and one danger: TG (full swing, no gain), pseudo-nMOS (few transistors, static power), dynamic (fast, charge sharing and monotonicity). Exams love asking for exactly that pair.
lessons.task: Draw a dynamic 3-input NAND gate with precharge pMOS and foot nMOS. Assume the output node is 15 fF and each of the two internal stack nodes is 5 fF at 0 V. Compute the worst-case output voltage after charge sharing when VDD = 1.0 V.

quiz.q: Why does a transmission gate use both an nMOS and a pMOS?
options: nMOS passes a strong 0 and pMOS passes a strong 1, giving full swing
To reduce the number of control signals
quiz.explain: Each device alone degrades one logic level; in parallel they pass both levels fully.

quiz.q: How many transistors does an N-input pseudo-nMOS gate need?
quiz.explain: N nMOS in the pull-down plus one always-on pMOS load.

quiz.q: In a dynamic gate, what happens during the precharge phase?
options: The output is charged to 1 while the foot transistor is off
quiz.explain: With clock = 0 the pMOS precharge is on and the foot is off, so the output rises to VDD.

quiz.q: A 20 fF dynamic node at 1.0 V shares charge with a 10 fF node at 0 V. What is the final voltage?
quiz.explain: 20 fC spread over 30 fF gives 0.67 V.

quiz.q: Why can't one dynamic gate directly drive another dynamic gate's input?
options: The first output starts high and may falsely discharge the second before it falls
quiz.explain: This is the monotonicity problem; domino logic inserts an inverter so inputs only rise during evaluation.

lessons.title: How Chips Are Made: The CMOS Fabrication Process
lessons.content:
Think of how a saree with a detailed block print is made. A craftsman takes plain cloth, presses a carved wooden block dipped in dye onto it, lets it dry, then uses another block with a different pattern and colour, and repeats this many times. The final design is built up layer by layer, and each block must line up perfectly with the earlier prints. A chip is made in a strikingly similar way, except the cloth is a disc of pure silicon, the blocks are patterns of light, the dyes are chemicals, metals and ions, and the lines are thousands of times thinner than a hair. This lesson walks through that process so that the layout rules and design choices in the next lessons make sense.

Why a designer needs to know fabrication: You will never run a fab yourself, but every rule you follow comes from it. Why must two wires be a minimum distance apart? Because the lithography cannot print them closer reliably. Why does a big chip cost so much more than a small one? Because of defects and yield. Why do we have a pMOS inside an n-well? Because of how the process builds both transistor types on one wafer. A designer who understands the factory makes better decisions about area, cost and reliability.

From sand to wafer: Silicon is the second most common element in the Earth's crust, found in sand as silicon dioxide. It is refined into extremely pure silicon, with impurities at around one part in a billion or better. Pure silicon is melted, and a small seed crystal is dipped in and slowly pulled up while rotating; this is the Czochralski method. The result is a single-crystal cylinder called an ingot. The ingot is sliced into thin discs called wafers, which are polished mirror-smooth. Modern logic fabs mostly use wafers 300 mm in diameter, a bit bigger than a dinner plate.

The cleanroom: A single dust particle can be larger than a transistor, so chips are made in cleanrooms where the air is filtered constantly and the number of particles is kept extremely low, far cleaner than a hospital operating theatre. Workers wear full suits, often called bunny suits, and wafers are moved in sealed boxes by robots. The whole process can take a few months and hundreds of steps from bare wafer to finished chips.

The basic operations: Almost everything in fabrication is a repetition of a few basic operations. Oxidation grows a layer of silicon dioxide on the surface by heating the wafer with oxygen or steam. Deposition adds layers of other materials, such as polysilicon, silicon nitride or metals, often by chemical vapour deposition, where gases react on the surface. Photolithography prints a pattern. Etching removes material where the pattern says. Ion implantation shoots dopant atoms, like boron or phosphorus, into selected regions to make them p-type or n-type. Annealing heats the wafer to repair crystal damage and activate dopants. Chemical mechanical polishing, CMP, grinds the surface flat so the next layer can be printed accurately.

Photolithography step by step: This is the heart of the process. Step 1: coat the wafer with a light-sensitive chemical called photoresist. Step 2: shine light through a mask, a plate carrying the pattern of one layer, so only some areas of the resist are exposed. Modern tools use a lens system that shrinks the mask pattern by about 4 times onto the wafer. Step 3: develop the resist; with positive resist, the exposed areas wash away. Step 4: etch or implant: wherever the resist is gone, the layer below is etched away or receives dopants, while the remaining resist protects the rest. Step 5: strip the remaining resist.
