One mask equals one pattern; a modern process can use many dozens of masks. Every mask must line up with the previous ones, which is called alignment or overlay.

Wavelength and resolution: The smallest feature you can print depends on the wavelength of the light. For many years fabs used deep ultraviolet light at 193 nm, and with tricks like immersion lithography, where water between the lens and wafer improves resolution, and multiple patterning, where a dense layer is split over two or more masks, they printed features far smaller than 193 nm. Extreme ultraviolet, EUV, at 13.5 nm entered high-volume production around 2019, letting fabs print fine layers with fewer masks. EUV machines are among the most complex and expensive machines ever built.

The n-well CMOS process, simplified: Let us build an nMOS and a pMOS on a p-type wafer. Step 1, wells: implant an n-well where pMOS transistors will go, since pMOS needs an n-type body. Step 2, isolation: etch shallow trenches between transistor areas and fill them with oxide, called shallow trench isolation, so neighbouring transistors do not talk. Step 3, gate oxide: grow the very thin gate dielectric. Step 4, gate: deposit and pattern the gate material, polysilicon in classic processes. Step 5, source and drain: implant n+ dopants for nMOS and p+ dopants for pMOS. Because the gate is already there, it blocks the implant underneath, so the source and drain line up perfectly with the gate edges. This is called a self-aligned process, and it is a key reason MOSFETs could be shrunk so well. Step 6, silicide and contacts: form low-resistance contacts on source, drain and gate. Step 7, interconnect: add layers of insulator and metal with vias between them.

Front end and back end: The steps that build transistors in the silicon are called front end of line, FEOL. The steps that build the wiring above are called back end of line, BEOL. A modern chip may have 10 to 15 or more metal layers. Lower layers are thin and dense for local connections; upper layers are thick and wide for long-distance signals, power and clocks. Since the late 1990s most fabs use copper wires made by the damascene process: etch trenches in insulator, fill them with copper, then polish the excess off with CMP. Aluminium was used before, and copper won because of its lower resistance.

Process nodes and their names: Processes are named by a node, like 180 nm, 90 nm, 28 nm, 7 nm, 5 nm or 3 nm. Long ago the node number roughly matched the gate length. Today it is mostly a marketing label for a generation; no feature on a 5 nm chip is literally 5 nm in the old sense. Compare processes by real metrics like transistor density, contacted gate pitch and metal pitch, speed and power. Older nodes like 180 nm or 130 nm are still widely used for cheap microcontrollers, sensors, power and analog chips.

FinFET and gate-all-around, briefly: In a planar transistor, the gate sits only on top of the channel, and in very short channels it loses control, leading to leakage. A FinFET raises the channel into a thin vertical fin and wraps the gate around three sides, giving much better control. FinFETs entered high-volume production around 2011 to 2012 at the 22 nm generation. Gate-all-around transistors, using stacked nanosheets with the gate wrapping all four sides, are the next step, entering production at the most advanced nodes from around 2022 onward. Lesson 15 explains why this was needed.

Wafer, die and yield: After processing, each wafer holds many copies of the chip; each copy is a die. A common estimate of dies per wafer is pi r squared divided by die area, minus pi d divided by the square root of twice the die area, to account for partial dies at the edge. For a 300 mm wafer, r = 150 mm and d = 300 mm, and a 100 square-millimetre die: 70,686 / 100 minus 942.5 / 14.1, which is about 707 minus 67, so roughly 640 dies. Not all dies work. Random defects land on some dies and kill them. A simple Poisson yield model says yield = e to the power minus D times A, where D is the defect density and A the die area. With D = 0.1 defects per square centimetre and A = 1 square centimetre, yield = e to the minus 0.1, about 90.5 percent, so about 579 good dies.

Why big chips are expensive: If a processed wafer costs, say, 10,000 dollars, each good 100 square-millimetre die costs about 10,000 / 579, roughly 17 dollars. Now make the die four times bigger, 400 square millimetres. Dies per wafer drop to about 143, yield falls to e to the minus 0.4, about 67 percent, leaving about 96 good dies, roughly 104 dollars each. Four times the area gave about six times the cost. This is why designers fight for every square millimetre, and why large designs are increasingly split into smaller chiplets.

After the wafer: Each die is tested on the wafer by a probe card, a step called wafer sort. Then the wafer is diced with a saw or laser, good dies are put in packages, connected by wire bonds or by flip-chip solder bumps, and tested again. Lesson 24 covers testing. Packaging matters more and more: advanced packages place several dies side by side or stack them.

Real-life example 1, printing a wedding card: A printing press in Nilkhet prints a multicolour wedding card using one plate per colour. If the red plate is shifted by a millimetre against the blue, the card looks blurry. Fabrication is the same, with dozens of plates (masks) and alignment needed within a few nanometres. A printing error ruins a card; an alignment error ruins dies. Also, a bigger card means more chances for an ink spot to land on it, just like bigger dies have lower yield.

Real-life example 2, why your phone chip came from Taiwan or Korea: Bangladesh imports almost all its chips. The most advanced logic foundries are in places like Taiwan and South Korea, because a leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars and needs huge supporting industries. But the design of chips, the subject of most of this course, can be done anywhere with skilled engineers and computers, which is why design centres exist in Dhaka.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think node names like 5 nm are real gate lengths. Many confuse etching (removing material) with deposition (adding it), or positive resist with negative resist. Some forget that a pMOS needs an n-well in a p-substrate process. Others think doubling die area doubles cost, ignoring yield. Exam questions: list and explain the steps of photolithography; describe the n-well CMOS process; explain self-alignment; explain FEOL versus BEOL; compute dies per wafer and yield; explain why EUV was needed; compare planar transistors and FinFETs.

Recap: Chips start as purified silicon grown into ingots and sliced into 300 mm wafers. A few operations, oxidation, deposition, photolithography, etching, implantation, annealing and CMP, are repeated through many masks. The n-well process builds both nMOS and pMOS, with self-aligned sources and drains. Front end makes transistors; back end makes copper wiring over many layers. Node names are labels, not sizes. Dies per wafer and yield make big chips disproportionately expensive: about 17 dollars for a 100 square-millimetre die but about 104 dollars for a 400 square-millimetre one in our example. Next, we learn how designers draw the patterns for these masks: layout and design rules.
key_points: Silicon is purified, grown as a single-crystal ingot (Czochralski) and sliced into 300 mm wafers.
Repeated operations: oxidation, deposition, photolithography, etching, ion implantation, annealing, CMP.
Photolithography: resist, expose through mask, develop, etch or implant, strip; one mask per pattern.
n-well process builds pMOS in an n-well; source/drain are self-aligned to the gate.
FEOL builds transistors; BEOL builds copper wiring (damascene) over 10-15+ metal layers.
Node names (7 nm, 5 nm) are generation labels, not literal feature sizes; FinFET and GAA improve gate control.
Yield = e^(-DA): 100 mm^2 die gives about 579 good dies per wafer (about 17 dollars each); 400 mm^2 gives about 96 (about 104 dollars).
lessons.tip: Draw the cross-section of an inverter after each process step (well, isolation, gate, implants, contacts, metal). Six small pictures will lock the process in your memory far better than a list of steps.
lessons.task: Using the formula dies = pi r^2 / A - pi d / sqrt(2A) and yield = e^(-DA), compute the number of good dies and cost per good die for a 50 mm^2 die on a 300 mm wafer costing 10,000 dollars with D = 0.1 per cm^2. Compare with the 100 mm^2 case in the lesson.

quiz.q: In photolithography, what does the mask do?
options: Carries the pattern so light exposes only selected areas of the resist
quiz.explain: Light shines through the mask's pattern onto photoresist, defining where etching or implanting happens.

quiz.q: Why is the source/drain implant called self-aligned?
options: The gate itself blocks the implant, so source and drain line up with the gate edges
It needs no mask at all for any layer
quiz.explain: Implanting after the gate is formed uses the gate as a mask, guaranteeing perfect alignment.

quiz.q: With defect density 0.1 per cm^2 and a 1 cm^2 die, the Poisson yield is about:
What does a node name like 5 nm mean today?
options: The gate length is exactly 5 nm
It is mainly a label for a process generation, not a literal feature size
The metal wires are 5 nm wide
quiz.explain: Node names became marketing labels; compare processes using density and pitch figures.

quiz.q: Which part of the process builds the metal interconnect layers?
quiz.explain: BEOL adds insulators, vias and metal wiring above the transistors.

lessons.title: Layout and Design Rules: Drawing the Masks
lessons.content:
Imagine an architect planning a new building in Uttara. The client describes the rooms they want, but the builder needs exact drawings: where every wall stands, how thick it is, where every pipe runs. The city also has rules: buildings must be a minimum distance from the road, stairs must be at least a certain width. A chip layout is that exact drawing, and design rules are the city code. Layout is the set of coloured polygons, one colour per mask layer, that the factory uses to make the masks you met in lesson 7. This lesson teaches you to read and draw layout, why the rules exist, and how designers keep billions of shapes correct.

Why layout matters: The transistor circuit only says which transistors connect to which. The layout decides how big the chip is, how long the wires are, how much capacitance each node has and therefore how fast and power-hungry the chip is. A clever layout can be noticeably smaller and faster than a careless one with the same circuit. In standard-cell design, cell layouts are drawn once by experts and reused millions of times, so every square nanometre saved is multiplied across the chip.

The layers: A basic CMOS layout uses a handful of layers. N-well marks where pMOS transistors live. Active, also called diffusion, marks where transistors and their source and drain regions are; it is split by select layers into n+ regions for nMOS and p+ regions for pMOS. Polysilicon, or poly, is the gate material. Contact connects metal 1 to active or poly. Metal 1, metal 2 and higher layers are the wires, and via layers connect one metal layer to the next. Each layer gets its own colour in layout editors, for example green for active, red for poly, blue for metal 1.

Where a transistor appears: In layout, a transistor is simply where a poly line crosses an active region. The poly over the active becomes the gate, and the active on either side becomes the source and drain. The width of the active strip under the poly is the transistor width W, and the width of the poly line is the channel length L. So to make a wider transistor, draw a wider active strip; to use minimum length, draw the poly at its minimum width. This is why one simple rectangle crossing gives you a MOSFET.

Why design rules exist: Fabrication is not perfect. Lithography blurs edges, layers misalign slightly, and etching may eat a little more or less than intended. Design rules are the minimum widths, spacings and overlaps that guarantee the chip works despite these imperfections. If two metal wires are too close, they may short. If a poly line is too thin, it may break. If poly does not extend far enough past the active edge, the gate might not fully cut the channel, leaving a leaky path from source to drain. If a contact is not surrounded by enough metal, misalignment could leave it half-connected.

Kinds of rules: Width rules give the minimum width of shapes on one layer. Spacing rules give the minimum gap between shapes on the same layer or on different layers. Enclosure or overlap rules say how much one layer must surround another, like metal around a contact. Extension rules say how far poly must stick out beyond active. Modern processes add many more: density rules, requiring a certain percentage of metal in every window so CMP polishes evenly; antenna rules, limiting how much metal can connect to a gate during manufacturing, because charge collected during plasma etching can damage thin gate oxide; and many special rules for multi-patterning and EUV layers.

Lambda rules: In the 1980s, Mead and Conway proposed expressing all rules as multiples of one unit called lambda, roughly half the minimum feature size. The minimum transistor length is then 2 lambda. A typical lambda rule set says something like: poly width at least 2 lambda, metal 1 width at least 3 lambda and spacing at least 3 lambda, poly extends at least 2 lambda past active, contacts are 2 by 2 lambda. Exact values differ between rule sets, so always use the one given. The beauty of lambda rules is scalability: draw a layout once and shrink it to a new process by changing the value of lambda. For example, with lambda = 0.3 micrometres, the metal spacing of 3 lambda is 0.9 micrometres.

Micron rules: Real modern processes do not scale perfectly, because different layers shrink differently. So foundries give rules in absolute units, micrometres or nanometres, for each layer, in a design rule manual that can be hundreds of pages long. Lambda rules are still excellent for learning and for quick estimates, and university courses use them; industry uses the foundry's micron rules inside a process design kit, PDK.

Stick diagrams: Before drawing exact polygons, designers sketch a stick diagram: each layer is a coloured line, with no widths, showing only the relative positions and connections. Typically VDD rail runs along the top, ground along the bottom, the pMOS active strip near the top, the nMOS active strip near the bottom, and vertical poly lines for each input crossing both strips. A stick diagram lets you plan the order of transistors and the wiring before worrying about exact sizes.

Euler paths: For compact layout, we want each active strip to be one unbroken row of transistors, with neighbouring transistors sharing a source or drain region. That is possible if we can order the inputs so that, in the graph of the pull-down network and also in the graph of the pull-up network, there is a path that uses every transistor edge exactly once, in the same order. Such a path is an Euler path. Example: Y = NOT(A AND B OR C). PDN: A and B in series between Y and ground, C in parallel from Y to ground. PUN: A and B in parallel from VDD to a middle node, then C in series to Y. Try the order A, B, C. In the PDN: Y through A to the middle node, through B to ground, through C back to Y. In the PUN: from the middle node through A to VDD, through B back to the middle node, through C to Y. Both work, so three vertical poly lines in the order A, B, C cross unbroken nMOS and pMOS strips. Without an Euler path, the strip must be broken, wasting space.

The standard-cell template: Standard cells follow a strict template so they can sit side by side in rows. Every cell has the same height, often measured in metal tracks, for example 9 or 12 tracks. VDD runs as a horizontal metal 1 rail along the top edge and ground along the bottom edge, so when cells sit next to each other their rails join automatically. The n-well covers the top half, so pMOS transistors go on top and nMOS at the bottom. Rows are often flipped alternately so neighbouring rows can share a rail. Cell widths are multiples of a placement grid, and input and output pins sit on the routing grid so the router can reach them.

Walk-through, an inverter cell: Draw the VDD rail at the top and the ground rail at the bottom in metal 1. Draw an n-well over the top half. Inside it, draw a p+ active rectangle for the pMOS; at the bottom, an n+ active rectangle for the nMOS. Draw one vertical poly line crossing both: that is input A, and where it crosses each active you get the two transistors. Contact the left side of the pMOS active up to VDD and the left side of the nMOS active down to ground. Contact the right sides of both actives and join them with a vertical metal 1 strip: that is output Y. Add a contact from the poly to a metal 1 pin for input A. Finally, add well and substrate tap contacts so the n-well connects to VDD and the p-substrate to ground. A NAND2 is the same with two poly lines, the nMOS strip shared in series, and the pMOS strip with the output in the middle and VDD contacts on both ends, making the two pMOS parallel.

Verification: DRC, extraction and LVS: Humans make mistakes and chips have billions of shapes, so software checks everything. Design rule check, DRC, scans every polygon against every rule and flags violations. Layout versus schematic, LVS, extracts the transistors and connections from the layout and compares them with the intended schematic or netlist; a missing contact or a short between two nets is caught here. Parasitic extraction computes the resistance and capacitance of every wire, which feeds timing analysis. A chip is not sent to the factory until DRC and LVS are clean.

Real-life example 1, the RAJUK building code: Dhaka's building rules set minimum setbacks from the road, minimum gaps between buildings, and limits on height. An inspector checks the plan before approval. Design rules are the same kind of code, written by the foundry, and DRC is the inspector who checks every corner of every shape. Breaking a building rule might cause a fire hazard; breaking a design rule might cause a short circuit that kills the chip.

Real-life example 2, packing a bazaar lane: In a crowded market lane, shops of equal depth stand side by side, sharing walls, with a common drain along the back and a common path in front. Standard cells are the same: equal height, shared power rails like the common drain, and shared source and drain regions between neighbouring transistors like shared walls. This uniformity is what lets software place millions of cells automatically.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up W and L in layout: W is the active width under the poly, L is the poly width. Many forget well and substrate taps, which are needed to bias the bodies and prevent latch-up. Some forget that contacts cannot be placed on the gate over active in classic rule sets. Others try to share diffusion without checking for an Euler path. Exam questions: list the layers and their purpose; state typical lambda rules and why each exists; draw a stick diagram or layout of an inverter, NAND2 or NOR2; find an Euler path for a given function; explain DRC, LVS and extraction; compare lambda and micron rules.

Recap: Layout is the set of polygons on each mask layer; a transistor appears where poly crosses active, with W set by the active width and L by the poly width. Design rules, widths, spacings, enclosures and extensions, protect against fabrication imperfections. Lambda rules scale nicely and suit learning; real foundries use micron rules in a PDK. Stick diagrams plan topology, Euler paths allow unbroken diffusion strips, and standard cells follow a fixed-height template with shared rails. DRC, LVS and extraction check everything before tape-out. Next, we turn those shapes into numbers: the resistance and capacitance that set speed.
key_points: Layout is coloured polygons per mask layer: n-well, active, select, poly, contact, metals and vias.
A transistor is where poly crosses active: W = active width under the gate, L = poly width.
Design rules (width, spacing, enclosure, extension, density, antenna) protect against fabrication imperfections.
Lambda rules express everything in units of lambda (min length 2 lambda) and scale; foundries use micron rules in a PDK.
Stick diagrams plan topology; an Euler path common to PDN and PUN gives unbroken diffusion strips.
Standard cells: fixed height, VDD rail on top, ground at bottom, n-well on top half, pins on a grid.
DRC checks rules, LVS compares layout to schematic, extraction gives R and C for timing.
lessons.tip: Free layout tools such as Magic or KLayout let you draw an inverter with real layers. Ten minutes of drawing and running DRC teaches more than an hour of reading rule tables.

They remove the need for DRC

quiz.explain: A fixed height with rails at fixed positions lets placement tools butt cells together in rows.

lessons.title: Resistance and Capacitance: The RC View of a Chip
lessons.content:
Imagine filling a row of buckets using a garden hose. The buckets are capacitors: they store water, like charge. The hose is a resistor: a thin or long hose slows the flow. How long it takes to fill all the buckets depends on two things only, how hard it is to push water through the hose and how much water the buckets hold. A digital chip is exactly this game played billions of times per second. Every gate output must fill or empty the capacitance of the wires and gates it drives, through the resistance of its transistors and the wires. This lesson teaches you to estimate those resistances and capacitances and to combine them into a delay with the Elmore formula.

Why RC thinking is the key to speed: In lesson 3 we had exact current equations, but nobody solves those by hand for a million gates. Designers instead replace each ON transistor with a resistor and each node with a capacitor, then use simple RC formulas. These estimates are accurate enough to compare designs, size transistors and find slow paths. Timing tools use more detailed versions of the same idea. Lessons 10, 11, 14 and 17 all build on this lesson.

Wire resistance and sheet resistance: A wire's resistance is R = rho L / (t W), where rho is the material's resistivity, L the length, W the width and t the thickness. On a chip, the thickness of each layer is fixed by the process, so we combine rho / t into one number called the sheet resistance, Rs, measured in ohms per square. Then R = Rs x (L / W). The ratio L / W is the number of squares: a wire 10 units long and 1 unit wide is 10 squares, whatever the units. A square of any size has the same resistance, because doubling both length and width cancels out.

Worked example, a long wire: Take a metal wire with Rs = 0.08 ohms per square, 1,000 micrometres long and 0.1 micrometres wide. Squares = 1,000 / 0.1 = 10,000. R = 10,000 x 0.08 = 800 ohms. That is surprisingly large for a piece of metal one millimetre long, and it is why long wires on modern chips are slow. Thin lower metal layers have higher sheet resistance than thick upper layers, so long wires are routed on upper layers when possible.

Other resistances: Polysilicon has a much higher sheet resistance than metal, even with a silicide layer on top to lower it, so poly is used only for short connections such as gates, never for long wires. Diffusion also has relatively high resistance. Each contact and via adds resistance too, from a few ohms to tens of ohms depending on the layer; designers place several vias in parallel on important nets to lower resistance and improve reliability.

Gate capacitance: The transistor gate sits on thin oxide over the channel, forming a parallel plate capacitor: C = Cox x W x L, where Cox is the oxide capacitance per unit area. Since designers usually keep L at minimum, gate capacitance is proportional to width. A handy rule is to describe it as a capacitance per micrometre of width, roughly on the order of 1 femtofarad per micrometre in many processes; treat this as an illustrative number and use your process data in practice. For the RC model we simply say: a transistor of width k has gate capacitance kC, where C is the gate capacitance of a unit transistor.

Diffusion capacitance: The source and drain regions form reverse-biased junctions with the body, and these junctions also have capacitance, both along their bottom area and around their edges. This parasitic capacitance appears at every gate output. In the simple RC model from Weste and Harris, the diffusion capacitance of a transistor's source or drain is taken as about equal to its gate capacitance, also proportional to width. Sharing a diffusion between two series transistors, as in the Euler-path layouts of lesson 8, reduces it.

Wire capacitance: A wire couples to the substrate and to layers below and above it, like a parallel plate, plus fringing fields from its edges, plus coupling to neighbouring wires on the same layer. In modern processes, coupling to neighbours is a large part of the total because wires are tall and close together. A typical rough figure for a minimum-pitch wire is around 0.2 femtofarads per micrometre, which is the number we use in examples. So the 1,000 micrometre wire above has about 200 fF. Lesson 14 treats coupling and crosstalk in more depth.

The effective resistance of a transistor: An ON transistor does not have one fixed resistance, because its current depends on its voltages. But for delay estimates we can define an effective resistance that gives the right average behaviour. Call the effective resistance of a unit-width nMOS R. A transistor k times wider has resistance R / k, because it carries k times more current. A pMOS of the same width has about 2R, because hole mobility is about half. So a pMOS of width 2 has resistance about R, matching a unit nMOS. That is why the unit inverter is drawn with nMOS width 1 and pMOS width 2: both pull with resistance R.

The RC model of a gate: Now replace every gate with a circuit: a switch in series with its effective resistance from the output to VDD or ground, the parasitic diffusion capacitance at the output, and gate capacitance at each input. For a unit inverter with nMOS width 1 and pMOS width 2: input capacitance 3C, output diffusion capacitance about 3C, pull-down resistance R, pull-up resistance R. For a NAND2 sized for equal drive (nMOS width 2 in series, pMOS width 2 in parallel): each input sees 4C, and the two series nMOS each have R / 2, adding to R. This is how we will compute delays in the next two lessons.

Lumped RC delay: If a resistor R charges a single capacitor C from 0 to VDD, the voltage rises as 1 - e to the power minus t / RC. The time to reach 50 percent is ln 2 x RC, about 0.69 RC. So a gate with resistance 1 kilo-ohm driving 20 fF takes about 0.69 x 20 ps, about 14 ps to cross the midpoint. Many textbooks simply use RC as the delay estimate, because the constant factor is the same for every gate and cancels when you compare designs.

The Elmore delay: Real paths are chains of resistors and capacitors, for example a transistor driving a wire that has resistance and capacitance along its length. The Elmore delay is a simple, surprisingly good estimate for any RC tree. Rule: for each capacitor, multiply its capacitance by the total resistance of the path from the driver to that capacitor, shared with the path to the output; then add them all. For a simple chain, each capacitor is multiplied by the sum of all resistors between the source and that capacitor.

Worked example, two-stage chain: A driver with R1 = 1 kilo-ohm charges node 1 with C1 = 10 fF, then through R2 = 2 kilo-ohms charges node 2 with C2 = 20 fF. Elmore delay at node 2 = R1 x C1 + (R1 + R2) x C2 = 1k x 10f + 3k x 20f = 10 ps + 60 ps = 70 ps. Notice that C2 sees both resistors, so far-away capacitance costs more. Another example: a ladder of three equal sections, each R = 1 kilo-ohm and C = 10 fF. Delay at the end = R x C + 2R x C + 3R x C = 6RC = 60 ps.

Distributed wires: A long wire has resistance and capacitance spread evenly along it. Cut it into N tiny sections and apply Elmore: the sum is R x C x (1 + 2 + ... + N) / N squared, which approaches RC / 2 as N grows. So the Elmore delay of a distributed wire is half its total RC. The more exact 50 percent delay of a distributed line is about 0.38 RC, compared with 0.69 RC for a lumped one. For our 800 ohm, 200 fF wire: RC = 160 ps; Elmore gives 80 ps; the 50 percent delay is about 61 ps; a lumped model would wrongly give about 110 ps. Key fact: R and C both grow with length, so wire delay grows with length squared. Doubling the wire length quadruples its delay. Lesson 14 shows how repeaters fix this.

Real-life example 1, filling water bottles at a mosque tap: Picture a long row of people with bottles waiting along a pipe from the tank. The people near the tank fill quickly, those at the far end wait longest, because water must pass through the whole pipe to reach them, and the pipe also feeds everyone before them. That is the Elmore idea: far capacitance is multiplied by more resistance. And if the pipe were twice as long with twice as many people, the last person waits about four times as long, the length-squared effect.

Real-life example 2, why your phone processor uses thick top metals: Chip designers route the clock, power and long buses on the thickest upper metal layers, which have the lowest sheet resistance, and keep short local connections on thin lower layers. They also widen important wires and stack multiple vias. All these choices come straight from the formulas in this lesson: lower R, controlled C, smaller RC.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget that sheet resistance is per square, not per unit length, and multiply by length only. Others treat a distributed wire as a lumped RC and overestimate delay. Many forget that pMOS resistance is about twice nMOS for the same width. In Elmore calculations, a frequent error is multiplying each capacitor only by its own nearest resistor. Exam questions: compute wire resistance from sheet resistance; compute gate and wire capacitance; build the RC model of an inverter or NAND; compute the Elmore delay of an RC chain or tree; explain why wire delay grows with length squared.

Recap: Wire resistance is Rs times the number of squares, so a 1 mm long, 0.1 micrometre wide wire at 0.08 ohms per square is 800 ohms. Gate and diffusion capacitances scale with transistor width; wires have around 0.2 fF per micrometre. An ON transistor is modelled as an effective resistance R / k for width k, with pMOS about twice nMOS. Lumped RC gives 0.69 RC to 50 percent; the Elmore delay sums each capacitance times its upstream resistance (70 ps in our chain); distributed wires give RC / 2 by Elmore and 0.38 RC more exactly, growing with length squared. Next, we use this model to measure gate delay in a clean unit called tau.
key_points: Wire R = Rs x (L/W); 1,000 um x 0.1 um at 0.08 ohm/square = 800 ohms.
Gate capacitance = Cox W L, proportional to width; diffusion capacitance is roughly similar per unit width.
Wire capacitance about 0.2 fF/um (illustrative); coupling to neighbours is a large share.
Effective resistance: unit nMOS R, width k gives R/k, pMOS of the same width about 2R.
Lumped RC: 50 percent delay = 0.69 RC.
Elmore delay = sum of each C times the resistance from the source to it; example 70 ps.
Distributed wire: Elmore RC/2, true 50 percent about 0.38 RC; delay grows with length squared.
lessons.tip: In every Elmore problem, draw the RC chain first and write the upstream resistance next to each capacitor. Then the answer is just a sum of products and you will not miss a term.

lessons.title: Gate Delay: Tau, Parasitic Delay and the FO4 Inverter
lessons.content:
Think of a relay race at a school sports day in Dhaka. Each runner takes some time to run their part, and also some time to hand over the baton. A strong runner carrying a light baton is fast; a weak runner carrying a heavy load is slow; and if one runner must hand batons to four teammates at once, the handover takes longer. A chain of logic gates is a relay race of signals. Each gate's delay depends on how strong it is, how much it has to drive, and its own internal baggage. This lesson turns the RC model of lesson 9 into a simple, powerful way of measuring gate delay in units that do not depend on the process.

Why measure delay this way: The clock speed of a chip is set by its slowest path of gates, the critical path. To design fast circuits, you must estimate how long each gate takes, choose sizes, and compare alternatives quickly. Absolute picoseconds change from one process to the next, but ratios stay similar. So designers express delays in a process-independent unit, tau, and in FO4 inverter delays. This also lets you compare designs from different generations fairly.

Definitions of delay: When an input switches, the output responds after a while. Propagation delay, tpd, is the maximum time from the input crossing 50 percent of VDD to the output crossing 50 percent. Contamination delay, tcd, is the minimum time from an input change until the output starts to change; it matters for hold-time checks in lesson 16. Rise time and fall time, often called slew, describe how long the output takes to go from 20 to 80 percent of VDD or 80 to 20 percent. We often separate rising and falling propagation delay, tpdr and tpdf, because pull-up and pull-down strengths can differ.

The inverter's RC delay: Take the unit inverter of lesson 9: nMOS width 1, pMOS width 2, each pulling with effective resistance R. Its input capacitance is 3C, and its output has parasitic diffusion capacitance of about 3C. Let it drive h identical inverters, a load of 3hC. The output node then has 3C + 3hC, charged through R. Using RC as the delay estimate, delay = R x (3C + 3hC) = 3RC x (1 + h).

The unit tau: Notice the factor 3RC. It is the delay of an ideal inverter driving another identical inverter with no parasitic capacitance. Call it tau. Then the inverter's delay is d = h + 1 in units of tau. The h part is the effort delay, which grows with the load. The 1 is the parasitic delay p, caused by the gate's own output capacitance; it does not depend on what the gate drives. Tau depends on the process; in modern processes it is a few picoseconds. For our examples, say tau = 3 ps, an illustrative number.

Fanout: The ratio h of output load capacitance to the gate's own input capacitance is called the electrical effort, or simply fanout when the load is identical gates. An inverter driving one copy of itself has h = 1 and delay 2 tau. Driving four copies, h = 4, delay 5 tau.

The FO4 inverter delay: An inverter driving four identical inverters is a common benchmark: the fanout-of-4 or FO4 delay, equal to 5 tau in this model. Why four? It is a realistic, well-balanced load, close to the stage effort that gives minimum delay in long chains, as lesson 11 shows. Designers often describe a processor's clock cycle in FO4 delays: a highly pipelined design might have a cycle of only around 10 to 20 FO4, while a simple low-power design might have many more. With tau = 3 ps, FO4 = 15 ps, so a cycle of 20 FO4 is 300 ps, about 3.3 GHz. Expressing cycles in FO4 lets you compare designs across processes.

Other gates: NAND2: Size the NAND2 for equal drive: nMOS width 2 each in series, pMOS width 2 each in parallel. Each input sees 4C, compared with 3C for the inverter. The output has diffusion capacitance from two pMOS of width 2 and one nMOS of width 2, about 6C. Pulling with resistance R, parasitic delay = 6RC / 3RC = 2 tau. If a NAND2 drives h copies of itself, the load is 4hC, so effort delay = R x 4hC / 3RC = (4/3) h. Total d = (4/3) h + 2. For h = 4, d = 5.33 + 2 = 7.33 tau, versus 5 tau for an inverter. NAND gates are slower than inverters at the same fanout, and the next lesson captures this with the logical effort g = 4/3.

The internal node: A more careful Elmore analysis of the NAND2 falling transition includes the internal node between the two series nMOS. Its capacitance is charged through only the lower nMOS, which adds a little delay, depending on which input switches last. That is why input ordering, from lesson 5, matters: putting the latest-arriving signal on the transistor nearest the output avoids discharging the internal node at the last moment.

The effect of sizing: Suppose you make a gate k times bigger, every transistor k times wider. Its resistance drops to R / k, its parasitic capacitance grows by k, so its parasitic delay stays the same. Its input capacitance grows by k, so the gate driving it now sees k times more load. Upsizing a gate helps it drive a big load but slows down the gate before it. This tension is the heart of transistor sizing, solved neatly by logical effort in lesson 11.

Stacks and fan-in: Gates with many series transistors are slow for three reasons: each series transistor must be wider, raising input capacitance; the output and internal nodes have more diffusion capacitance; and body effect raises the thresholds of upper transistors. Parasitic delay grows roughly with the number of inputs, so a NAND4 has about twice the parasitic delay of a NAND2. Breaking wide gates into trees of smaller gates often reduces delay.

Input slew matters too: The simple model assumes the input switches instantly. In reality, a slowly rising input turns the pull-down on gradually, so the gate's delay grows with the input transition time, and both transistors conduct for longer, adding short-circuit power. A gate with a slow output edge therefore also slows down every gate it drives. This is why timing tools carry slew along with arrival time through every path, and why libraries limit the maximum transition allowed on any net, inserting buffers when a net is too heavily loaded.

The ring oscillator: How do factories measure gate delay? They build a ring oscillator: an odd number N of inverters connected in a loop. The signal chases itself around the ring and the output oscillates with period 2 x N x tpd, because a full cycle needs the signal to travel around twice, once for each edge. Example: 31 stages with tpd = 15 ps gives a period of 2 x 31 x 15 = 930 ps, a frequency of about 1.08 GHz. Measuring this frequency on a test chip gives the gate delay directly, and ring oscillators are used to monitor process speed on production wafers.

Delay versus supply voltage: A gate's delay is roughly C x VDD / I, the charge to move divided by the current. With the alpha-power model, I is proportional to (VDD - Vt) to the power alpha. Lowering VDD reduces I much faster than it reduces the charge, so delay rises. Example with Vt = 0.3 V and alpha = 1.3: going from VDD = 1.0 V to 0.8 V multiplies delay by (0.8 / 1.0) x (0.7 / 0.5) to the power 1.3, about 1.24. So a 20 percent lower voltage gives roughly 24 percent more delay, while dynamic power falls by about 36 percent (lesson 12). As VDD approaches Vt, delay grows dramatically.

Temperature and process corners: Higher temperature reduces carrier mobility, slowing transistors, but also lowers Vt, speeding them up. At normal supply voltages the mobility effect usually wins, so hot chips are slower; at very low voltages the opposite can happen, called temperature inversion. Manufacturing variation means some chips have fast transistors and some slow ones. Designers check timing at corners like SS (slow nMOS, slow pMOS), TT (typical) and FF (fast), combined with voltage and temperature extremes. The chip must meet timing at the slow corner and hold timing at the fast corner.

Real-life example 1, a wedding feast queue: At a big biye bari in Dhaka, one server carries a pot of biryani to a table of four guests. Serving one plate is quick; serving four takes longer, the effort delay. But even before serving, the server spends some fixed time picking up the pot and walking to the table, the parasitic delay, which does not depend on how many guests are waiting. A stronger server is faster, but a stronger server also needs a bigger pot handed to them by the cook, slowing the cook. That is the sizing trade-off.

Real-life example 2, clock speed claims: When a phone maker says its processor runs at 3 GHz, the cycle is about 333 ps. If tau were 3 ps, that is about 22 FO4 delays per cycle, and every pipeline stage must fit its logic, flip-flop overhead and clock skew into that budget. When engineers say a design has 16 FO4 per stage, everyone in the industry understands how aggressive it is, regardless of the process node.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think upsizing a gate always makes the circuit faster; it can slow down the previous stage. Some forget the parasitic delay and compute delay as just h. Others confuse propagation delay with contamination delay, or think delay depends only on the number of gates in a path. Exam questions: define tpd, tcd, rise and fall time; derive the inverter delay d = h + 1 in tau; compute FO4 delay; compute NAND2 delay for a given fanout; compute ring oscillator frequency; explain how VDD and temperature affect delay; explain process corners.

Recap: Delay is measured from 50 percent input to 50 percent output. With the RC model, tau = 3RC is the delay of an ideal inverter driving its twin. A gate's delay is d = effort delay + parasitic delay; for the inverter, d = h + 1, so FO4 = 5 tau, about 15 ps if tau = 3 ps. A NAND2 driving h copies has d = (4/3)h + 2, 7.33 tau at h = 4. Upsizing keeps parasitic delay but loads the previous stage. A ring oscillator of 31 stages at 15 ps oscillates near 1.08 GHz. Lower VDD and higher temperature usually slow gates, and designs are checked at process corners. Next, logical effort turns these ideas into a method for sizing whole paths.
key_points: tpd: 50 percent input to 50 percent output (max); tcd: minimum time before output starts changing.
tau = 3RC, the delay of an ideal inverter driving an identical one.
Gate delay d = gh + p; inverter: d = h + 1; FO4 inverter delay = 5 tau (about 15 ps if tau = 3 ps).
NAND2 driving h copies: d = (4/3)h + 2, e.g. 7.33 tau at h = 4.
Upsizing a gate keeps its parasitic delay but loads the gate before it.
Ring oscillator period = 2 N tpd; 31 stages at 15 ps gives about 1.08 GHz.
Lower VDD raises delay (1.0 to 0.8 V gives about 1.24x here); designs are checked at SS/TT/FF corners.
lessons.tip: Memorise one anchor: FO4 = 5 tau. Whenever you see a delay in tau, divide by 5 to get FO4 and you will instantly feel whether a path is short or long.

quiz.explain: d = h + p = 4 + 1 = 5 tau.

A ring oscillator has 21 inverters, each with tpd = 20 ps. Its period is:

quiz.explain: Resistance halves but output capacitance doubles, so their product, the parasitic delay, stays constant.

lessons.title: Logical Effort: Sizing a Path for Minimum Delay
lessons.content:
Imagine you need to move a very heavy almirah up to the fifth floor of a Dhaka building. One person cannot lift it at all. If you hire a giant, he is too expensive and too slow to arrive. The smart way is a team in stages: a few people lift it to the first landing, more join for the next, and the strongest group carries it the last bit. Each stage should do a similar share of the work. Driving a big electrical load through a chain of gates is the same problem, and logical effort is the elegant method, invented by Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull, that tells you how many stages to use and how big each gate should be.

Why logical effort is needed: In lesson 10 you saw that making a gate bigger helps it drive its load but slows down the gate before it. With a long path of different gates, trying every combination of sizes by simulation is slow and gives no insight. Logical effort gives a pencil-and-paper answer: the best possible delay of a path, the best number of stages, and the size of every gate, in a few lines of arithmetic. It also explains why some circuit structures are inherently faster than others.

The delay equation: From lesson 10, the delay of any gate, in units of tau, is d = f + p, where p is the parasitic delay and f is the stage effort. The stage effort itself splits into two factors: f = g x h. Here h is the electrical effort, output capacitance divided by input capacitance, which says how big the load is relative to the gate. And g is the logical effort, which says how much worse this kind of gate is at driving current than an inverter with the same input capacitance. So d = g h + p.

What logical effort means: Logical effort g is the ratio of a gate's input capacitance to the input capacitance of an inverter that can deliver the same output current. An inverter has g = 1 by definition. A NAND2 sized for equal drive has 4C per input versus 3C for the inverter, so g = 4/3. A NOR2 has 5C per input, so g = 5/3. More generally, an n-input NAND has g = (n + 2) / 3 and an n-input NOR has g = (2n + 1) / 3, so NAND3 is 5/3 and NOR3 is 7/3. Logical effort depends only on the topology of the gate, not on its size. It captures the cost of computing a logic function rather than just inverting.

Parasitic delays: Using the same model, the inverter has p = 1, NAND2 and NOR2 have p = 2, and an n-input NAND or NOR has p of about n. Notice that NOR is worse than NAND in g but the same in p in this simple model.

From one gate to a path: Now consider a path of N stages. Define path logical effort G as the product of all the g values. Define path electrical effort H as the load capacitance at the end divided by the input capacitance of the first gate. If the path has branches, where a gate's output also drives gates off the path, define branching effort b at each stage as (on-path capacitance + off-path capacitance) / on-path capacitance, and B as the product of all b. Then path effort F = G x B x H. Path parasitic delay P is the sum of the p values.

The key result: The total path delay is D = sum of (g h) + P. It can be proven that D is smallest when every stage has the same stage effort. That best stage effort is f-hat = F to the power 1/N, the Nth root of the path effort. The minimum delay is then D = N x F to the power 1/N + P. This is the almirah rule: share the work equally among the stages.

Worked example, sizing a 3-stage path: A path consists of an inverter, then a NAND2, then an inverter, driving a load 64 times bigger than the input capacitance of the first inverter. No branching. G = 1 x 4/3 x 1 = 4/3. H = 64. B = 1. F = 4/3 x 64 = 85.3. With N = 3, f-hat = cube root of 85.3, about 4.40. P = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. D = 3 x 4.40 + 4 = 17.2 tau.

Finding the sizes: Now work backwards from the load. Each gate's input capacitance must be Cin = g x Cout / f-hat. Last inverter: Cin = 1 x 64 / 4.40, about 14.5 units. NAND2: Cin = 4/3 x 14.5 / 4.40, about 4.4 units. First inverter: Cin = 1 x 4.4 / 4.40 = 1 unit, which matches the given input capacitance, a good check that the arithmetic is right. So the gates grow by a factor of roughly 4.4 in effort per stage, and the NAND2, which has g = 4/3, is a little smaller than a pure geometric progression would suggest.

Reading the answer in real time: Our 17.2 tau path is about 3.4 FO4 delays, since one FO4 is 5 tau. If tau were 3 ps, that is about 52 ps. Now compare with a careless design where all three gates are minimum size: the last inverter would have h = 64 alone, giving a delay of 64 + 1 = 65 tau in that stage, roughly four times the optimised total. The difference between a sized and an unsized path is often this dramatic, which is why sizing is one of the first things a timing tool does after synthesis.

How many stages: Adding inverters changes N without changing the logic, if you add them in pairs or adjust the polarity. Which N is best? Solving for the minimum of N x F to the power 1/N + N x p_inv gives a best stage effort of about 3.6 when the inverter parasitic is 1, and in practice a stage effort of about 4 is a good rule. So the best number of stages is roughly log base 4 of F. For our example, log4 of 85.3 is about 3.2, so 3 stages is right. The delay curve is also flat near the optimum: stage efforts anywhere from about 2.4 to 6 give delays within about 15 percent of the best, so you do not need to be exact.

Worked example, driving a big load: An inverter must drive a load 1,000 times its input capacitance, for example a long clock wire or an off-chip pad. With one inverter, D = 1,000 + 1 = 1,001 tau. With 3 inverters, f = 10, D = 30 + 3 = 33 tau. With 5 inverters, log4 of 1,000 is about 5, f = 3.98, D = 19.9 + 5 = 24.9 tau. With 7 inverters, f = 2.68, D = 18.8 + 7 = 25.8 tau. Five stages is best, and the improvement from 1 stage to 5 is about 40 times. This chain of growing inverters is called a buffer tree or tapered buffer, and it is how chips drive large loads.

Branching example: Suppose a NAND2 output drives the next gate on the critical path and also an identical gate on another path. Half of its output current goes off-path, so b = 2 at that stage. This doubles the path effort, and the only way to recover is to make gates bigger. Branching is why signals that fan out widely, like select lines and enables, are slow and are often buffered separately.

Comparing structures with logical effort: Logical effort also tells you which design is fundamentally faster. For example, an 8-input AND can be built as a NAND8 followed by an inverter, or as NAND4, NOR2 and so on, or as NAND2, NOR2, NAND2, inverter. Compute G and P for each, combine with the given H, and the minimum D shows the winner. For large H, trees of small gates usually win because they allow more stages with modest logical effort, while a single big gate has huge g and p. This is a classic exam problem.

Limitations: Logical effort assumes simple RC models, ignores wire capacitance unless added to the load, treats rising and falling delays as averaged, and assumes gates can be sized continuously, while real libraries offer only discrete sizes like X1, X2, X4. It also does not handle interconnect-dominated paths well; for long wires, lesson 14's repeater analysis is better. Still, logical effort is the fastest way to reason about gate-dominated paths and is used by experienced designers to sanity-check synthesis results.

Real-life example 1, moving furniture up stairs: Back to the almirah. If one stage does almost everything and the others barely help, the slow stage dominates the time. If you use too many stages, the time spent handing over between groups, the parasitic delay, adds up. The best plan is a moderate number of stages, each carrying a similar share, exactly what F to the power 1/N says.

Real-life example 2, a chip's clock and enable signals: Inside a processor, one control signal such as a pipeline stall might need to reach thousands of flip-flops. The designers drive it through a tree of buffers whose sizes grow by roughly 4 at each level, the FO4 rule in action. Synthesis and timing tools use logic very close to logical effort when they insert and size buffers on high-fanout nets.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget the branching effort or compute H using the wrong reference capacitance. Some multiply the parasitic delays instead of adding them. Many forget that logical effort does not change with size. Another common error is computing sizes forward from the input instead of backward from the load. Exam questions: give the logical effort and parasitic delay of common gates; compute G, B, H, F, f-hat and D for a path; find the best number of stages; size each gate; compare two implementations of the same function; explain why the best stage effort is about 4.

Recap: Gate delay is d = gh + p. Logical effort g measures how much worse a gate is than an inverter: 1 for the inverter, 4/3 for NAND2, 5/3 for NOR2, (n + 2)/3 for NANDn, (2n + 1)/3 for NORn. Path effort F = GBH; minimum delay D = N F to the power 1/N + P, reached when every stage has the same effort. Our 3-stage example gave F = 85.3, f-hat = 4.4, D = 17.2 tau and input sizes 1, 4.4 and 14.5. The best number of stages is about log4 F, so driving a 1,000x load takes about 5 stages for 24.9 tau instead of 1,001 tau with one inverter. Next, we turn from speed to the other half of every design decision: power.
key_points: d = gh + p: g logical effort, h electrical effort (Cout/Cin), p parasitic delay.
g: inverter 1, NAND2 4/3, NOR2 5/3, NANDn (n+2)/3, NORn (2n+1)/3; p about n for n-input gates.
Path effort F = G x B x H; minimum D = N F^(1/N) + P when all stages share equal effort.
Example: inv-NAND2-inv, H = 64: F = 85.3, f = 4.4, D = 17.2 tau, input sizes 1, 4.4, 14.5.
Size backwards from the load: Cin = g Cout / f-hat.
Best number of stages is about log4 F; stage effort near 4 is good and the optimum is flat.
Driving a 1,000x load: 5 inverters give 24.9 tau versus 1,001 tau for one inverter.
lessons.tip: Write the logical effort recipe as a fixed ritual: G, B, H, then F, then N and f-hat, then D, then sizes from the back. Following the same order every time makes exam problems almost mechanical.
lessons.task: A path is NAND2 -> NOR2 -> inverter driving a load 100 times the first gate's input capacitance, no branching. Compute G, F, f-hat, P and the minimum delay D in tau, then find the input capacitance of each gate working backwards from the load.

quiz.q: What is the logical effort of a static CMOS NOR2 gate?
quiz.explain: Each input sees 1 + 4 = 5 units versus 3 for an inverter, so g = 5/3.

quiz.q: A path has G = 2, B = 1 and H = 32. What is the path effort F?
quiz.explain: F = G x B x H = 2 x 1 x 32 = 64.

quiz.q: For a 3-stage path with F = 64 and P = 5, what is the minimum delay?
About how many stages are best for a path effort of F = 256?
quiz.explain: log4(256) = 4, so about 4 stages each with effort near 4.

quiz.q: A gate drives one gate on the critical path and three identical gates off the path. The branching effort at that stage is:
quiz.explain: b = (on-path + off-path) / on-path = (1 + 3) / 1 = 4.

lessons.title: Power and Energy: Where a Chip's Watts Go
lessons.content:
Look at an electricity bill at home in Bangladesh. The fan, the fridge and the lights each add to it. Some appliances use power only when switched on and working, like an iron. Others quietly use a little all the time, like a TV on standby. A chip has the same two kinds of costs: power spent every time a signal switches, and power that leaks away even when nothing happens. In a phone, power decides battery life; in a laptop, how hot it gets on your lap; in a data centre, the electricity bill and the size of the cooling plant. This lesson explains where a chip's power goes and how to calculate it.

Why power became the main limit: For decades designers mostly chased speed. But around the mid-2000s, chips hit a power wall: making them faster by raising the clock meant more heat than a small package and fan could remove. Since then, power and energy efficiency have been first-class goals, often more important than raw speed. Every technique in lesson 13, and many architecture choices like multicore processors, exist because of the formulas in this lesson.

Power and energy are different: Power is the rate of using energy, measured in watts, joules per second. Energy is the total amount, measured in joules. A battery stores energy. If a task takes 2 seconds at 1 watt, it uses 2 joules. If a faster design does it in 1 second at 1.5 watts, it uses only 1.5 joules, less energy despite more power. For battery devices, energy per task usually matters most; for cooling, peak power and power density matter most.

The three components: A CMOS chip's power has three parts. Dynamic switching power: charging and discharging capacitances when signals change. Short-circuit power: the brief current through both pull-up and pull-down during a transition. Static or leakage power: current that flows even when nothing switches, through transistors that are supposed to be off and through thin gate oxides. In older processes, dynamic power dominated. In modern processes, leakage can be a substantial share, especially in chips that sit idle a lot.

Energy of one switching event: Consider a gate output with load capacitance C. When the output rises from 0 to VDD, the supply delivers charge Q = C x VDD at voltage VDD, so it supplies energy C x VDD squared. Half of that, one half C VDD squared, ends up stored in the capacitor; the other half is turned into heat in the pull-up transistor. When the output falls back to 0, the stored half is dumped as heat in the pull-down. So a full cycle, 0 to 1 and back to 0, costs C VDD squared, all ending as heat. Example: a 10 fF node at 1.0 V costs 10 femtojoules per full cycle. Tiny, but there are billions of nodes switching billions of times per second.

The dynamic power formula: Multiply by how often switching happens. If a node goes through a full 0 to 1 to 0 cycle with probability alpha in each clock cycle, the average dynamic power is P = alpha x C x VDD squared x f, where f is the clock frequency. Alpha is the activity factor. By the common convention, the clock signal itself has alpha = 1, since it rises and falls every cycle. A data signal can switch at most once per cycle, so its maximum alpha is 0.5; truly random data gives 0.25; and typical logic is often much lower, around 0.1 or less, because many signals do not change every cycle.

Worked example: A chip has a total switched capacitance of 1 nF across all its nodes, an average activity factor of 0.1, VDD = 1.0 V and f = 2 GHz. P = 0.1 x 1 nF x 1.0 squared x 2 GHz = 0.1 x 10 to the minus 9 x 2 x 10 to the 9 = 0.2 W. Now look at the knobs. Doubling f doubles power. Halving alpha halves power. But reducing VDD from 1.0 to 0.8 V multiplies power by 0.64, saving 36 percent, because of the square. Voltage is the strongest knob for dynamic power.

Glitches add hidden activity: The activity factor counts every transition, not just the final value. When inputs of a gate arrive at different times, its output may briefly flip and flip back before settling, a glitch. In a ripple-carry adder, for example, the high-order sum bits can toggle several times in one cycle as the carry ripples through. Each glitch charges and discharges capacitance and costs energy, even though the final answer is the same. Balancing path delays, so that inputs of a gate arrive together, and registering signals before they fan out widely, are standard ways to cut glitch power.

Short-circuit power: During a transition, while the input passes through the middle, both transistors conduct briefly and current flows straight from VDD to ground. Its size depends on how slow the input edges are compared with the output edges. With well-designed, roughly balanced edges, short-circuit power is usually a small fraction of dynamic power, often quoted as under about 10 percent. Slow input edges and very lightly loaded outputs make it worse. Keeping slews under control in timing analysis also keeps this term small.

Subthreshold leakage: From lesson 3, a transistor below threshold still conducts a small current that falls exponentially with lower VGS and rises exponentially with lower Vt. Every off transistor in a gate leaks a little. Example: if each of 1 billion transistors leaks 1 nanoamp on average at 1.0 V, leakage power is 10 to the 9 x 10 to the minus 9 x 1.0 = 1 W, even when the chip does nothing. Leakage also rises steeply with temperature, so a hot chip leaks more, which makes it hotter: a feedback loop that can lead to thermal runaway if cooling is poor.

Other leakage paths: Gate leakage is tunnelling current through very thin gate oxides; it grew rapidly as oxides thinned in the early 2000s and was tamed by high-k dielectrics. Junction leakage flows through the reverse-biased source and drain diodes. Gate-induced drain leakage appears at high drain-gate fields. For a designer, the key point is that static power is proportional to the number of transistors that are powered, their Vt, temperature and VDD.

The stack effect: Two off transistors in series leak much less than one, often several times less. The intermediate node rises a little, giving the upper transistor a negative VGS and a body effect that raise its effective threshold. This is why NAND gates with off stacks leak less in some input states, and designers sometimes force idle circuits into low-leakage input states.

Metrics: power-delay and energy-delay: Comparing designs by power alone is unfair, since a slower circuit can always use less power. The power-delay product, PDP, equals energy per operation. The energy-delay product, EDP, multiplies energy by delay, rewarding designs that are both efficient and fast. For example, design A takes 1 ns and 2 pJ per operation, EDP = 2 pJ-ns; design B takes 2 ns and 1.2 pJ, EDP = 2.4 pJ-ns. A is better by EDP, although B uses less energy. Which metric to use depends on the product: a sensor node cares about energy, a server about EDP or throughput per watt.

Power density and heat: A modern high-performance processor can dissipate around 100 W or more on a die of a few square centimetres. That heat must flow through the package to a heat sink and fan, or in a phone to the case. If heat cannot escape, temperature rises, leakage grows and transistors slow down. Phones therefore throttle, lowering clock and voltage when hot. You have seen this when a phone playing a heavy game for a long time gets warm and starts to lag.

Dark silicon: Since around the end of Dennard scaling (lesson 15), the number of transistors per chip kept rising faster than the power each transistor saved. As a result, not all transistors on a modern chip can switch at full speed at the same time without exceeding the power budget. Some areas must be idle or slower at any moment; researchers call this dark silicon. It pushed designers toward specialised accelerators, like image signal processors and neural engines, which do particular jobs with far less energy than a general CPU, and are switched on only when needed.

Real-life example 1, a phone battery: A phone battery of 4,000 mAh at about 3.85 V stores about 4 x 3.85 = 15.4 watt-hours. If the whole phone averages 1 W, the battery lasts roughly 15 hours. If a game pushes the processor to 4 W, the processor alone would drain it in under 4 hours. That is why chip designers fight for every milliwatt: lower alpha by not switching unneeded logic, lower VDD when speed is not needed, lower leakage by switching off idle blocks. These are exactly the techniques of lesson 13.

Real-life example 2, load-shedding and IPS: Many Dhaka homes use an IPS during load-shedding. People quickly learn which appliances drain it: a fan running continuously versus lights that are mostly off. A chip designer thinks the same way: which blocks switch constantly, like the clock network, and which leak quietly, like large caches. The clock network alone can be a large fraction of a chip's dynamic power because its activity factor is 1 and it reaches every flip-flop.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget that energy per full cycle is C VDD squared, not half, or think that the capacitor's stored energy is returned to the supply; in standard CMOS it is turned into heat. Many forget the activity factor or use alpha = 1 for data signals. Some think leakage is negligible in modern chips. Others confuse power with energy. Exam questions: derive the energy per transition; compute dynamic power for given alpha, C, V and f; compute savings from voltage scaling; explain the sources of leakage and their dependence on Vt and temperature; compare designs with PDP and EDP; explain the power wall and dark silicon.

Recap: Chip power has dynamic, short-circuit and leakage parts. A full 0 to 1 to 0 cycle of a node costs C VDD squared, all ending as heat. Dynamic power is alpha C VDD squared f; our example gave 0.2 W, and lowering VDD from 1.0 to 0.8 V saves 36 percent. Short-circuit power is small with good slews. Leakage grows exponentially with lower Vt and higher temperature; a billion transistors at 1 nA leak about 1 W. PDP measures energy per operation and EDP balances energy and speed. Power density limits clock speed and leads to throttling and dark silicon. Next, we learn the toolkit designers use to cut power.
key_points: Power = rate of energy use (W); energy = total (J); battery devices care about energy per task.
Three parts: dynamic switching, short-circuit, leakage (subthreshold, gate, junction).
A full 0-1-0 cycle of a node costs C VDD^2, all turned into heat.
Dynamic power P = alpha C VDD^2 f; example 0.1 x 1 nF x 1 V^2 x 2 GHz = 0.2 W.
Activity factor: clock 1, data at most 0.5, random data 0.25, typical logic about 0.1.
Leakage rises exponentially as Vt drops and temperature rises; 1e9 transistors x 1 nA x 1 V = 1 W.
PDP = energy per operation, EDP = energy x delay; power density leads to throttling and dark silicon.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a power question, first write P = alpha C V^2 f and mark which of the four factors the question is changing. Voltage changes are squared; the rest are linear.
lessons.task: Your phone battery capacity is printed in mAh (check settings or the box). Multiply by about 3.85 V and divide by 1,000 to get watt-hours. Estimate how many hours it would last at 0.5 W, 1 W and 3 W, and relate this to how a voltage drop from 1.0 V to 0.8 V would change processor dynamic power.

quiz.explain: The supply delivers Q = C VDD at voltage VDD; half is stored, half is lost as heat in the pull-up.

quiz.explain: The clock rises and falls every cycle, so alpha = 1.

lessons.title: Low-Power Design: Cutting Watts Without Losing the Plot
lessons.content:
Think of how a careful family runs a house during a hot summer with frequent load-shedding. They turn off lights in empty rooms. They run the fan at a lower speed at night when it is cooler. They unplug the TV instead of leaving it on standby. They use the IPS only for the most important things. Each trick is simple, but together they cut the bill a lot. Low-power chip design is the same family of habits applied to transistors: switch off what is not needed, slow down when speed is not needed, lower the voltage whenever possible, and choose leaky fast parts only where they matter.

Why low-power design matters: A phone, a smartwatch, a wireless earbud and an IoT sensor all live on batteries. Laptops and servers are limited by heat and electricity costs. From lesson 12 you know the formulas: dynamic power is alpha C VDD squared f, and leakage grows with lower Vt and higher temperature. Every low-power technique attacks one of these terms: alpha (switch less), C (smaller or fewer capacitances), VDD (lower voltage), f (slower clock), or leakage (higher Vt, off transistors, lower temperature). A good designer knows which knob each technique turns and what it costs.

Voltage scaling, the biggest knob: Because dynamic power and energy go with VDD squared, lowering voltage is the most effective single technique. Energy per operation is proportional to C VDD squared, so going from 1.0 V to 0.8 V cuts energy per operation to 0.64 of the original, a 36 percent saving, for the same work. The price is speed: from lesson 10, lower voltage means less transistor current and longer delays. So voltage scaling works best when the circuit has spare time, or when we can do the work in a different way that needs less speed per circuit.

Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: DVFS changes VDD and f at run time depending on the workload. When you are just reading messages, the phone processor runs at a low frequency and low voltage; when you open the camera or a game, it ramps up. Example: lowering from 1.0 V and 2 GHz to 0.8 V and 1.5 GHz multiplies dynamic power by 0.64 x 0.75 = 0.48, less than half. The operating system picks among a table of supported voltage and frequency pairs, called operating performance points. Changing voltage takes a voltage regulator some microseconds, so the system cannot switch arbitrarily fast.

Race to idle versus slow and steady: Sometimes it is better to finish quickly at high speed and then shut everything down, because leakage stops when the block is power gated; this is race to idle. At other times, running slowly at low voltage is more efficient, because energy per operation falls with the square of voltage. Which wins depends on how large leakage is compared with dynamic energy, and on how deeply the system can sleep. Modern phones measure and choose dynamically.

Parallelism to save power: An old but beautiful trick: replace one fast unit with two copies running at half the frequency, alternating jobs, so the throughput is the same. Each copy now has twice the time per operation, so it can run at a lower voltage. Example: suppose the delay model says the circuit at 0.6 V is about 1.8 times slower than at 1.0 V, which fits within the doubled time. Two copies with 10 percent extra capacitance for the multiplexing logic give power = 2 x 1.1 C x 0.6 squared x f/2 = about 0.40 of the original. Same throughput, about 60 percent less power, at the cost of more area. This is one reason processors moved to multiple cores rather than ever higher clock speeds.

Clock gating: The clock network switches every cycle, alpha = 1, and drives every flip-flop. If a block has no new work in a cycle, there is no reason to clock its registers. Clock gating inserts a gating cell, usually a latch plus an AND gate called an integrated clock gate, so that the clock to a group of flip-flops stops when an enable signal says the block is idle. The latch prevents glitches on the gated clock. Example: if a block consumes 30 percent of a chip's dynamic power and is idle 70 percent of the time, gating it saves up to 0.3 x 0.7 = 21 percent of dynamic power, minus the small overhead of the gating cells. Synthesis tools insert clock gating automatically when the RTL has enable conditions on registers.

Operand isolation and reducing alpha: Even if registers are not clocked, combinational logic can toggle when its inputs change for unrelated reasons. Operand isolation holds the inputs of an unused block, like a multiplier, constant, so its internal nodes do not switch. Other alpha reducers: choosing encodings with fewer transitions, such as Gray code for counters and addresses on buses, and avoiding glitches by balancing paths, as seen in lesson 12.

Power gating: Clock gating stops dynamic power, but the block still leaks. Power gating cuts the supply itself. A large high-Vt transistor, called a sleep transistor or header switch, sits between the real VDD and the virtual VDD of the block. When the block is not needed for a long time, the sleep transistor turns off and leakage drops dramatically. Costs: the sleep transistor adds a little resistance and IR drop when on, waking up takes time and energy to recharge the block, and all state inside is lost. Isolation cells clamp outputs of a powered-down block to safe values so they do not confuse active neighbours.

State retention: To avoid losing important register contents during power gating, designers use retention flip-flops. Each has a small, always-powered, low-leakage storage element. Before power-down, the state is saved into it; after wake-up, it is restored. This lets a block sleep deeply and wake quickly without a full restart. Power-management controllers sequence all this: save, isolate, switch off; then switch on, wait for stable power, restore, release isolation.

Memories in sleep: Large on-chip SRAMs leak a lot simply because they hold millions of transistors. Fully switching them off loses their contents, so many designs instead lower the memory supply to a retention voltage, just high enough for each cell to keep its bit but too low to read or write. Leakage drops sharply while the data survives, and the memory returns to normal voltage before use. Choosing which memories to keep, retain or flush is a key power-management decision.

Multi-threshold libraries: Foundries offer transistors with several threshold voltages, such as low-Vt, standard-Vt and high-Vt. With a subthreshold slope of about 100 mV per decade, raising Vt by 100 mV cuts leakage by about 10 times, but the gate becomes slower. The trick is that only a small fraction of paths are timing-critical. Tools build the design mostly from high-Vt cells and swap in low-Vt cells only on critical paths. Many designs end up with most cells high-Vt, cutting leakage substantially at almost no speed cost.

Body biasing: The threshold voltage depends on the body voltage. Reverse body bias raises Vt, reducing leakage in standby; forward body bias lowers Vt, speeding up a slow chip. Some processes, especially fully depleted silicon on insulator, offer strong body-bias control, and chips can tune each block after manufacture to compensate for process variation.

Multiple voltage domains: Not every part of a chip needs the same voltage. A design might run the CPU cores at a variable DVFS voltage, the always-on control logic at a low fixed voltage, and the I/O at a higher voltage for external standards. Each region is a voltage island or power domain. Signals crossing between domains need level shifters, which convert a low-voltage logic 1 into a full high-voltage 1. Without them, a low-voltage 1 entering a high-voltage gate might leave its pMOS partly on, causing static current, the same problem as the weak 1 from lesson 2.

Near-threshold and subthreshold operation: Push VDD very low, close to or even below Vt, and energy per operation can drop a lot, sometimes several times, because of the squared term. Delay grows enormously and sensitivity to process and temperature variation becomes severe, so this is used for very low-rate applications like sensor nodes and some wearable devices, where speed hardly matters and battery life is everything.

Architecture and software matter too: The biggest savings often come from higher levels: using a specialised accelerator for video decoding instead of a CPU, keeping data close to where it is used to avoid expensive memory accesses, and letting the operating system put idle blocks to sleep. Heterogeneous designs, such as ARM's big.LITTLE idea of pairing high-performance cores with small efficient cores, let a phone run light tasks on efficient cores and wake the big ones only when needed.

Real-life example 1, your phone overnight: While you sleep, your phone screen is off, but it still receives messages. Most of the SoC is power gated. A small always-on domain at low voltage keeps the clock and listens for the modem. When a WhatsApp message arrives, the power controller wakes a small efficient core, restores its state from retention registers, processes the message, and returns to sleep within milliseconds. This is why a phone can lose only a few percent of battery overnight.

Real-life example 2, a solar-powered sensor in a rice field: Agricultural sensors measuring soil moisture or water level in Bangladesh may run from a small solar panel and battery. They wake once every few minutes, take a reading, send a short radio packet, and sleep again. Their chips use high-Vt transistors, deep power gating, very low VDD for the always-on timer and aggressive duty cycling. The average power can be in the microwatt range, so the battery lasts through cloudy monsoon days.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think lowering frequency alone saves energy per operation; it reduces power, but energy per operation depends on C VDD squared, so voltage must drop too. Many confuse clock gating, which stops switching, with power gating, which stops leakage. Some forget level shifters and isolation cells, or think high-Vt cells are always better. Exam questions: compute savings from DVFS; explain clock gating with a circuit and why a latch is used; explain power gating, sleep transistors, isolation and retention; explain multi-Vt optimisation; explain the parallelism trick with numbers; compare race to idle with slow operation.

Recap: Low-power design attacks alpha, C, VDD, f and leakage. Voltage scaling gives the biggest win; DVFS from 1.0 V and 2 GHz to 0.8 V and 1.5 GHz gives 0.48 times the power. Parallel units at lower voltage can keep throughput at about 40 percent of the power in our example. Clock gating stops idle switching; operand isolation and good encodings cut activity; power gating with sleep transistors stops leakage, helped by isolation and retention cells. Multi-Vt libraries, body bias, voltage islands with level shifters and near-threshold operation complete the toolkit. Next, we look at the wires that connect everything, which have become a speed and power problem of their own.
key_points: Every technique targets alpha, C, VDD, f or leakage; VDD is the strongest knob (energy goes with VDD^2).
DVFS: 1.0 V, 2 GHz to 0.8 V, 1.5 GHz gives 0.64 x 0.75 = 0.48 of the power.
Parallelism: two copies at f/2 and lower V (0.6 V, 10 percent overhead) give about 0.40 of the power.
Clock gating (integrated clock gate with latch) stops switching in idle blocks; 30 percent block idle 70 percent saves up to 21 percent.
Power gating with sleep transistors stops leakage; needs isolation cells, retention flip-flops and wake-up time.
Multi-Vt: about 10x less leakage per 100 mV higher Vt; use low-Vt only on critical paths.
Voltage islands need level shifters; body bias, near-threshold and architecture choices complete the toolkit.
lessons.tip: For each low-power technique, write which term of P = alpha C V^2 f + leakage it attacks and what it costs (area, speed, wake-up time). That two-column table answers most exam questions.
lessons.task: A block uses 0.5 W of dynamic power at 1.0 V and 1 GHz. Compute its power at 0.9 V and 800 MHz, and at 0.7 V and 500 MHz. Then suppose it is idle 60 percent of the time: how much more would clock gating save at the first operating point?

quiz.q: Which change cuts energy per operation the most for the same work?
quiz.explain: Energy per operation is proportional to C VDD^2, independent of frequency.

quiz.q: What does clock gating mainly reduce?
options: Dynamic switching power in idle registers and clock wires
quiz.explain: It stops the clock from toggling idle flip-flops; leakage still flows unless power gating is used.

quiz.q: Lowering from 1.0 V, 2 GHz to 0.8 V, 1.5 GHz changes dynamic power to:
Why are level shifters needed between voltage domains?
options: A low-voltage 1 may not fully turn off the pMOS of a higher-voltage gate
quiz.explain: Without shifting, the receiving gate sees a weak 1 and may draw static current.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of using high-Vt cells?
quiz.explain: Higher threshold reduces leakage but also reduces drive current, so gates are slower.

lessons.title: Interconnect: When the Wires Become the Problem
lessons.content:
Dhaka's traffic shows something important. Cars have become faster and more powerful over the years, but the trip from Mirpur to Motijheel has not become shorter, because the roads are crowded and long. Chips went through the same story. Transistors kept getting faster with every generation, but the wires connecting them did not keep up. In modern chips, the delay, power and noise of wires often matter as much as the transistors. This lesson explains why wires became a bottleneck and what designers do about it: repeaters, careful routing, shielding, power grids and new materials.
