Why interconnect matters: In lesson 9 you learned that a wire's resistance and capacitance both grow with length, so its delay grows with length squared. A large share of a chip's dynamic power is spent charging wire capacitance, including the clock network. Neighbouring wires disturb each other, causing noise and timing changes. The power supply itself is delivered through wires, which drop voltage. Ignoring interconnect gives a chip that simulates beautifully at the gate level and fails in silicon.

The metal stack: As seen in lesson 7, a modern process has many metal layers. The lowest layers have the smallest pitch, the width plus spacing of wires, for dense local connections inside and between cells. Middle layers carry signals across blocks. The top layers are thick and wide, with low resistance, used for global signals, clocks and the power grid. Routing tools usually alternate preferred directions, horizontal on one layer and vertical on the next, so wires can cross by switching layers through vias.

How wires scale: When a process shrinks, a wire's width and thickness shrink, so its cross-section area falls and its resistance per unit length rises, roughly by the square of the scale factor. Its capacitance per unit length stays about the same, because both the wire and its distance to neighbours shrink together. For local wires, which connect nearby gates, the length shrinks too, so their total delay stays roughly constant or improves slightly. But global wires, which cross the whole chip, do not get shorter, because the chip does not get smaller; often it grows. Their RC delay per unit length rises every generation while gates get faster. The gap between gate delay and global wire delay keeps widening.

Resistivity problems at small sizes: Copper's bulk resistivity is low, but very narrow copper wires need a thin barrier liner around them to stop copper atoms diffusing into the insulator, and this liner does not conduct well. Electrons also scatter off the wire surfaces and grain boundaries. As wires shrink to tens of nanometres, effective resistivity rises well above the bulk value. Foundries are exploring other metals for the tightest layers for this reason.

Low-k dielectrics: Wire capacitance depends on the insulator between wires. Silicon dioxide has a relative permittivity, k, of about 3.9. Modern processes use low-k materials with lower values, sometimes with tiny pores or air gaps, to reduce capacitance. They are mechanically weaker, which makes manufacturing and packaging harder, a classic engineering trade-off.

Worked example, a long wire without repeaters: A global wire 10 mm long has r = 0.1 ohms per micrometre and c = 0.2 fF per micrometre. Total R = 10,000 x 0.1 = 1,000 ohms; total C = 10,000 x 0.2 = 2,000 fF = 2 pF. RC = 1,000 x 2 pF = 2 ns. Using the 0.38 RC rule for a distributed wire, the delay is about 0.76 ns, 760 ps. At a 2 GHz clock, that is more than one full clock cycle, just to cross the wire.

Repeaters: The fix is to cut the wire into segments and put a buffer, called a repeater, at each cut. Each segment is shorter, so its delay falls with the square of its length, and the total wire delay now grows only linearly with length. Example: split the 10 mm wire into 5 segments of 2 mm each. Each segment has R = 200 ohms and C = 0.4 pF, so 0.38 RC = 0.38 x 80 ps = 30.4 ps. Five segments give 152 ps. Adding, say, 20 ps for each of 5 repeaters gives about 252 ps, three times faster than 760 ps. There is an optimum: too few repeaters and the wire's quadratic delay dominates; too many and the repeaters' own delays add up. Repeater insertion is done automatically by physical design tools, and a modern chip can contain a very large number of repeaters.

The cost of repeaters: Repeaters burn power, take area, and must be placed in specific spots, which can be awkward over large blocks like memories. They also need vias down from the upper metal layers to the transistors and back up again. Designers therefore plan floorplans so that blocks that communicate a lot sit close together, avoiding long wires in the first place. Architecture also adapts: in large chips, a signal may need more than one clock cycle to cross the chip, so designers add pipeline registers on long wires.

Crosstalk and coupling capacitance: In modern processes, wires are tall and close together, so a large part of a wire's capacitance is to its neighbours, not to ground. Call the coupling capacitance to each neighbour Cc and the capacitance to ground Cg. If a neighbour switches in the same direction as our wire, the voltage across Cc stays constant, so it behaves like zero capacitance. If the neighbour switches in the opposite direction, the voltage across Cc changes by twice VDD, so it behaves like 2 Cc. This is the Miller effect. Example with Cg = 0.1 and Cc = 0.05 fF per micrometre on each side: quiet neighbours give a total of 0.1 + 2 x 0.05 = 0.2; both neighbours switching the same way give 0.1; both switching the opposite way give 0.1 + 2 x 2 x 0.05 = 0.3 fF per micrometre. The delay of the same wire can vary by a factor of 3 depending on its neighbours. Timing tools must consider these worst cases.

Crosstalk noise: Coupling also causes noise. If our wire is supposed to stay at 0 and a neighbour rises, charge couples onto our wire and creates a bump. For a floating node, like a dynamic gate output, the bump is a capacitive divider: delta V = VDD x Cc / (Cc + Cg). With Cc = 20 fF, Cg = 80 fF and VDD = 1.0 V, the bump is 0.2 V. A driven wire recovers faster, so the bump is smaller, but if it exceeds the noise margin of the receiving gate, or arrives at a flip-flop near the clock edge, the chip can malfunction.

Fixing crosstalk: Designers have several tools. Increase spacing between sensitive wires. Shield critical wires, such as clocks, by running grounded wires on both sides. Route sensitive wires on different layers or perpendicular to aggressors. Make victim drivers stronger. Avoid long parallel runs. Signal integrity tools find likely problem nets and apply fixes.

The clock as the most important wire: The clock net reaches every flip-flop, switches every cycle and must arrive everywhere at nearly the same moment. It is usually routed on wide upper-layer wires, shielded on both sides, and driven by a carefully balanced tree of buffers, which lesson 17 describes. Because it is so long and so active, the clock network is a prime example of interconnect dominating both timing and power.

The power grid and IR drop: Every gate gets its power through a grid of wires from the package pins. Current through the grid's resistance causes a voltage drop, called IR drop. Example: if 1 A flows through an effective grid resistance of 0.05 ohms, the drop is 50 mV, which is 5 percent of a 1.0 V supply. Gates far from the pins see a lower effective VDD and switch more slowly, possibly causing timing failures. The grid is therefore a mesh of wide wires on the top metal layers, with many vias down to every cell row, and the package provides many power and ground pins or bumps. Decoupling capacitors placed across the chip supply sudden bursts of current locally, smoothing fast changes; package and wire inductance makes sudden current changes cause additional L di/dt noise.

Electromigration: When high current density flows through a thin metal wire for a long time, the moving electrons gradually push metal atoms along, creating voids that eventually break the wire, or hillocks that short neighbours. This is electromigration, and it can make a chip fail after months or years. Design rules limit the current density for each layer and wire width; power wires and high-activity signal wires are made wider, and multiple vias are used. Electromigration checks are part of sign-off.

Real-life example 1, Dhaka's flyovers and bus stops: A long road without stops is like an unbuffered wire: traffic piles up and the trip time grows faster than the distance. Adding regular stations where buses refresh their passengers, like repeaters, keeps the trip time growing only in proportion to distance. But too many stops slow the bus again. City planners and chip designers both choose a sensible spacing. Floorplanning is like putting the market close to the homes that use it most, so long trips are not needed at all.

Real-life example 2, why your phone processor has many power bumps: If you could look under a phone SoC, you would see a large array of tiny solder bumps, and a big fraction of them carry power and ground, not signals. When the processor suddenly goes from idle to full speed, its current can jump quickly. Without many power paths, a wide grid and on-chip decoupling capacitance, the voltage would sag, gates would slow, and the chip could crash. Power delivery is a whole engineering discipline inside VLSI design.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think wires shrink with transistors and so stay fast; global wires do not get shorter. Many forget that wire delay is quadratic without repeaters and linear with them. Some ignore the Miller effect and treat coupling capacitance as constant. Others confuse IR drop with crosstalk. Exam questions: compute wire R, C and delay; compute the improvement from repeaters; explain wire scaling for local and global wires; compute effective capacitance with the Miller effect; compute crosstalk noise on a floating node; compute IR drop; explain electromigration and its fixes.

Recap: Wires matter as much as transistors in modern chips. Local wires scale reasonably, but global wire delay per unit length grows as wires get thinner, while chips do not shrink. A 10 mm wire with 1,000 ohms and 2 pF has about 760 ps of delay; cutting it into 5 repeated segments brings it near 250 ps. Coupling capacitance makes delay depend on neighbours, from 1x to 3x in our example, and causes noise bumps like 0.2 V on a floating node. The power grid suffers IR drop, 50 mV for 1 A through 0.05 ohms, and inductive noise, and high current density causes electromigration. Next, we step back and see how transistor scaling itself has changed: Dennard scaling, its end, and the new transistors that followed.
key_points: Local wires scale reasonably; global wires stay long while resistance per length rises, so wire delay outpaces gate delay.
Narrow copper suffers from barrier liners and surface scattering; low-k dielectrics reduce capacitance.
10 mm wire, 1 kohm, 2 pF: about 0.38 RC = 760 ps; 5 repeated segments give about 252 ps.
Repeaters make wire delay linear in length instead of quadratic; floorplanning avoids long wires.
Miller effect: same-direction neighbour acts as 0, opposite-direction as 2Cc; delay can vary about 3x.
Crosstalk on a floating node: delta V = VDD Cc / (Cc + Cg), e.g. 0.2 V.
IR drop (1 A x 0.05 ohm = 50 mV), L di/dt noise and electromigration shape power-grid design.
lessons.tip: Remember one sentence: an unbuffered wire is quadratic, a buffered wire is linear. Whenever a question mentions a long wire, ask yourself whether repeaters are allowed.
lessons.task: A 6 mm wire has r = 0.08 ohm/um and c = 0.2 fF/um. Compute its unbuffered delay using 0.38 RC. Then compute the wire delay for 2, 3 and 6 equal segments, add 15 ps per repeater, and find which segment count is fastest.

quiz.q: Why do global wires get relatively slower as processes shrink?
options: Their resistance per unit length rises while their length does not shrink
quiz.explain: Thinner cross-sections raise R per length, but a global wire still spans the chip.

quiz.q: A wire has R = 1,000 ohms and C = 2 pF. Using 0.38 RC, its delay is about:
If a neighbouring wire switches in the opposite direction, the coupling capacitance behaves like:
quiz.explain: The voltage across Cc changes by 2 VDD, so it acts like twice the capacitance (Miller effect).

quiz.q: A floating node has Cc = 25 fF to an aggressor and Cg = 75 fF to ground, VDD = 1.0 V. The noise bump is:
What is electromigration?
options: Metal atoms pushed by high current density over time, creating voids or hillocks
Voltage drop in the power grid
quiz.explain: Long-term high current density moves metal atoms, eventually opening or shorting wires.

lessons.title: Scaling and Its Limits: Dennard, the Power Wall and New Transistors
lessons.content:
Imagine a magic photocopier that can shrink a city map by 30 percent. Every road, house and pipe becomes smaller, and somehow the shrunken city works even better: cars arrive faster, the electricity bill per house goes down, and the whole city still uses the same amount of power per square kilometre. For about thirty years, shrinking transistors felt exactly like this magic photocopier. Then, in the mid-2000s, the magic partly stopped working. This lesson explains the rules of the magic, called Dennard scaling, why it ended, and how the industry kept going with new materials, new transistor shapes and new ways of building chips.

Why this history matters: Many things about today's chips only make sense in this light. Why do processors have many cores instead of one super-fast core? Why have clock frequencies stayed in the range of a few gigahertz for nearly two decades? Why does your phone have special engines for AI and images? Why are transistors now three-dimensional fins? All of these are answers to the end of Dennard scaling. Understanding it also helps you judge news about new process nodes and chip claims.

What scaling means: Each new process generation shrinks the dimensions of transistors and wires by a factor, traditionally about 0.7 each time. Write it as 1/S with S about 1.4. A linear shrink of 0.7 means area shrinks to 0.7 times 0.7, about 0.5, so twice as many transistors fit in the same area. That is the engine behind Moore's law: roughly every two years, a new node doubled the density.

Dennard's rules: In 1974, Robert Dennard and colleagues at IBM showed what happens if you scale everything consistently, a recipe called constant-field scaling. Shrink all dimensions, including gate length, width and oxide thickness, by 1/S. Shrink the supply voltage VDD and threshold Vt by 1/S as well, so electric fields stay the same. Increase doping by S. Then: current per transistor scales by 1/S; capacitance scales by 1/S; gate delay, about CV/I, scales by 1/S, so frequency can rise by S; power per transistor, C V squared f, scales by (1/S)(1/S squared)(S) = 1/S squared; and transistor density rises by S squared. Multiply power per transistor by density and power per unit area stays constant.

Worked numbers: With S = 1.4 per generation: area per transistor about 0.51, density about 1.96 times, delay about 0.71, frequency about 1.4 times, power per transistor about 0.51, and power density 1.0. In words: twice as many transistors, each 40 percent faster, the whole chip using the same power for the same area. That is why for decades each new generation brought faster, cheaper, cooler chips almost for free.

What broke, part 1, voltage: Dennard scaling needs VDD and Vt to fall every generation. But Vt cannot fall freely, because of the subthreshold slope from lesson 3: at room temperature, current falls by at most about 10 times per 60 mV below threshold. Every 60 to 100 mV cut in Vt raises off-state leakage by about 10 times. With hundreds of millions of transistors, leakage power exploded. So Vt stopped falling, and to keep enough overdrive for speed, VDD also stalled, staying roughly around 1 V and below for many years instead of dropping steadily.

What broke, part 2, power density: Now redo the arithmetic with VDD fixed. Density still doubles. If we also hold frequency constant, power per transistor, C V squared f, only falls by the capacitance factor, 1/S, about 0.71. Power density then rises by S squared times 1/S = S, about 1.4 times per generation. If we tried to raise frequency as before, power density would rise even faster. This is the power wall. Around 2004 to 2005, mainstream processor clock rates stopped climbing and settled in the range of a few gigahertz, and designers turned to multiple cores and other forms of parallelism, which give more performance per watt than a faster single core.

What broke, part 3, the oxide: Gate oxide thickness also had to shrink to keep the gate in control of the channel. By the mid-2000s, silicon dioxide gate layers were only a few atomic layers thick, around a nanometre or so, and electrons tunnelled through them, causing gate leakage. The industry's answer was high-k metal gate technology, introduced in high-volume production around 2007: replace silicon dioxide with a high-permittivity material such as a hafnium-based oxide, which gives the same capacitance with a physically thicker layer, and replace polysilicon gates with metal gates to work well with it.

Short-channel effects and variability: As channels shortened, the drain's field increasingly influenced the channel (DIBL, lesson 3), so the gate lost control, especially in the off state. Also, a tiny transistor's channel may contain only a small number of dopant atoms, so the random number and position of these atoms change Vt from one transistor to the next. Line-edge roughness from lithography adds more variation. Variability means designers must add margins, which costs speed and power, and memory cells, which use the smallest transistors, are especially sensitive.

Strained silicon: One of the first new tricks, introduced in the early 2000s around the 90 nm generation, stretched or compressed the silicon crystal in the channel to raise carrier mobility, giving more current without shrinking. Engineers used different stress for nMOS and pMOS, since electrons and holes benefit from different strain.

FinFET: The big structural change was to stop making flat transistors. In a FinFET, the channel is a thin vertical fin of silicon, and the gate wraps around its top and two sides. Because the gate surrounds the channel, it controls it much better, reducing leakage and short-channel effects, so Vt and VDD can be managed better. FinFETs entered high-volume production at around the 22 nm generation in 2011 to 2012. One consequence for designers: transistor width now comes in steps, by the number of fins, so sizing is quantised.

Gate-all-around: As fins became too narrow and tall, the next step was to surround the channel completely. Gate-all-around transistors use horizontal nanosheets or nanowires stacked on top of each other, with the gate filling the space around each one. This gives even better electrostatic control and lets designers choose sheet widths more flexibly. They began production at the most advanced nodes from around 2022 onwards. Further ideas, such as stacking nMOS and pMOS vertically, are being researched.

Wires did not scale nicely either: Dennard's paper was about transistors. As lesson 14 showed, wires get worse as they shrink, because resistance per unit length rises while global distances stay the same. So even when transistors kept getting faster, the time to send a signal across a chip did not improve at the same rate. Architects responded by keeping communication local: clusters of cores with their own caches, networks-on-chip with short hops, and pipelined long wires.

Reading node claims sensibly: Because node names stopped describing real sizes, engineers compare processes with concrete numbers: transistor density in millions of transistors per square millimetre for a standard mix of cells, contacted gate pitch, minimum metal pitch, SRAM bit-cell area, and measured speed and power for a reference circuit. Two foundries' 5 nm or 3 nm processes can differ noticeably on these metrics. When you read that a new chip uses a smaller node, ask what happened to density, power and cost rather than the label.

What the end of Dennard means for designers: Since every new generation no longer brings automatic speed and power gains, the designer's choices matter more. Clock gating, power gating, multi-Vt cells, DVFS and accelerators from lesson 13 became essential rather than optional. Energy per operation, not peak frequency, became the main figure of merit for most products, from phones to data centres.

The economics of Moore's law: For decades, each node also made each transistor cheaper. At the most advanced nodes, wafers have become much more expensive because of EUV lithography, multiple patterning and many more process steps. Transistors still get denser, but the cost per transistor no longer falls as quickly as it used to, and the fixed cost of designing a chip at a leading node, including masks, tools and verification, is very high. This is why only products with very large volumes or high value use the newest nodes, and many chips stay on older, cheaper ones.

More than Moore: When shrinking alone gives less, designers find gains elsewhere. Specialised accelerators do particular jobs far more efficiently than general cores. Chiplets split a large design into several smaller dies, each with good yield, connected inside one package; different chiplets can even use different nodes. 3D stacking places memory directly on top of logic or stacks dies with dense vertical connections. Advanced packaging is now a major area of innovation. Lesson 25 returns to these ideas.

Real-life example 1, phone processors and clock speeds: If clock speeds had kept growing at the 1990s pace, phones today would run at tens of gigahertz. Instead, phone processors run at a few gigahertz but have several CPU cores of different sizes, a GPU, an image signal processor and an AI engine. That design is a direct response to the power wall: more parallel, specialised, energy-efficient units rather than one ever-faster engine.

Real-life example 2, why old nodes still matter in Bangladesh: Many products used every day in Bangladesh, such as electricity meters, garment-factory machine controllers, motorbike electronics and simple IoT devices, use chips built at mature nodes like 180, 130, 65 or 40 nm. These nodes are cheap, reliable, good for analog and high-voltage parts, and fast enough. Chip design jobs are not only at the bleeding edge; a huge share of the industry works on mature nodes.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think Moore's law and Dennard scaling are the same thing; Moore is about transistor count, Dennard about how voltage, speed and power scale with size. Many think scaling ended completely; density keeps improving, but voltage and frequency scaling largely stopped. Some believe FinFET was mainly for speed, but its main purpose was better gate control and lower leakage. Exam questions: write the Dennard scaling table; compute density, delay and power density for given S; explain why Vt and VDD stopped scaling; compute power density growth with fixed VDD; explain high-k metal gate, strained silicon, FinFET and gate-all-around; discuss the end of frequency scaling and the move to multicore.

Recap: Dennard constant-field scaling shrank dimensions and voltages by 1/S, giving S squared density, S speed, 1/S squared power per transistor and constant power density; with S = 1.4 that is about 2x density and 1.4x speed per generation. The subthreshold slope limited Vt, so VDD stalled and power density began rising about 1.4x per generation even at fixed frequency: the power wall of the mid-2000s. Thin oxides led to high-k metal gates, short channels to FinFETs and then gate-all-around transistors, and rising costs to chiplets, 3D stacking and specialised accelerators. Next, we return to circuits and build the storage elements that make chips remember: latches and flip-flops.
key_points: Scaling shrinks dimensions by about 0.7 (1/S, S about 1.4), doubling density each node.
Dennard (1974): scale V and Vt by 1/S too; delay 1/S, power per transistor 1/S^2, power density constant.
Vt could not keep falling (subthreshold slope at least about 60 mV/decade), so VDD stalled near 1 V and below.
With fixed VDD and fixed frequency, power density rises about S (1.4x) per generation: the power wall.
Clock rates plateaued in the mid-2000s; designers moved to multicore and specialised accelerators.
Fixes: strained silicon (early 2000s), high-k metal gate (about 2007), FinFET (about 2011-12), gate-all-around (from about 2022).
Cost per transistor falls more slowly now; chiplets, 3D stacking and mature nodes are key strategies.
lessons.tip: Build the Dennard table yourself from three facts: everything scales by 1/S, delay = CV/I, power = CV^2 f. If you can derive it, you never have to memorise it, and you can redo it for fixed VDD in seconds.
lessons.task: Using S = 1.4, fill a table for two consecutive generations under (a) ideal Dennard scaling and (b) fixed VDD with fixed frequency: density, power per transistor and power density. Write one sentence explaining the difference.

quiz.q: Under ideal Dennard scaling, what happens to power density?
quiz.explain: Power per transistor falls by 1/S^2 while density rises by S^2, so power per area is constant.

quiz.q: Why did threshold voltage stop scaling down?
options: Lowering Vt raises subthreshold leakage exponentially
quiz.explain: The subthreshold slope limits how fast current turns off, so lower Vt means much more leakage.

quiz.q: With VDD fixed, frequency fixed and S = 1.4, power density per generation rises by about:
quiz.explain: Density rises by S^2 and power per transistor falls only by 1/S, giving S, about 1.4.

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of high-k metal gate technology?
options: To reduce gate leakage while keeping high gate capacitance
quiz.explain: A high-k dielectric gives the same capacitance with a thicker layer, cutting tunnelling leakage.

quiz.q: What is the key advantage of a FinFET over a planar transistor?
options: The gate wraps around the channel, giving better control and less leakage
It works only at high voltage
quiz.explain: Surrounding the fin on three sides lets the gate control the channel much better.

lessons.title: Latches, Flip-Flops and the Timing Rules of Sequential Circuits
lessons.content:
Think of the gates of a cricket stadium in Mirpur. During entry time, the gate is open and people flow through; when the gate closes, whoever is inside stays inside, and whoever is outside waits for the next opening. A chip's memory elements work like this. A latch is a gate that is open for a whole phase of the clock; a flip-flop is a gate that opens for just an instant, at the clock edge. Between them, the combinational logic does its work. In this lesson we build latches and flip-flops from transistors and learn the timing rules, setup, hold and clock-to-q, that decide how fast a chip can run and whether it works at all.

Why sequential circuits matter: Every processor, controller and pipeline needs to remember values from one clock cycle to the next: registers, state machines, counters, pipeline stages. In Digital Logic Design you used flip-flops as black boxes with D, clock and Q. In VLSI you must know what is inside, because their delays and constraints become part of every timing path, and their power is a large share of a chip's total, together with the clock that drives them.

Static versus dynamic storage: There are two ways to store a bit. Dynamic storage keeps it as charge on a capacitor, like the gate of an inverter, with nothing actively holding it; it is small but leaks away, so it must be refreshed or used quickly. Static storage uses positive feedback: two inverters connected in a loop, each driving the other, hold a value forever while power is on. A 0 at one inverter's input forces a 1 at its output, which forces a 0 at the other's output, which reinforces the first input. This cross-coupled pair is bistable, with two stable states.

The dynamic latch: The simplest latch is a transmission gate followed by an inverter. When the clock is high, the TG is on, so the input D passes through and the inverter output follows D (inverted); the latch is transparent. When the clock goes low, the TG turns off, and the value is held as charge on the inverter's input capacitance. It uses only 4 transistors, but the stored charge leaks and is sensitive to noise, so it only works if the clock never stops for long.

The static latch: To make the latch robust, add feedback. A common design: the input TG feeds a node X, an inverter drives the output from X, and a feedback path made of another inverter and a second TG (or a clocked inverter) drives X back from the output. When the clock is high, the input TG is on and the feedback TG is off, so X follows D. When the clock is low, the input TG is off and the feedback TG is on, closing the loop and holding the value indefinitely. Many library latches use clocked inverters, also called tristate inverters, in place of the TGs. A positive latch is transparent when the clock is high; a negative latch is transparent when the clock is low.

The master-slave flip-flop: A flip-flop samples its input only at a clock edge. The classic static CMOS design is two latches in series with opposite clock phases. The first, the master, is a negative latch, transparent when the clock is low; the second, the slave, is a positive latch, transparent when the clock is high. While the clock is low, the master follows D and the slave holds the old Q. When the clock rises, the master closes and holds whatever D was at that instant, while the slave opens and passes that value to Q. So Q changes only just after the rising edge, to the value D had right before it. This is a positive-edge-triggered D flip-flop, typically around 20 or more transistors in a standard library, depending on features like reset.

Timing parameters of a flip-flop: Setup time, tsetup, is how long before the clock edge the input D must be stable. If D changes too close to the edge, the master may not have time to settle, and the flip-flop can capture the wrong value or go metastable (lesson 17). Hold time, thold, is how long after the edge D must stay stable, because the master takes a moment to fully close. Clock-to-Q delay has two values: tpcq, the maximum time from the clock edge until Q is stable, and tccq, the minimum time until Q can start changing. These four numbers come from the library datasheet and are used in every timing check.

The max-delay constraint: Consider a path from one flip-flop, through combinational logic, to the next flip-flop, both clocked by the same clock with period Tc. On a rising edge, the first flip-flop's Q changes after up to tpcq. The signal then passes through the logic, taking up to tpd. It must arrive at the second flip-flop at least tsetup before the next edge. So Tc must be at least tpcq + tpd + tsetup. This is the setup or max-delay constraint, and it sets the maximum clock frequency.

Worked example, max delay: tpcq = 50 ps, tsetup = 30 ps, and the slowest logic path is tpd = 400 ps. Tc must be at least 50 + 400 + 30 = 480 ps, so the maximum frequency is 1 / 480 ps, about 2.08 GHz. Notice that 80 ps of every cycle, about 17 percent, is spent in the flip-flops themselves; this is the sequencing overhead. Deep pipelines with very little logic per stage lose a big fraction of each cycle to this overhead, which is why pipelining has diminishing returns.

Clock skew: The clock does not arrive at every flip-flop at exactly the same time; wires and buffers differ. The difference in arrival times between two flip-flops is the clock skew. If the receiving flip-flop gets its clock earlier than the launching one, it effectively shortens the cycle. With 20 ps of such skew, the constraint becomes Tc at least 50 + 400 + 30 + 20 = 500 ps, so the maximum frequency drops to 2.0 GHz. Jitter, random variation of the clock edge from cycle to cycle, takes away timing in the same way.

The min-delay or hold constraint: There is a second, sneakier danger. On a clock edge, the first flip-flop's output starts changing after tccq, and the fastest path through the logic takes tcd. If this new value reaches the second flip-flop before its hold time has passed for the same edge, it corrupts the value being captured. So we need tccq + tcd at least thold + tskew, where tskew here is how much later the receiving flip-flop's clock can arrive. Notice that the clock period does not appear: a hold violation cannot be fixed by slowing the clock. That is why hold failures are especially dangerous.

Worked example, hold: tccq = 40 ps, thold = 20 ps, and skew up to 30 ps. We need tcd at least 20 + 30 - 40 = 10 ps. If two flip-flops are connected directly with no logic between them, as in a shift register, tcd is about 0 and the constraint fails. The fix is to insert buffers or delay cells on short paths to add contamination delay, a routine step called hold fixing in physical design. If the skew grew to 50 ps, you would need at least 30 ps of minimum logic delay.

Latch-based design and time borrowing: Some high-performance designs use two-phase latches instead of flip-flops. Since a latch is transparent for half a cycle, a slow logic stage can borrow time from the next stage: the signal can pass through the latch late, as long as it arrives before the latch closes. This makes the design tolerant of unbalanced stages and clock skew, at the cost of more complex timing analysis. Pulsed latches, latches opened by a short pulse at each clock edge, act like fast flip-flops with lower overhead.

Flip-flop power: Every flip-flop presents its clock input capacitance, several transistor gates inside both latches, to the clock network, and that capacitance toggles every cycle even when D does not change. Multiply by hundreds of thousands of flip-flops and it becomes a major power cost. Library designers therefore minimise clock-pin capacitance, and synthesis tools merge flip-flops into multi-bit cells that share clock buffering.

Reset and enable: Real flip-flops often include a reset input, synchronous (acting at the next clock edge) or asynchronous (acting immediately), and an enable, which is often implemented by a multiplexer feeding D back into itself or, better for power, by clock gating from lesson 13. Scan flip-flops, with a multiplexer on the input for testing, are covered in lesson 24.

Real-life example 1, the train at Kamalapur station: A train leaves at exactly 8:00. Passengers must be on the platform a few minutes before departure, the setup time, and must not jump out in the first moments after the doors close, the hold time. If the station clock is a little off for some platforms, the skew, the timetable must allow extra margin. And the train's travel time to the next station, the logic delay, plus boarding time, decides how often trains can run, the clock period.

Real-life example 2, a processor pipeline: In a 5-stage pipeline from Computer Architecture, each stage boundary is a row of flip-flops. If one stage, such as memory access, has 400 ps of logic and the flip-flops add 80 ps, the whole pipeline cannot run faster than about 2.08 GHz, no matter how fast the other stages are. Engineers rebalance stages or split the slow one, but each extra stage adds another 80 ps of overhead, so splitting has limits.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think increasing the clock period fixes every timing problem; it fixes setup violations but not hold violations. Many mix up tpcq and tccq. Others forget the direction of skew: it hurts setup in one direction and hold in the other. Some draw a master-slave flip-flop with both latches on the same phase, which makes it transparent. Exam questions: draw a dynamic latch, a static latch and a master-slave flip-flop and explain their operation; define setup, hold, tpcq and tccq; compute the maximum frequency with and without skew; check a hold constraint and compute the needed delay; explain time borrowing.

Recap: Storage is dynamic (charge) or static (cross-coupled feedback). A latch is transparent for one clock phase; a master-slave flip-flop of two opposite-phase latches captures D at the edge. Setup requires Tc at least tpcq + tpd + tsetup (480 ps, about 2.08 GHz in our example, 500 ps and 2 GHz with 20 ps of skew). Hold requires tccq + tcd at least thold + tskew (here tcd at least 10 ps), and it cannot be fixed by slowing the clock. Latches allow time borrowing; pulsed latches cut overhead. Next, we learn how tools check these constraints across millions of paths, how the clock is distributed, and what happens when an input arrives at exactly the wrong moment.
key_points: Dynamic storage holds charge (small, leaks); static storage uses cross-coupled inverters (bistable).
A latch is transparent for one clock phase; a master-slave flip-flop (negative + positive latch) captures D at the rising edge.
Parameters: tsetup, thold, tpcq (max clock-to-Q), tccq (min clock-to-Q).
Setup: Tc >= tpcq + tpd + tsetup; 50 + 400 + 30 = 480 ps, about 2.08 GHz.
Skew adds to the setup budget: with 20 ps, Tc >= 500 ps, 2.0 GHz.
Hold: tccq + tcd >= thold + tskew; independent of clock period, fixed by adding delay on short paths.
Latch-based design allows time borrowing; sequencing overhead limits deep pipelines.
lessons.tip: Draw one timing diagram with two flip-flops and mark tpcq, tpd, tsetup on the setup side and tccq, tcd, thold on the hold side of the same edge. Every timing question is a variation of that one picture.
lessons.task: Given tpcq = 60 ps, tccq = 35 ps, tsetup = 40 ps, thold = 25 ps and a clock skew of 15 ps, find the maximum clock frequency for a path with tpd = 650 ps, and the minimum contamination delay needed to avoid hold violations.

quiz.q: In a positive-edge master-slave flip-flop, the master latch is transparent when:
quiz.explain: The master is a negative latch, open while the clock is low, and closes at the rising edge.

quiz.q: tpcq = 50 ps, tpd = 400 ps, tsetup = 30 ps, no skew. Minimum clock period?
Which timing violation cannot be fixed by lowering the clock frequency?
quiz.explain: The hold constraint does not contain the clock period, so slowing the clock does not help.

quiz.q: tccq = 40 ps, thold = 20 ps, tskew = 30 ps. Minimum tcd needed?
quiz.explain: tcd >= thold + tskew - tccq = 20 + 30 - 40 = 10 ps.

quiz.q: What makes a static latch hold its value indefinitely?
quiz.explain: Two inverters driving each other form a bistable loop that keeps the value while powered.

lessons.title: Timing Analysis, Clock Distribution and Metastability
lessons.content:
Imagine you are organising a huge wedding in Dhaka with guests arriving from many places: Gazipur, Narayanganj, Savar, Uttara. The ceremony starts at 8 pm sharp. You do not need to watch every guest's whole journey; you only need, for each guest, the latest time they could leave and still arrive before 8, and you want to find the guest with the least spare time. That is static timing analysis. And if two families use different clocks, one running a little fast, someone will arrive exactly at the wrong moment and be confused about whether the ceremony has started. That is metastability. This lesson covers how chips check timing on millions of paths, how the clock is delivered everywhere, and how to safely pass signals between unrelated clocks.

Why this matters: Lesson 16 gave you the setup and hold rules for one path. A real chip has millions of flip-flops and billions of paths between them. You cannot simulate every possible input pattern to find the slowest one. Instead, tools perform static timing analysis, which checks every path without simulation. And since every flip-flop depends on the clock, delivering it with low skew and low power is one of the hardest physical design tasks. Finally, nearly every real system has several clock domains, and getting data across them safely is a classic source of rare, hard-to-find bugs.

Static timing analysis: STA models the design as a graph. Nodes are pins of cells; edges are cell delays and wire delays, taken from the library and extraction. Timing starts at launch points, flip-flop clock pins and primary inputs, and ends at capture points, flip-flop D pins and primary outputs. STA computes for every node the latest arrival time, by taking the maximum over all incoming paths, and the earliest arrival time, by taking the minimum. It does not need input vectors, which is why it is called static. It checks every path at once in time roughly proportional to the size of the graph.

Worked example, arrival times: Two signals start at time 0. Gate A takes 100 ps on the path from the first input; gate B takes 150 ps on the path from the second. Gate C takes both as inputs and has a delay of 80 ps. The latest arrival at C's output is max(100, 150) + 80 = 230 ps, through gate B. The earliest arrival is min(100, 150) + 80 = 180 ps, which matters for hold checks.

Required time and slack: For setup, the required time at a capture flip-flop is the next clock edge, minus the setup time, minus clock uncertainty, which covers skew and jitter. Slack is required time minus arrival time. Positive slack means the path meets timing with that much to spare; negative slack means a violation. Example: clock period 500 ps, setup 30 ps, uncertainty 20 ps, so required time = 500 - 30 - 20 = 450 ps. A path arriving at 430 ps, launched at the clock edge and including tpcq, has slack +20 ps: it passes. Another arriving at 470 ps has slack -20 ps: it fails, and the designer must speed it up or slow the clock. The path with the worst slack is the critical path.

Hold checks and fixing: STA also checks hold using earliest arrival times against the same clock edge. Setup violations are fixed by upsizing gates, restructuring logic, using faster low-Vt cells, moving flip-flops (retiming) or relaxing the clock. Hold violations are fixed by adding delay to fast paths. A good tool flow fixes both without breaking the other.

Exceptions and corners: Not every path in the graph is real. A false path is one that can never be activated, for example because two multiplexers are always selected in a way that blocks it; designers tell the tool to ignore it. A multicycle path is allowed to take two or more cycles by design. Timing must also hold across corners: slow and fast transistors, low and high voltage, cold and hot temperature, and different modes like test mode or low-power mode. Tools run multi-corner multi-mode analysis and add on-chip variation margins because two nearby gates on the same die can differ slightly.

Clock distribution, the goal: Deliver the clock to every flip-flop with small skew, controlled slew, low jitter and as little power as possible. This is hard because the clock may drive hundreds of thousands of flip-flops spread over the whole die, switches every cycle with alpha = 1, and its wires are long.

H-trees: A classic structure is the H-tree. Start at the centre of the chip, run a wire to two points left and right, then from each, wires up and down, then left and right again, forming nested letters H. Because every path from the root to a leaf has the same length and the same number of buffers, skew is ideally zero. In practice, uneven loads and process variation create some skew, but the symmetry helps a lot.

Grids and clock-tree synthesis: High-performance processors often drive a clock grid, a mesh of wires across the chip fed at many points by a tree; shorting all branches together averages out differences and gives very low skew, at the cost of extra power. Most ASICs use clock-tree synthesis, CTS, in which a tool builds a buffered tree tuned to the actual positions of the flip-flops, balancing delays so skew stays within a target such as a few tens of picoseconds. Useful skew is a further trick: deliberately delaying the clock to a flip-flop that captures a slow path, which gives that path more time.

Generating the clock, PLLs: The clock usually comes from a quartz crystal oscillator outside the chip, running at tens of megahertz. A phase-locked loop on the chip multiplies it to the needed frequency. For example, a 25 MHz reference multiplied by 80 gives 2 GHz. A PLL compares the phase of a divided-down copy of its output with the reference and adjusts a voltage-controlled oscillator until they match. PLLs also allow frequency changes for DVFS and cleaning up jitter. Their analog design is a specialty of its own.

Metastability: A flip-flop must decide between 0 and 1. If its input changes inside the setup-hold window, the cross-coupled latch can be left balanced near the middle voltage, like a ball resting on top of a hill. It will eventually fall to one side, but the time it takes is unbounded in principle; the longer you wait, the less likely it is still undecided. The probability of still being metastable after time t falls exponentially as e to the power minus t / tau, where tau is a small time constant of the latch, often tens of picoseconds.

Mean time between failures: For a flip-flop sampling an asynchronous input, a standard estimate is MTBF = e to the power (t / tau) / (T0 x fclk x fdata), where t is the time allowed to resolve, T0 is a constant related to the window width, fclk is the clock frequency and fdata the rate of input changes. Example: tau = 20 ps, T0 = 50 ps, fclk = 1 GHz, fdata = 10 MHz, and t = 900 ps of a 1 ns cycle. MTBF = e to the 45 / (50e-12 x 1e9 x 1e7), about 7 x 10 to the 13 seconds, roughly 2.2 million years. That sounds safe, but a product sold in millions of units with many such synchronisers might still see failures.

Synchronisers: The standard fix is a two-flip-flop synchroniser: the asynchronous signal goes into one flip-flop, whose output goes into a second flip-flop on the same clock. The first flip-flop may go metastable, but it gets almost a full extra cycle to resolve before the second samples it. In our example, t grows to about 1,900 ps, and MTBF becomes e to the 95 / (5 x 10 to the 5), on the order of 10 to the 28 years, far longer than the age of the universe. Very high-speed or safety-critical designs sometimes use three stages.

Clock domain crossing: A single-bit control signal can cross domains through a synchroniser. But a multi-bit bus cannot simply be synchronised bit by bit, because different bits may resolve in different cycles and form a value that never existed. Safe methods include handshakes, where a request and acknowledge are synchronised and the data is held stable meanwhile, and asynchronous FIFOs, where read and write pointers are passed across in Gray code, so only one bit changes at a time. Tools perform CDC checks to find unsafe crossings.

Retiming: Since flip-flops can sometimes be moved across logic without changing the function seen at the outputs, a retiming tool can shift registers to balance stage delays. For example, moving a register from after a slow adder to the middle of it can cut the longest stage. This is a powerful optimisation used in synthesis.

Real-life example 1, the wedding organiser's checklist: For each guest, compute the latest departure time, like required time, and their estimated travel time, like path delay. The difference is their slack. The guest with the smallest slack, perhaps coming from Gazipur through traffic, is your critical path. Calling every guest is static timing analysis; following one guest's car is simulation. The first is complete; the second is not.

Real-life example 2, a USB or Bluetooth chip: Your phone's USB controller receives data timed by the cable's clock while the processor runs on its own clock. Between them, an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers and two-flip-flop synchronisers carries data safely. Without careful CDC design, the system might work in the lab for weeks and then fail randomly in the field, the most frustrating kind of bug.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes think STA simulates input patterns; it does not. Many forget clock uncertainty in required time, or mix up the setup and hold directions of skew. Some think metastability can be eliminated; it can only be made extremely unlikely. Others synchronise a multi-bit bus bit by bit. Exam questions: compute arrival times on a small graph; compute slack and identify the critical path; explain false and multicycle paths; compare H-tree, grid and CTS; explain a PLL; compute MTBF and show the effect of a two-flop synchroniser; explain safe CDC for buses.

Recap: STA computes latest and earliest arrival times over a timing graph without vectors; slack = required minus arrival, with 450 ps required and 430 ps arrival giving +20 ps. Exceptions, corners and variation margins make the checks realistic. Clocks are distributed by H-trees, grids or synthesised trees with low skew, generated by PLLs from crystal references. Metastability cannot be avoided but decays exponentially; with tau = 20 ps a single flip-flop gives about 2.2 million years MTBF and a two-flop synchroniser about 10 to the 28 years. Multi-bit crossings need handshakes or Gray-coded FIFOs. Next, we use all this to build fast arithmetic: adders, shifters and multipliers.
key_points: STA computes latest/earliest arrival times over a graph of cell and wire delays, without input vectors.
Slack = required time - arrival time; required = period - setup - uncertainty (500 - 30 - 20 = 450 ps).
False paths, multicycle paths, multi-corner multi-mode analysis and on-chip variation make STA realistic.
Clock distribution: H-tree (symmetric), grid (low skew, more power), clock-tree synthesis; PLL multiplies a crystal reference.
Metastability: unresolved state decays as e^(-t/tau); MTBF = e^(t/tau) / (T0 fclk fdata).
Example: tau 20 ps, 900 ps to resolve gives about 2.2 million years; a two-flop synchroniser gives about 1e28 years.
Multi-bit CDC needs handshakes or async FIFOs with Gray-coded pointers, not per-bit synchronisers.
lessons.tip: For every timing problem, write three lines: arrival, required, slack. Negative slack means fix; positive means pass. For metastability problems, write the MTBF formula first and plug in the exponent separately to avoid calculator overflow.
lessons.task: Draw a small timing graph: input X at 0 ps feeds gate G1 (120 ps) and gate G2 (60 ps); G2 feeds G3 (90 ps); G1 and G3 feed G4 (70 ps), which goes to a flip-flop with setup 25 ps on a 300 ps clock with 15 ps uncertainty. Compute the latest arrival at G4, the required time and the slack.

quiz.q: Why is static timing analysis called static?
options: It checks paths without simulating input vectors
It runs only once per year
quiz.explain: STA propagates worst-case and best-case delays through the graph instead of simulating specific inputs.

quiz.q: Clock period 400 ps, setup 25 ps, uncertainty 15 ps, arrival 370 ps. What is the slack?
quiz.explain: Required = 400 - 25 - 15 = 360 ps; slack = 360 - 370 = -10 ps, a violation.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of an H-tree clock network?
options: Equal path lengths from root to every leaf, giving low skew
quiz.explain: The symmetric structure makes every branch the same length, ideally giving zero skew.

quiz.q: Why does a two-flip-flop synchroniser greatly improve MTBF?
options: It gives the first flip-flop almost a full extra cycle to resolve, and MTBF grows exponentially with that time
It converts data to Gray code
quiz.explain: MTBF depends on e^(t/tau), so roughly one more cycle of resolution time multiplies it enormously.

quiz.q: How should a multi-bit counter value be passed safely between asynchronous clock domains?
options: Synchronise each bit with its own two-flop synchroniser
Use Gray code (as in an async FIFO pointer) or a handshake
quiz.explain: Per-bit synchronisation can capture a mix of old and new bits; Gray code changes one bit at a time.

lessons.title: Datapath Subsystems: Fast Adders, Shifters and Multipliers
lessons.content:
Think about how a bazaar shopkeeper adds a long bill. A slow shopkeeper adds digit by digit from the right, carrying one at a time, and waits for each carry before moving left. A clever one looks at groups of digits and quickly sees whether a carry will come out of each group, so the groups can be finished almost in parallel. Chip designers faced exactly this problem: addition is the most common operation in any processor, and the naive way is slow. This lesson shows how real chips build adders, comparators, shifters and multipliers that are fast enough for gigahertz clocks, and the area, delay and power trade-offs between them.

Why datapath design matters: The ALU, address calculations, loop counters, DSP filters, graphics and AI accelerators are all built from adders and multipliers. These blocks often sit on the critical path that sets the clock frequency. In Computer Architecture you studied ripple-carry and carry-lookahead adders and Booth's algorithm logically. Here we look at them as circuits: how many gate delays, how many transistors, and why industry chooses particular structures.

The full adder recap: A 1-bit full adder takes inputs A, B and carry-in C and produces Sum = A XOR B XOR C and Cout = AB + AC + BC. Two helper signals make adders easier to reason about. Generate, G = A AND B: this bit position creates a carry no matter what comes in. Propagate, P = A XOR B (or A OR B in some formulations): this bit passes an incoming carry through. Then Cout = G + P C. Every fast adder is a clever way to compute all the carries using G and P.

Ripple-carry adder: Chain N full adders, each carry-out feeding the next carry-in. It is small and simple, but in the worst case a carry must ripple through all N positions, for example adding 1 to 0111...1. The delay grows linearly with N. Example: if each carry step takes 20 ps, a 32-bit ripple adder takes about 32 x 20 = 640 ps in the worst case, too slow for a 2 GHz processor whose whole cycle is 500 ps. Ripple adders are fine for small widths or slow, low-power designs.

Carry-lookahead: Instead of waiting, compute carries directly from G and P. For a 4-bit group: C1 = G0 + P0 C0; C2 = G1 + P1 G0 + P1 P0 C0; and so on. Each carry is a two-level AND-OR expression, so all four come out at roughly the same time. The group also produces a group generate and group propagate, which can be combined at the next level in the same way. A hierarchy of lookahead blocks gives delay growing roughly with the logarithm of N rather than linearly. The cost is more gates and more wiring, and the high fan-in AND terms grow quickly, so groups are kept to about 4 bits.

Carry-select adder: Another idea: for the upper half of the adder, compute the sum twice, once assuming the carry into it is 0 and once assuming it is 1, at the same time as the lower half computes its real carry. When the real carry arrives, a multiplexer picks the right answer. For a 32-bit adder split into two 16-bit halves, delay is about 16 x 20 = 320 ps for the lower half plus one multiplexer, say 20 ps, giving about 340 ps instead of 640 ps. Splitting into more blocks of increasing size improves it further. The cost is nearly double the hardware for the upper part.

Carry-skip adder: A carry-skip adder adds a bypass around each block: if every bit in the block propagates, the group propagate is 1, and the incoming carry can skip straight to the block's output through a multiplexer instead of rippling. It is cheap and gives a useful speedup for medium widths, though its worst-case analysis is subtle.

Parallel prefix adders: The most important high-performance family. Computing all carries is a prefix problem: each carry depends on the combination of all (G, P) pairs to its right. Define a combining operation on pairs: (G, P) combined with (G', P') gives (G + P G', P P'). This operation is associative, so it can be done as a tree. In the Kogge-Stone adder, every bit computes its prefix in log2 N levels, with fan-out kept at 2 at each level: for 32 bits, 5 levels. It is very fast but uses many cells, N log2 N - N + 1 = 129 prefix cells for N = 32, and lots of long wires. The Brent-Kung adder uses only 2N - 2 - log2 N = 57 cells for 32 bits but needs about twice as many levels, 2 log2 N - 1 = 9. Sklansky and Han-Carlson adders sit between, trading fan-out, wiring and depth. Modern high-performance processors typically use parallel prefix adders of these families or hybrids.

Comparators: To compare two numbers A and B, compute A - B, which is A + NOT B + 1 using an adder. The result is zero exactly when A equals B; the carry-out or the sign, depending on signed or unsigned interpretation, says which is larger. Equality alone is cheaper: XNOR each pair of bits and AND all the results together in a tree. Comparators appear in branch units, sorting hardware and address-matching logic like cache tags.

Shifters: Shifting a 32-bit word by any amount from 0 to 31 in one cycle needs a barrel shifter. A logarithmic barrel shifter uses log2 N stages: the first stage shifts by 0 or 1 based on bit 0 of the shift amount, the next by 0 or 2, then 4, 8 and 16. Each stage is a row of 2-to-1 multiplexers. For 32 bits that is 5 stages of 32 multiplexers, 160 multiplexers in all, and the delay is 5 multiplexer delays regardless of the shift amount. Rotations, arithmetic right shifts (filling with the sign bit) and logical shifts are small variations.

Array multiplier: Multiplying two N-bit numbers produces N partial products, each the multiplicand ANDed with one bit of the multiplier and shifted. For 8 x 8, that is 64 AND gates producing 64 partial product bits. An array multiplier adds these rows with a regular grid of adders: about N(N - 2) full adders and N half adders, 48 and 8 for N = 8. It is regular and easy to lay out, but the critical path runs diagonally and down through the array, so the delay grows roughly in proportion to 2N adder delays.

Booth recoding: Radix-4 modified Booth recoding examines the multiplier in overlapping groups of three bits and recodes it into digits from -2 to +2. Each digit selects 0, plus or minus the multiplicand, or plus or minus twice the multiplicand, all easy to form by shifting and inverting. This roughly halves the number of partial products: an 8-bit multiplier gives about 4 rows instead of 8 (one more is needed for unsigned operands). Fewer rows mean fewer adders and a faster sum.

Wallace and Dadda trees: Instead of adding rows one after another, use carry-save adders: a row of full adders takes three rows and produces two, a sum row and a carry row, with no carry propagation within the row. Repeatedly reduce 3 rows to 2 until only 2 remain, then use one fast carry-propagate adder. For 8 rows: 8 to 6 to 4 to 3 to 2, four levels of full adders. For 16 rows: 16, 11, 8, 6, 4, 3, 2, six levels. The number of levels grows with the logarithm of N, so tree multipliers are much faster than arrays for large N, though their wiring is irregular. Dadda trees arrange the same idea to use slightly fewer adders.

Worked example, lookahead in action: Take A = 0101 and B = 0011, carry-in 0. Bit by bit from bit 0: G = 1, 0, 0, 0 and P = 0, 1, 1, 0. Then C1 = G0 = 1; C2 = G1 + P1 C1 = 0 + 1 = 1; C3 = G2 + P2 C2 = 0 + 1 = 1; C4 = G3 + P3 C3 = 0 + 0 = 0. The sum bits are P XOR C: 0, 0, 0, 1, giving 1000, which is 8, and indeed 5 + 3 = 8. The lookahead logic computes all four carries at once instead of waiting for each one.

Trade-offs: Ripple adders are smallest and lowest power but slow. Carry-select and carry-skip give moderate speed at moderate cost. Prefix adders are fastest but use the most area and wire. Multipliers can be arrays for small, low-power cases, or Booth plus Wallace trees plus a fast final adder for high performance. Synthesis tools often choose the architecture automatically from a library of adder and multiplier implementations, based on the timing constraint: tight timing gets a prefix adder; loose timing gets a ripple adder to save area and power.

Real-life example 1, the bKash transaction server: Behind every transfer in a mobile wallet, server processors compute balances, fees and checksums billions of times a day. Each addition passes through a 64-bit adder inside the ALU, built as a parallel prefix structure so it fits within a fraction of a nanosecond. If it were a ripple adder, the server's clock would have to be several times slower, and the system would need many more machines.

Real-life example 2, AI on your phone: The neural engine in a phone performs huge numbers of multiply-accumulate operations, often on small 8-bit numbers, to recognise faces in photos or translate speech. Designers pack thousands of small multipliers next to adders, using Booth recoding and compressor trees, and choose low-power structures since the work is massively parallel and does not need each unit to be extremely fast. The same building blocks are tuned differently for a different goal.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think carry-lookahead removes all delay; it reduces growth from linear to roughly logarithmic, but the lookahead logic itself has delay. Many confuse carry-save with carry-select. Some forget the extra partial product for unsigned Booth. Others think a barrel shifter's delay depends on the shift amount. Exam questions: derive G, P and carry equations; compute ripple and carry-select delays; draw a 4-bit carry-lookahead unit; explain the prefix operator and compare Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung; design a barrel shifter and count multiplexers; explain Booth radix-4 and count partial products; count Wallace tree levels.

Recap: Fast arithmetic is all about carries. Ripple carry is linear: 32 x 20 ps = 640 ps. Carry-lookahead and carry-select cut this; a 2-block carry-select gives about 340 ps. Parallel prefix adders compute all carries in log2 N levels: Kogge-Stone needs 5 levels and 129 cells for 32 bits, Brent-Kung 9 levels and 57 cells. A 32-bit barrel shifter uses 5 stages of 32 multiplexers. Multipliers form N squared partial product bits, reduce them with Booth recoding (about half as many rows) and carry-save trees (8 rows in 4 levels), then finish with a fast adder. Next, we look at the largest blocks on most chips: memory arrays.
key_points: Generate G = AB, propagate P = A XOR B, Cout = G + P Cin underlie all fast adders.
Ripple-carry delay is linear: 32 bits x 20 ps = 640 ps.
Carry-lookahead and carry-select cut delay; 2-block 32-bit carry-select is about 340 ps.
Prefix adders: Kogge-Stone log2 N levels (5 for 32 bits, 129 cells); Brent-Kung 2log2 N - 1 levels (9, 57 cells).
Barrel shifter: log2 N stages of N 2:1 muxes; 32 bits = 5 stages, 160 muxes, fixed delay.
Array multiplier: N^2 partial product bits, about N(N-2) full adders; Booth radix-4 halves the rows.
Wallace/Dadda trees reduce 3 rows to 2 per level: 8 rows in 4 levels, 16 rows in 6 levels.
lessons.tip: Remember every fast adder as an answer to one question: how do we know the carry into bit i without waiting? Lookahead computes it, select guesses both, skip bypasses, prefix builds a tree. That one question organises the whole topic.
lessons.task: For A = 1011 and B = 0110 with carry-in 0, compute G and P for each bit, then compute C1 to C4 using the lookahead equations, and check the sum against ordinary binary addition. Then count Wallace tree levels for a 12 x 12 multiplier.

quiz.q: In a ripple-carry adder where each carry step takes 25 ps, the worst-case delay of a 16-bit adder is about:
quiz.explain: 16 x 25 ps = 400 ps; the carry may ripple through all 16 bits.

quiz.q: How many prefix levels does a Kogge-Stone adder need for 64 bits?
quiz.explain: log2 64 = 6 levels.

quiz.q: How many 2:1 multiplexers does a 16-bit logarithmic barrel shifter need?
quiz.explain: log2 16 = 4 stages of 16 multiplexers = 64.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of radix-4 Booth recoding?
options: It roughly halves the number of partial products
quiz.explain: Recoding into digits -2 to +2 processes two multiplier bits per partial product.

quiz.q: A Wallace tree starts with 8 partial product rows. How many carry-save levels until 2 rows remain?
quiz.explain: 8 -> 6 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 takes four levels.

lessons.title: Memory Arrays: SRAM, DRAM, ROM and Flash
lessons.content:
Picture a huge post office at Gulistan with a wall of tiny letter boxes arranged in rows and columns. To find a letter, the clerk does not search every box; he takes the address, picks the right row, then the right column, and opens one box. Chip memories work exactly like this. A memory array is a grid of tiny storage cells, with a row decoder choosing a row and column circuits choosing and reading the right cells. On a modern processor, caches made of SRAM can take up half the chip area. In this lesson we see how SRAM, DRAM, ROM and flash cells are built from transistors, how the array around them works, and how designers keep huge memories working even when a few cells are faulty.

Why memory design matters: Every processor needs registers, caches and main memory; every phone needs storage for photos and apps; every microcontroller needs flash for its program. Memory cells are repeated millions or billions of times, so saving even one transistor or a fraction of a square micron per cell matters enormously. Memories also push manufacturing to its limits, since the cells are the densest structures on the chip. Understanding memory arrays explains why cache is expensive, why DRAM needs refresh, and why your phone's storage wears out slowly.

The array organisation: A memory with 2 to the power n words is organised as a square-ish grid. Suppose we have 1 megabit, which is 1,048,576 bits, organised as 1024 rows and 1024 columns. The address is split: 10 bits go to the row decoder, which turns on exactly one of 1024 wordlines, and 10 bits go to the column decoder, which selects which bitline or group of bitlines to read. A square shape keeps both the wordlines and the bitlines from becoming too long, since long wires are slow and power hungry. Real arrays are split into many smaller sub-arrays or banks for the same reason.

The 6T SRAM cell: The standard static RAM cell uses 6 transistors. Four form two cross-coupled inverters, the bistable storage from lesson 16, holding a value at node Q and its complement at node Q-bar. Two nMOS access transistors connect Q and Q-bar to a pair of bitlines, BL and BL-bar, when the wordline is high. As long as power is on, the cell holds its value without refresh. It is fast, a few hundred picoseconds to a nanosecond in caches, and uses the same CMOS process as the logic, so it can sit right next to the processor.

How an SRAM read works: First, both bitlines are precharged high. Then the wordline of the chosen row rises. In each cell of that row, the side storing 0 pulls its bitline down slightly through the access transistor and the pull-down nMOS. The bitlines are long and heavily loaded, so the voltage drops only slowly, perhaps 100 millivolts in a short time. A sense amplifier, a sensitive cross-coupled circuit at the bottom of the column, detects this small difference between BL and BL-bar and quickly amplifies it to a full 0 or 1. Waiting only for a small swing makes reads fast and saves power.

Read stability and writability: The cell must survive a read: when the access transistor connects the 0 node to a precharged bitline, the node rises a little; if it rises too far, the inverter could flip and destroy the data. So the pull-down nMOS must be stronger than the access transistor, a ratio of maybe 1.5 to 2. For a write, the bitlines are driven hard to the new value, one low and one high, and the access transistor must be strong enough to overpower the pull-up pMOS on the 1 side. So the access nMOS must be stronger than the pull-up pMOS. Sizing an SRAM cell is a careful balance of these three transistor strengths, made harder by process variation in tiny transistors.

Worked example, how many transistors: A 1 megabyte SRAM cache has 1,048,576 bytes times 8 = 8,388,608 bits. At 6 transistors per bit, that is 50,331,648 transistors, about 50 million, just for the cells, before decoders, sense amplifiers and redundancy. A processor with 32 MB of on-chip cache has well over 1.6 billion transistors in SRAM cells alone. This is why caches dominate chip area and why architects think hard before making a cache bigger.

The DRAM cell: Dynamic RAM uses only one transistor and one capacitor per bit, the 1T1C cell. The capacitor stores charge for a 1 or no charge for a 0; the access transistor connects it to the bitline when the wordline is high. Because each cell is so small, DRAM gives far more bits per square millimetre than SRAM, which is why main memory is DRAM. The capacitors are built in special ways, as deep trenches in the silicon or tall stacked cylinders above the transistors, to get enough capacitance in a tiny footprint.

DRAM read and refresh: Reading a DRAM cell connects its small capacitor to a long bitline with much larger capacitance, so the charge is shared and the bitline voltage changes only a tiny bit, perhaps tens of millivolts. A sense amplifier detects and amplifies this. But the read is destructive: the cell's charge has been spread out, so the sense amplifier must write the value back. Also, charge leaks away through the transistor and junctions within milliseconds, so every row must be refreshed regularly, typically every 64 milliseconds. With 8192 rows to refresh in a 64 millisecond window, the controller issues a refresh command about every 7.8 microseconds. DRAM uses a special process optimised for low leakage, so it is usually made on separate chips, not on the processor die.

ROM and flash: Read-only memory stores fixed data, for example by placing or omitting a transistor at each crossing of wordline and bitline when the chip is made; it is very dense but cannot change. Flash memory, used in phones, SSDs and USB drives, uses a floating-gate or charge-trap transistor: an extra layer between the gate and the channel stores trapped electrons, which shift the threshold voltage. A cell with trapped charge has a high Vt and reads as one value; without charge, a low Vt and the other value. Charge is pushed in and pulled out with high voltages through a thin oxide by tunnelling, and it stays for years without power, so flash is non-volatile. Each program-erase cycle slightly damages the oxide, which is why flash wears out after thousands of cycles and why SSDs spread writes evenly, called wear levelling. Modern flash stores 3 or 4 bits per cell by using 8 or 16 different threshold levels, and stacks over 200 layers of cells vertically in 3D NAND.

Content-addressable memory: A CAM works backwards: instead of giving an address and getting data, you give data and the CAM tells you which addresses hold it, comparing all entries in parallel. Each cell has storage plus comparison transistors. CAMs are used in network routers to look up addresses and in processors for translation lookaside buffers and fully associative caches. They are fast but use much more area and power than SRAM.

Redundancy and error correction: With billions of cells, a few will almost always be faulty after manufacturing. Memories therefore include spare rows and columns. After testing, faulty rows are mapped to spares by blowing tiny fuses or programming non-volatile registers, a process called memory repair, which greatly improves yield. In operation, cosmic rays and alpha particles can flip a stored bit, a soft error. Error-correcting codes add extra check bits to each word; a common code adds 8 check bits to 64 data bits and can correct any single-bit error and detect any double-bit error. Servers, such as those in a bank's data centre, use ECC memory for exactly this reason.

Peripheral circuits and the memory compiler: Around the cell array sit the row decoders, wordline drivers, precharge circuits, column multiplexers, sense amplifiers, write drivers and timing control. These peripherals can take a significant fraction of the area. Designers rarely draw SRAM arrays by hand for each chip; a memory compiler supplied with the process generates an SRAM block of any requested size, with layout, timing models and test structures, ready to drop into the design.

Register files and multi-port cells: A processor's register file must let several instructions read and write at the same time, for example two reads and one write per cycle. Each extra port adds a wordline and one or two bitlines to every cell, plus access transistors, so a cell with two read ports and one write port may need 8 to 12 transistors and grows quickly in area, because wires, not transistors, dominate. This is one reason processors keep register files small, typically 32 to a few hundred entries, and use plain single-port SRAM for big caches.

Real-life example 1, your phone's memory hierarchy: Inside your phone, the processor has small, very fast SRAM caches holding the data it is using right now. Next to it, a few gigabytes of LPDDR DRAM hold running apps and refresh themselves thousands of times per second. Finally, flash storage holds your photos, messages and apps even when the battery dies. Each layer uses a different cell, chosen for its balance of speed, density, cost and volatility.

Real-life example 2, the bank server: A bank's core banking server in Motijheel stores account balances in DRAM while processing transactions. If a cosmic ray flipped one bit in a balance, a customer's account could be wrong by thousands of taka. ECC memory detects and corrects such single-bit errors automatically, and logs them so technicians can replace modules that show too many errors. This small extra circuitry protects real money.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think SRAM needs refresh; it does not, DRAM does. Many forget that DRAM reads are destructive and must be written back. Some confuse the sizing rules: for read stability the pull-down must beat the access transistor; for writability the access transistor must beat the pull-up. Others think flash is volatile. Exam questions: draw a 6T SRAM cell and explain read and write; state the sizing constraints; draw a 1T1C DRAM cell and explain refresh; compute the number of transistors in an SRAM; compute row and column address bits for an array; explain flash cells and wear; explain redundancy and ECC.

Recap: Memories are grids of cells with row decoders, column selection and sense amplifiers; a 1024 by 1024 array uses 10 row and 10 column address bits. The 6T SRAM cell is fast and static but large: 1 MB needs about 50 million transistors. Its sizing balances read stability and writability. The 1T1C DRAM cell is dense but needs refresh, about every 64 ms, and destructive reads are written back. ROM is fixed; flash stores charge on a floating gate, is non-volatile and wears out; CAM searches by content. Spare rows and columns repair defects; ECC corrects soft errors. Next, we learn how to describe whole digital systems in a hardware description language, Verilog.
key_points: Memory = grid of cells + row decoder + column select + sense amps; 1024 x 1024 needs 10 row and 10 column address bits.
6T SRAM: two cross-coupled inverters + two access nMOS; static, fast, no refresh.
SRAM sizing: pull-down > access (read stability); access > pull-up (writability).
1 MB SRAM = 8,388,608 bits x 6 = 50,331,648 transistors.
1T1C DRAM: dense, destructive read with write-back, refresh about every 64 ms.
Flash stores charge on a floating gate: non-volatile, multi-level cells, limited program-erase cycles.
Spare rows/columns repair faults (yield); ECC such as 64 + 8 bits corrects single-bit soft errors.
lessons.tip: For SRAM sizing, remember the strength ranking: pull-down strongest, access in the middle, pull-up weakest. Reads must not flip the cell; writes must flip it. That one ordering answers most cell questions.
lessons.task: A cache has 256 KB of data organised as a square-ish array of 2048 rows. Compute the total number of bits, the number of columns, the row address bits, and the number of transistors if 6T cells are used. Then estimate how many refresh commands per second a DRAM with 8192 rows and a 64 ms refresh period needs.

quiz.q: How many transistors does a standard SRAM cell use?
quiz.explain: The 6T cell: four transistors in two cross-coupled inverters and two access transistors.

quiz.q: Why must DRAM be refreshed?
options: Its stored charge leaks away within milliseconds
quiz.explain: The tiny capacitor loses charge through leakage, so each row is rewritten periodically.

quiz.q: A memory array has 4096 rows. How many row address bits are needed?
For read stability in a 6T SRAM cell, which must be stronger?
options: The pull-up pMOS stronger than the pull-down
The access transistor stronger than the pull-down
The pull-down nMOS stronger than the access transistor
quiz.explain: A strong pull-down keeps the 0 node low when the precharged bitline is connected.

quiz.q: What makes flash memory non-volatile?
options: It is refreshed by a battery
Charge trapped on a floating gate stays for years without power
quiz.explain: Trapped charge shifts the transistor threshold and remains when power is removed.

lessons.title: Verilog I: Describing Hardware with Code
lessons.content:
Imagine an architect designing a 20-storey building in Gulshan. She does not draw every brick; she writes a plan: this floor has four flats, each flat has three rooms, use this standard window everywhere. Builders and software then turn the plan into detailed drawings. Chip designers work the same way. Nobody draws a billion transistors by hand. Instead, they write a description of the hardware in a hardware description language, HDL, and tools turn it into gates and layout. Verilog is the most widely used HDL in industry. In this lesson you learn how Verilog describes modules, wires, registers, combinational and sequential logic, and how to test a design with a testbench.

Why an HDL: As chips grew from thousands to billions of transistors, drawing schematics became impossible. An HDL lets you describe behaviour at a higher level, simulate it to catch bugs early, and then synthesise it automatically into a gate-level netlist using a standard-cell library. The same description can target an ASIC or an FPGA. It also brings software engineering habits to hardware: version control, reuse, code review and automated tests.

The big mindset shift: Verilog looks like C, but it is not a program that runs step by step. It describes hardware where everything exists at the same time and works in parallel. If you write two assign statements, they are not executed one after another; they are two pieces of wiring that both exist all the time. Beginners who think of Verilog as sequential software write code that simulates fine but synthesises into something unexpected, or not at all.

Modules and ports: The basic building block is a module, like a chip or a component with pins. A module has a name and a list of ports, each declared input, output or inout, with a width. For example, a module named and2 might have inputs a and b and output y, and inside it the single line assign y = a and b, written with the ampersand operator. Larger designs are built by instantiating modules inside other modules and connecting their ports with wires, just like placing chips on a circuit board and wiring them up. This is structural description.

Data types: wire and reg: A wire represents a physical connection; it has no memory and simply carries whatever drives it, usually from an assign statement or a module output. A reg is a variable assigned inside an always block. Despite the name, a reg does not always become a hardware register; it becomes a flip-flop only if it is assigned on a clock edge. In SystemVerilog, the single type logic replaces most uses of both. Vectors give width: wire with range 7 down to 0 is an 8-bit bus, and individual bits can be selected, such as bit 3, or ranges such as bits 7 to 4.
